description: NCERT Grade 4 English, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: Unit 1: My Land
chapters.summary: In this chapter: together we can; think, discuss and speak; let us learn a: groups and animal teams; let us learn b: places and prepositions.

lessons.title: Together We Can

activities.prompt: What happens when everyone joins hands and works together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What the poem is about
activities.body: 'Together We Can' is a poem about working with others. Teamwork means working together as one team. The poem says standing together makes us strong and tall. Nobody falls when we help each other, and joining hands brings our goal nearer. Teamwork can beat any difficulty. We cheer, sing, and share wins and losses. A bond of trust is always there, and team spirit fills the air with joy.
keyPoints: Standing together makes people strong and tall.
Helping each other means nobody falls.
Teamwork brings joy, cheer and trust.
activities.explanation: This poem tells us that people are stronger and happier when they work together.

activities.prompt: Two classmates face a difficult task. What should they do together?
steps: Standing together makes them strong, so they can face the task.
Helping each other keeps them from falling, so they can continue.
Teamwork can overcome any difficulty, so the task is not too hard.
Joining hands brings the goal nearer, so they should try together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do the people in the poem do together?
options: They sit apart and say nothing
They cheer and sing
They walk away from each other
They keep quiet all day
activities.explanation: The poem says that people cheer and sing together.

activities.prompt: When people join hands, the goal comes ______.
activities.hint: It comes closer to us.
activities.explanation: The poem says that joining hands brings the goal nearer.

activities.prompt: According to the poem, what can teamwork do?
options: It can make games shorter
It can bring only bad news
It can overcome any difficulty
It can make people sit alone
activities.explanation: The poem says teamwork can overcome any difficulty.

activities.prompt: Match each action to what the poem says about it.
activities.explanation: Every action in the poem has a good result for the team.

activities.prompt: Put these poem lines in the order they come in the poem.
items: Standing together makes people strong and tall.
People do not fall when they help each other.
People share whether they win or lose.
activities.explanation: Read the poem and these lines will fall into place one after another.

activities.prompt: Your class team lost a match today. What does the poem tell you?
options: We should stop practising for games
We share whether we win or lose
Only the winners matter in a team
We should leave the team behind
activities.explanation: The poem says people share whether they win or lose, and trust is always there.

activities.prompt: Two classmates call a task too hard. What should they try?
options: Work with others and keep trying together.
Keep trying alone so nobody can stop them.
Give up because the task is too hard.
Wait until the task becomes much easier.

why.Keep trying alone so nobody can stop the: This mistakes one person's effort for teamwork that overcomes difficulty.
This assumes teamwork cannot help with a difficult task.
This assumes the difficulty will pass without teamwork.

activities.explanation: Teamwork can overcome any difficulty, so trying together is best.

activities.prompt: A child loses balance. A friend helps. How might the child feel?
options: They may feel safe because the friend is there.
They may feel ignored because the friend is there.
They may feel angry because the friend is there.
They may feel worried because the friend is there.

why.They may feel ignored because the friend: This mistakes help for leaving the person alone.
why.They may feel angry because the friend i: This mistakes losing balance for anger at the helper.
why.They may feel worried because the friend: This mistakes support for a reason to worry.

activities.explanation: Helping each other keeps them from falling, so the child can feel safe.

activities.prompt: A child finishes a difficult task with teammates. How might the child feel?
options: They may feel joyful because teamwork brought happiness.
They may feel lonely because teamwork brought happiness.
They may feel bored because teamwork brought happiness.
They may feel afraid because teamwork brought happiness.

why.They may feel lonely because teamwork br: This confuses teamwork's joy with loneliness.
why.They may feel bored because teamwork bro: This confuses teamwork's joy with boredom.
why.They may feel afraid because teamwork br: This confuses teamwork's joy with fear.

activities.explanation: The poem says that being in a team brings joy.

activities.prompt: A team loses a game. What does the poem suggest they do?
options: They stand together and share the losing result.
They blame a teammate for the losing result.
They hide the losing result from their teammates.
They celebrate alone because the result was a loss.

why.They blame a teammate for the losing res: This assumes sharing a loss means blaming a teammate.
why.They hide the losing result from their t: This mistakes keeping apart for sharing the result together.
why.They celebrate alone because the result: This assumes celebrating together matters only after a win.

activities.explanation: The poem says people share whether they win or lose.

lessons.title: Think, Discuss and Speak

activities.prompt: How can joining hands with our team make us feel stronger and more joyful?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Working Together
activities.body: Think about teamwork, helping and unity. You will consider what happens when you join hands with your team. You will think about how you feel after losing a game. You will also think about joyful feelings and a leader bringing teammates together. You will talk with a friend and share foods and festivals you like most. Different traditions, foods, festivals and languages can exist while people stand in unity.
keyPoints: Bokali says they stand together in unity.
The book asks about teamwork, helping, joyful feelings and losing.
Children exchange a conversation and share foods and festivals.
activities.explanation: The lesson connects teamwork, feelings, conversation and unity.

activities.prompt: How can a leader help teammates who disagree to stand in unity?
steps: Ask them to join hands, because joining hands brings the team together.
Ask each teammate to think of the others, because helping each other matters.
Help them choose one way forward, because unity means standing together.
The leader unites them by bringing everyone together in one team.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Question About Helping
activities.prompt: Which question does the book ask?
options: When the game ends
Why it is important
Who will win the game
Where the game is played
activities.explanation: The book asks why helping each other is important.

activities.title: Together as a Team
activities.prompt: Bokali says that they stand together in ______.
activities.hint: This word means being joined together.
activities.explanation: The missing word is unity, which means being joined together.

activities.title: Match the Topics
activities.prompt: Match each topic with the book question.
activities.explanation: These pairs match each topic with the question in the book.

activities.title: Talk with a Friend
activities.prompt: What are children asked to do with a friend?
options: Start a new game
Choose different foods
Exchange a conversation
Find a new leader
activities.explanation: Children are asked to turn to a friend and exchange a conversation.

activities.title: Our Different Country
activities.prompt: What do people do despite these differences?
options: People stand in unity
People share one language
People eat only one food
People join only one festival
activities.explanation: Different traditions and languages do not stop people from standing together in unity.

activities.title: Love for Our Country
activities.prompt: Darsana loves her country. Which idea also shows that people can stay together?
options: People keep traditions apart
Children avoid sharing food
People separate from friends
People stand in unity
activities.explanation: Darsana says she loves her country. The lesson also says its people stand in unity.

activities.prompt: Two teammates disagree about what to do. Their leader helps them join hands. Why should the leader do this?
options: It helps the teammates stand farther apart.
It helps the teammates stand together in unity.
It makes the teammates stop helping each other.
It turns every disagreement into a separate team.

why.It helps the teammates stand farther apa: This is right because joining hands helps unite teammates who disagree.
why.It makes the teammates stop helping each: This mistakes joining hands for stopping teamwork.
why.It turns every disagreement into a separ: This mistakes disagreement for needing separate teams.

activities.explanation: This mistakes joining hands for standing farther apart.

activities.prompt: A child thinks about what makes her joyful. She remembers how she felt after losing a game. What is she doing?
options: Choosing what her friends should eat.
Deciding which festival should be cancelled.
Counting how many games she has won.
Exploring her feelings about joy and loss.

This is right because she thinks about joy and her feelings after losing.
why.Deciding which festival should be cancel: This mistakes thinking about feelings for choosing food.
This mistakes thinking about feelings for cancelling a festival.

activities.explanation: This mistakes thinking about feelings for counting wins.

activities.prompt: A country has different traditions, foods, festivals and languages. Its people still stand in unity. Why can this happen?
options: They can choose unity while keeping their differences.
They must forget their traditions and languages.
They should stop sharing foods and festivals.
They can argue because differences make unity impossible.

why.They must forget their traditions and la: This mistakes unity for forgetting traditions.
why.They should stop sharing foods and festi: This mistakes unity for stopping shared interests.
why.They can argue because differences make: This mistakes differences for making unity impossible.

activities.explanation: This is right because different traditions can exist within unity.

lessons.title: Let us Learn A: Groups and Animal Teams

activities.prompt: What special names do groups of animals, flowers, and boys have?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Special Group Words
activities.body: Different things can have special names for their groups. A group of sheep is a herd, while a group of wolves is a pack. Flowers can form a bouquet, and trees can grow in a grove. Bees gather in a swarm. The word box also includes group names for choir members, boys, keys, and a bundle of sticks.
keyPoints: A group of sheep is a herd.
A group of wolves is a pack.
Different groups can have different names.
activities.explanation: These special words help us name groups clearly.

activities.prompt: A child sees sheep walking together and wants to name the group.
steps: The word box gives names for groups, because it collects group words.
The child should look there, because it explains the special names.
Sheep form a herd, so the child can use that word.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the Group Word
activities.prompt: Which word names a group of sheep?
options: herd
pack
bouquet
swarm
activities.explanation: A group of sheep is called a herd.

activities.title: Complete the Group Word
activities.prompt: A group of sheep is called a ______.
activities.hint: Think of the word for a group of sheep.
activities.explanation: The correct word is herd.

activities.title: Match Groups with Their Names
activities.prompt: Match each group with its special name.
activities.explanation: Each group has its own special word.

activities.title: Ants Work Together
activities.prompt: What do ants use to work together?
options: signals
sticks
keys
flowers
activities.explanation: Ants use signals to work together.

activities.title: Order the Group Words
activities.prompt: Put these group words in alphabetical order.
activities.explanation: Alphabetical order starts with bouquet, then grove, herd and swarm.

activities.title: Find the First Example
activities.prompt: What is the first completed example?
options: bundle of sticks
pack of wolves
bouquet of flowers
herd of sheep
activities.explanation: The first completed example is a bundle of sticks.

activities.prompt: A story says, "A herd of sheep follows one another." What does this show?
options: They move as a group
They travel all alone
They stay far apart
Each sheep stops following

why.They travel all alone: This wrongly treats each sheep as separate from the group.
why.They stay far apart: This wrongly treats the sheep as spread out.
why.Each sheep stops following: This wrongly treats following as something the sheep stop doing.

activities.explanation: A herd is the sheep group, and the sheep follow one another.

activities.prompt: A path passes beside a grove. What might the child see there?
options: A group of trees
A group of sheep
A group of bees
A group of boys

why.A group of sheep: This mistake confuses trees with sheep.
why.A group of bees: This mistake confuses trees with bees.
why.A group of boys: This mistake confuses trees with boys.

activities.explanation: A grove is a group of trees, so trees fit the place.

activities.prompt: Bees form a swarm, while ants use signals. Why might ants follow signals?
options: To find food together
To make flowers bloom
To form a choir
To tie sticks together

why.To make flowers bloom: Making flowers bloom is not one of the ant group's jobs.
why.To form a choir: Ants use signals for food, defence, and nest building.
why.To tie sticks together: Ant signals are not used for tying sticks together.

activities.explanation: Following signals helps ants find food, so this is a valid reason.

lessons.title: Let us Learn B: Places and Prepositions

activities.prompt: Can you discover where the special places belong on our map?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Places and prepositions
activities.body: Pay attention to the map. It shows a hospital, bank, post office, road, school, book store and children’s park. Fill each blank using the box. The words are behind, between, near and in front of. Behind means at the back of a place. Between means in the middle of other places. Near means close by. In front of means at the front of another place.
keyPoints: The map includes a hospital, bank, post office, road, school, book store and children’s park.
The box words are behind, between, near and in front of.
The blanks ask about the positions of places.
activities.explanation: These prepositions help you describe where places are on the map.

activities.prompt: How can I choose the right preposition for places on a map?
steps: Read the place names, because the map must guide each answer.
Picture the two places together, because each box word describes a position.
Choose from the box, because it gives four possible position words.
Check each blank, because the answer must match the map's shown position.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Places in comparisons
activities.prompt: Match each place with the place used in the same comparison.
activities.explanation: Each pair appears together in a question about a position.

activities.title: A close position
activities.prompt: Choose the word that means close to another place: ______.
activities.hint: Choose a word from the box.
activities.explanation: Near means close to another place.

activities.title: The book shop comparison
activities.prompt: Which place is compared with the children’s park?
options: bank
book store
post office
school
activities.explanation: A blank asks for the book store’s position in relation to the children’s park.

activities.title: Preposition meanings
activities.prompt: Match each preposition with its plain meaning.
pairs: at the back of another place
in the middle of other places
at the front of another place
activities.explanation: Each preposition describes a position on the map.

activities.title: Suggested lesson steps
activities.prompt: Put the suggested lesson steps in order.
items: Notice the places on the map
Discuss the prepositions in the children’s mother tongue
Help children understand the English versions
activities.explanation: The children notice the map places. The teacher may then use the mother tongue before English.

activities.prompt: The post office is __ the hospital. Only a short walk separates them. Which word fits?
options: The post office is behind the hospital.
The post office is between the hospital and bank.
The post office is near the hospital.
The post office is in front of the hospital.

Behind means the hospital comes first, but the places are close.
why.The post office is between the hospital: Between needs two places with the post office in the middle.
why.The post office is in front of the hospi: It means the post office comes first, but the clue says they are close.

activities.explanation: Near fits because the two places are only a short walk apart.

activities.prompt: The bank is __ the school. You meet the bank before the school on the path. Which word fits?
options: The bank is behind the school.
The bank is between the school and post office.
The bank is near the school.
The bank is in front of the school.

Behind means the school comes first, but the bank comes first.
why.The bank is between the school and post: Between needs another place on the other side of the bank.
Near means close, but the clue gives their order on the path.

activities.explanation: It fits because the bank comes before the school on the path.

activities.prompt: The bookstore is __ the children's park. Their places appear next to each other on the map. Which word fits?
options: The bookstore is behind the children's park.
The bookstore is between the children's park and school.
The bookstore is near the children's park.
The bookstore is in front of the children's park.

why.The bookstore is behind the children's p: Behind means the park comes first, but their places stand together.
why.The bookstore is between the children's: Between needs one place on each side of the bookstore.
why.The bookstore is in front of the childre: It means the bookstore comes first, but their places stand together.

activities.explanation: Near fits because the two places appear next to each other.

activities.prompt: The ambulance is __ the post office and hospital. It stands in the middle of them. Which word fits?
options: The ambulance is behind the post office.
The ambulance is between the post office and hospital.
The ambulance is near the post office.
The ambulance is in front of the hospital.

It means one place comes first, but it stands in the middle.
It means close to one place, not in the middle of both.
why.The ambulance is in front of the hospita: It means before both places, but it stands in the middle.

activities.explanation: Between fits because the ambulance stands in the middle of two places.

activities.prompt: The book is __ the wall. The wall hides the book from view. Which word fits?
options: The book is behind the wall.
The book is between two walls.
The book is near the wall.
The book is in front of the wall.

Between needs two walls, but the wall blocks only one side.
Near does not explain why the wall hides the book.
In front of means visible before the wall, but the book is hidden.

activities.explanation: Behind fits because the wall hides the book from view.

lessons.title: Let us Write

activities.prompt: What will happen next after each picture?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Questions about Pictures
activities.body: In this lesson, you will look at pictures and answer the questions below them. Each question asks what the people are doing and what they will do next. The questions name Lubang, Obang, Manya, Tina, Anna, Zakir, Gulpreet and Gilashree. Your teacher will draw attention to the word ‘will’. You will learn that this word is used for events that will happen in the future.
keyPoints: Each picture has a question below it.
Questions ask about actions and what happens next.
‘Will’ is used for future events.
activities.explanation: This will help you answer each picture question clearly.

activities.prompt: Why do we use “will” when the teacher asks what will happen next?
steps: The teacher's next action has not happened yet, because it comes after the students' actions.
The word “will” points to an event that will happen in the future.
A future action needs “will,” because we are talking about what comes next.
So “will ask” is right, because the teacher's question is still to happen.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What are you asked to do after looking at the pictures?
options: Look at pictures and answer questions below them
Read names and copy each question
Draw new pictures for every answer
Listen to the teacher read a story
activities.explanation: Great choice! You must answer the questions written below the pictures.

activities.prompt: Each picture question asks what people are doing and what they will do next.
activities.explanation: Correct! Every question looks at an action and the next event.

activities.prompt: The teacher should draw attention to the word ‘______’.
activities.hint: This word is used for future events.
activities.explanation: Well done! ‘Will’ helps us talk about what will happen.

activities.prompt: Put the picture questions in their lesson order.
activities.explanation: Perfect! You placed all the questions in their correct order.

activities.prompt: Which option describes Anna’s picture question?
options: Anna’s action and the old lady’s next action
Anna’s action and the teacher’s next action
Tina’s action and Anna’s next action
Zakir’s action and the teacher’s next action
activities.explanation: Exactly right! Anna’s question asks about her and the old lady.

activities.prompt: The word ‘will’ shows an event happening now.
activities.explanation: Good try! ‘Will’ shows something happening in the future.

activities.prompt: The word ‘will’ is used for events that will happen in the ______.
activities.hint: Something in the future has not happened yet.
activities.explanation: You did it! ‘Will’ helps us write about future events.

activities.prompt: Lubang says, “I will help my injured friend.” He helps now. What does his action show?
options: He cares about his injured friend.
He wants his friend to leave.
He thinks his friend needs no help.
He is angry with his injured friend.

This mistake treats helping as wanting the friend to leave.
This mistake separates Lubang's action from what his friend needs.
This mistake mistakes an angry feeling for a caring action.

activities.explanation: Helping an injured friend shows that Lubang cares about him.

activities.prompt: A child says, “We will answer the picture questions.” The answer is not ready now. What can we tell?
options: The answer will be given later.
The answer was given earlier.
The answer is being given now.
The answer will never be given.

This mistake treats the future action as a past action.
This mistake treats the future action as happening now.
This mistake turns a future action into something impossible.

activities.explanation: This is right because “will” points to an action still to come.

lessons.title: Let us Do

activities.prompt: What could you create to show that everyone belongs together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Make a symbol for togetherness
activities.body: Make a symbol for togetherness by creating a paper person. Fold a sheet of paper, then draw one side of a boy or girl. Include the head, neck, hand, dress, leg and shoe. Cut along your drawing, unfold the paper gently, and colour it. Finally, paste a picture of your creation in the box.
keyPoints: Create a symbol for togetherness.
Draw one side of a body with all the needed parts.
Cut, unfold, colour and paste your creation.
activities.explanation: Follow the steps carefully and enjoy making your symbol.

activities.prompt: A child has folded a sheet of paper but does not know how to finish the symbol. What should the child do next?
steps: The child should draw one side of a body, because the scissors will follow the lines.
The drawing needs all the body parts, so it shows a whole person.
The child should cut and unfold gently, because this opens the shape while keeping it safe.
The child should colour it and paste it in the box, because this finishes the activity.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Follow the making steps
activities.body: Work through the making steps in order. Take a sheet of paper and fold it. Draw one side of a body with all the needed parts. Next, cut along the drawing with scissors. Unfold the paper gently, then colour the drawing with crayons or sketch pens.
keyPoints: Fold the paper before drawing.
Cut along the drawing and unfold gently.
Colour the drawing after unfolding.
activities.explanation: Good step-by-step work helps you make your creation.

activities.prompt: Use scissors to cut the paper along the drawing.
activities.explanation: Use scissors to cut the paper along your drawing.

activities.prompt: Colour the drawing with crayons or ______ pens.
activities.hint: Use one of the colouring tools in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The drawing can be coloured with crayons or sketch pens.

activities.prompt: Match each action with the correct step.
activities.explanation: Each action matches a step in making your creation.

activities.prompt: You have folded the paper. What comes next?
options: Colour the drawing
Paste the picture
Draw one side of a body
Cut the drawing
activities.explanation: After folding the sheet, draw one side of a body.

activities.prompt: Put these actions in the correct order.
items: Draw one side of a body
activities.explanation: Fold first, then draw. Cut next, unfold gently and colour afterwards.

activities.prompt: Children should unfold the paper roughly after cutting.
activities.explanation: The lesson says to unfold the paper gently.

activities.prompt: A child draws before cutting. What does the drawing do?
options: The drawing guides the scissors along its lines.
The drawing uses less crayon for colouring.
The drawing makes the paper become smaller.
The drawing hides the body from other children.

why.The drawing uses less crayon for colouri: This mistake confuses drawing with controlling crayon use.
why.The drawing makes the paper become small: This mistake thinks a drawing changes the paper's size.
why.The drawing hides the body from other ch: This mistake thinks the body must be hidden from others.

activities.explanation: The scissors need the drawing as a clear guide.

activities.prompt: The class needs a symbol for togetherness. Which picture fits best?
options: People joining their hands in a group.
A person standing alone far from others.
Shoes standing apart from one another.
Separate shapes placed far from each other.

This mistake thinks being alone can show togetherness.
This mistake treats shoes as a sign of joined people.
why.Separate shapes placed far from each oth: This mistake thinks being separate can show togetherness.

activities.explanation: Joined hands show people being together.

activities.prompt: After cutting, why should the paper be unfolded gently?
options: To keep the drawing from being damaged.
To make the paper become smaller.
To hide the cut lines from view.
To make the crayon colours darker.

This mistake thinks unfolding makes paper shrink.
This mistake thinks opening the paper hides the cuts.
This mistake thinks unfolding can change crayon colours.

activities.explanation: Gentle opening helps protect the newly cut drawing.

activities.prompt: The person may be a boy or a girl. What does this mean?
options: Children have freedom in choosing who to draw.
Only girls may join the activity.
The boy must always be drawn.
All children must draw the same person.

This mistake thinks the activity is only for girls.
This mistake thinks a boy is the only allowed choice.
This mistake thinks all children must make the same picture.

activities.explanation: Either a boy or a girl is allowed, so children can choose.

activities.context: A group faced a very difficult task. One member was struggling, so another reached out a hand. They kept helping each other instead of giving up. When the task was completed, they cheered and sang together. The group shared the happy feeling whether they had won or lost. Standing close together made them feel strong, and they trusted one another. They knew that joining hands would bring their goal nearer.
activities.prompt: If one member stopped helping and tried to face the difficulty alone, what would most likely happen?
options: The group would find it harder to overcome the difficulty.
The group would overcome the difficulty more easily.
The group would feel stronger and more confident.
The group would bring its goal nearer very quickly.

why.The group would overcome the difficulty: Working alone would remove the strength of teamwork.
why.The group would feel stronger and more c: Being together helps people feel strong.
why.The group would bring its goal nearer ve: Joining hands brings the goal nearer.

activities.explanation: The poem says teamwork can overcome any difficulty.

activities.context: A group faced a very difficult task. One member was struggling, so another reached out a hand. They kept helping each other instead of giving up. When the task was completed, they cheered and sang together. The group shared the happy feeling whether they had won or lost. Standing close together made them feel strong, and they trusted one another. They knew that joining hands would bring their goal nearer.
activities.prompt: After the group shared an outcome, one member felt left out. What should the others do?
options: Stay with the member and include them in the shared cheer.
Leave the member alone so the group can celebrate.
Tell the member that only they caused the outcome.
Wait until the member forgets about the group.

why.Leave the member alone so the group can: Cheering and singing together brings team spirit.
why.Tell the member that only they caused th: A bond of trust should always be there.
why.Wait until the member forgets about the: Being in a team brings joy to everyone.

activities.explanation: People should share whether they win or lose.

activities.prompt: How does teamwork help people overcome a difficulty?
activities.answer: Teamwork helps because people stand together, help each other, and join hands. This makes them strong and keeps them from falling. Their team spirit gives them cheer and joy. Together, they can overcome any difficulty and bring their goal nearer.
points: Standing together makes people strong.
Members help each other avoid falling.
Team spirit brings cheer and joy.
Teamwork can overcome any difficulty.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Darsana and Bokali are in the same class. When Darsana says that she loves her country, Bokali says that they stand together in unity. The country has different traditions, foods, festivals and languages, but its people still stand in unity. Their team joins hands. Then Darsana turns to a friend, and they exchange a conversation about the foods and festivals they like most. A team leader must also help teammates who disagree come together.
activities.prompt: Darsana's team joins hands. What is the most likely result?
options: The teammates become more united.
The teammates forget about their own traditions.
The teammates think that every festival is the same.
The teammates stop sharing their ideas.

why.The teammates forget about their own tra: Joining hands should not make anyone forget their traditions.
why.The teammates think that every festival: People can remain united even when their traditions are different.
A united team should continue sharing ideas.

activities.explanation: Joining hands helps the team stand together in unity.

activities.context: Darsana and Bokali are in the same class. When Darsana says that she loves her country, Bokali says that they stand together in unity. The country has different traditions, foods, festivals and languages, but its people still stand in unity. Their team joins hands. Then Darsana turns to a friend, and they exchange a conversation about the foods and festivals they like most. A team leader must also help teammates who disagree come together.
activities.prompt: What should Darsana do when a friend likes a different food or festival?
options: Turn to the friend, talk, and share what they like most.
Tell the friend that their choice is wrong.
Choose the food or festival for the friend.
Keep her own likes to herself.

why.Tell the friend that their choice is wro: A different choice should not make Darsana reject her friend.
why.Choose the food or festival for the frie: Each child should be allowed to share their own choice.
Keeping her likes to herself does not help the conversation.

activities.explanation: Children are asked to exchange conversations and share what they like.

activities.context: Darsana and Bokali are in the same class. When Darsana says that she loves her country, Bokali says that they stand together in unity. The country has different traditions, foods, festivals and languages, but its people still stand in unity. Their team joins hands. Then Darsana turns to a friend, and they exchange a conversation about the foods and festivals they like most. A team leader must also help teammates who disagree come together.
activities.prompt: Bokali notices that teammates disagree about festivals. What should the team leader do?
options: Invite each teammate to share what they like and talk together.
End the conversation so that no one feels different.
Ask only one teammate to make the decision.
Say that some traditions are less important.

why.End the conversation so that no one feel: Ending the conversation does not unite the teammates.
why.Ask only one teammate to make the decisi: One person should not decide alone when teammates disagree.
why.Say that some traditions are less import: The leader should respect different traditions and bring everyone together.

activities.explanation: Sharing and talking can help disagreeing teammates stand in unity.

activities.prompt: Explain why helping each other is important and how joining hands can show unity.
activities.answer: Helping each other is important because a team can stand together in unity. When children join hands, they show that they are willing to work as one team. Even though the country has different traditions, foods, festivals and languages, its people can remain united.
points: Helping each other supports teamwork.
Joining hands shows unity.
The country includes different traditions.
Different people can still stand together.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how ants use signals to help their colony.
activities.answer: Ants use signals when they work together. These signals help the colony find food, defend itself, and build complex nests. The signals help the ants coordinate their actions, so they can complete these important jobs as a team.
points: Signals help the ants work together.
They help the ants find food.
They help the ants defend their colony.
They help the ants build complex nests.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During an English lesson, children study a map with a hospital, bank, post office, road, school, book store and children’s park. The teacher asks them to fill blanks using words from the box. For practice, the teacher places the post office close to the hospital. The ambulance has the post office on one side and the hospital on the other. The book store is close to the children’s park, and the bank is close to the school.
activities.prompt: The teacher places the post office close to the hospital. Which word from the box should the children write for this blank?
options: near
behind
between
in front of

why.behind: “Behind” would mean one place is at the back of another.
why.between: “Between” would need something on each side.
why.in front of: “In front of” would mean one place is ahead of another.

activities.explanation: “Close to” describes the near position.

activities.context: During an English lesson, children study a map with a hospital, bank, post office, road, school, book store and children’s park. The teacher asks them to fill blanks using words from the box. For practice, the teacher places the post office close to the hospital. The ambulance has the post office on one side and the hospital on the other. The book store is close to the children’s park, and the bank is close to the school.
activities.prompt: What should the children write if the teacher keeps the book store close to the children’s park?
options: near
behind
between
in front of

why.behind: “Behind” would describe a position at the back of something.
why.between: “Between” would need another place on each side.
why.in front of: “In front of” would describe a position ahead of something.

activities.explanation: The book store and the park are close together.

activities.prompt: How does the ambulance’s position show the difference between being between two places and being near one place?
activities.answer: If the post office and hospital are on opposite sides of the ambulance, it is between them. If the ambulance is simply close to one place, it is near that place. The other places in the sentence help us understand the position.
points: Identifies that the ambulance is between two places.
Explains that near means close to one place.
Uses the other places to understand the position.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the “Let us Do” activity, Riya and her friend make a symbol for togetherness. Riya takes a plain sheet of paper and folds it. Next, she cuts along the drawing with scissors, unfolds the paper gently, and colours the drawing with crayons.
activities.prompt: Riya and her friend have finished colouring their creation. What should they do next?
options: Attach a picture of their creation to the box.
Fold the creation and put it away.
Use the creation to cut out another body shape.
Draw a new body on a separate sheet.

Folding it away does not show the finished work.
why.Use the creation to cut out another body: The creation should not be used for another cutting task.
A new drawing is not required at this stage.

activities.explanation: This completes the activity as instructed.

activities.context: During the “Let us Do” activity, Riya and her friend make a symbol for togetherness. Riya takes a plain sheet of paper and folds it. Using a pencil, she draws one side of a body with a head, neck, hand, dress, leg and shoe. She decides to draw a girl. Next, she cuts along the drawing with scissors, unfolds the paper gently, and colours the drawing with crayons.
activities.prompt: Riya notices that she forgot to draw a shoe before beginning to cut. What should she do?
options: Draw the missing shoe and then continue cutting.
Cut a shoe shape from a different sheet of paper.
Wait until the colouring stage and draw the shoe then.
Paste the picture in the box without a shoe.

why.Cut a shoe shape from a different sheet: The shoe should be part of the main drawing, not another sheet.
why.Wait until the colouring stage and draw: The required body parts should be drawn before cutting.
why.Paste the picture in the box without a s: The completed picture must show all the required parts.

activities.explanation: The drawing must include every listed body part before cutting.

activities.context: During the “Let us Do” activity, Riya and her friend make a symbol for togetherness. Riya takes a plain sheet of paper and folds it. Using a pencil, she draws one side of a body with a head, neck, hand, dress, leg and shoe. She decides to draw a girl. Next, she cuts along the drawing with scissors, unfolds the paper gently, and colours the drawing with crayons.
activities.prompt: Riya gently unfolds the paper, but she has not coloured the drawing yet. What should she do next?
options: Add colour to the opened drawing.
Cut another body outline around the drawing.
Fold the paper tightly along the drawing.
Paste the uncoloured picture in the box.

why.Cut another body outline around the draw: Another cut is not part of the next step.
why.Fold the paper tightly along the drawing: The paper should remain opened for colouring.
Colouring must be completed before the picture is pasted.

activities.explanation: Colouring comes after cutting and unfolding.

activities.prompt: How does the order of drawing and cutting help Riya complete the activity?
activities.answer: Riya draws the body parts on the folded paper before she cuts. This gives her a clear guide for the scissors. After she cuts along the drawing, she gently unfolds the paper and colours the created symbol for togetherness.
points: Folds the paper first.
Draws all the required body parts.
Cuts along the completed drawing.
Unfolds and colours the creation.

lessons.title: Chinna and the Tinkling Bells

activities.prompt: What would make Chinna’s heart sing like a little bell?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Chinna and Tara
activities.body: Chinna is a bright boy in grade 4. He lives in a village and likes reading storybooks. He loves playing with Tara, his little pet kid. Tara has milky white fur and is five months old. While returning from school, Chinna stops at Chacha’s shop. He sees shiny, tinkling bells, but his money is missing.
keyPoints: Chinna is a bright boy who lives in a village.
Tara is his little pet kid.
Chinna stops at Chacha’s shop on his way home.
activities.explanation: This tells you about Chinna, Tara, and the bells.

activities.prompt: Chinna wants the beautiful bells, but he cannot find his money. What should he do?
steps: First, Chinna checks every pocket, because the money may be there.
Next, he feels shocked, because he still cannot pay ten rupees.
He returns the bells, because taking them without paying is wrong.
Therefore, Chinna leaves the bells and walks home without buying them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Chinna Finds the Tinkling Bells
activities.body: Chinna stops at Chacha’s shop while returning from school. He notices a pair of beautiful, shiny, tinkling bells. He politely asks the shopkeeper to show them to him. The bells cost ten rupees. Chinna is shocked because his money is missing. He searches all his pockets. Sadly, he returns the bells and walks home.
keyPoints: Chinna politely asks to see the bells.
The bells cost ten rupees.
Chinna searches his pockets before returning the bells.
activities.explanation: This explains what happens when Chinna sees the bells.

activities.prompt: Chinna stopped at Chacha’s shop while going to school.
activities.explanation: He stopped there while returning from school.

activities.prompt: Chinna searched all his ______ for the missing money.
activities.hint: He checked the places on his clothes that hold things.
activities.explanation: He searched every pocket because his money was missing.

activities.prompt: Match each one with its detail from the story.
pairs: place where Chinna saw the bells
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important detail from Chinna’s day.

activities.prompt: Put Chinna’s actions in the order they happened.
items: Ask the shopkeeper to show them
activities.explanation: Chinna first saw the bells, then searched for his money.

activities.prompt: Why did Chinna return the bells?
options: Because his money was missing
Because the shop was closed
Because Tara wanted them
Because they were too heavy
activities.explanation: His money was missing, so he sadly returned the bells.

activities.prompt: Chinna put his shoes in the corner at home.
activities.explanation: Yes, Chinna put his shoes in the corner.

activities.prompt: Imagine your pocket is empty at a shop. How might you feel?
options: He feels shocked and very sad.
He feels very happy and excited.
He feels angry with the shopkeeper.
He feels calm and quite careless.

This misses the worry caused by missing money.
This wrongly blames the shopkeeper for the missing money.
This misses the worry shown by searching all pockets.

activities.explanation: This matches Chinna's shock and sadness after finding no money.

activities.prompt: Before buying, you check every pocket. What are you trying to find?
options: Someone else to pay for the item.
The coins kept by the shopkeeper.
The money needed to pay for the item.
A promise to pay for the item later.

This wrongly thinks another person will pay for the item.
This wrongly puts the money with the shopkeeper.
This wrongly thinks a promise can replace the missing money.

activities.explanation: This matches Chinna's search for money to buy the bells.

activities.prompt: You cannot pay for an item. What should you do?
options: Take the item and run outside quickly.
Keep the item hidden under your coat.
Ask the shopkeeper to shout for help.
Give the item back to the shopkeeper.

This wrongly suggests taking an unpaid item.
This wrongly suggests hiding an item you cannot pay for.
This wrongly expects another person to solve the problem.

activities.explanation: This matches Chinna's decision to sadly return the bells.

activities.prompt: The bells look shiny. What does “shiny” mean here?
options: They have a surface that shines.
They make a gentle ringing sound.
They have rough and dirty surfaces.
They are too small for little hands.

This confuses shiny with the bells' tinkling sound.
This confuses a shining surface with a dirty one.
This confuses the bells' appearance with their size.

activities.explanation: This is right because shiny means having a surface that shines.

activities.prompt: You want to see the bells at a shop. What should you do first?
options: Ask the shopkeeper politely to show them.
Push the bells into the shopkeeper's hands.
Take the bells without first asking anyone.
Shout until the shopkeeper comes closer.

why.Push the bells into the shopkeeper's han: This wrongly shows an impolite and forceful action.
why.Take the bells without first asking anyo: This wrongly suggests taking the bells before asking.
This wrongly shows a loud and impolite action.

activities.explanation: This matches Chinna's polite request to see the bells.

lessons.title: Kamala Helps Chinna

activities.prompt: Would you return extra money if it was not really yours?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Kamala's Kind Help
activities.body: Kamala first comforts Chinna. She offers him money for bells. Later, she buys two pineapples for forty-five rupees each. The seller gives too much change, and Chinna notices ten extra rupees. Kamala says keeping the extra money is stealing. Chinna pays for the bells, walks home with Kamala, and ties them around Tara’s neck.
keyPoints: Kamala comforts Chinna and offers money for bells.
Chinna notices ten extra rupees in his change.
Chinna pays for bells and puts them around Tara’s neck.
activities.explanation: This story shows Kamala’s kindness and Chinna’s honesty.

activities.prompt: A shop gives you ten extra rupees by mistake. What should you do, and why?
steps: Notice the extra money, because you need to know what you received.
Give it back to the seller, because the money is not yours.
Do not keep it, because Kamala says that keeping it is stealing.
The seller may praise you, because your choice shows honesty.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Asked What Happened?
activities.prompt: Who gently asked Chinna what had happened?
options: Kamala
Chinna
Tara
The seller
activities.explanation: Kamala gently asked what had happened. You spotted the right helper!

activities.title: Money for Bells
activities.prompt: Kamala offered Chinna money to buy the ______.
activities.hint: Think about the objects Chinna later bought.
activities.explanation: Kamala offered Chinna money so he could buy the bells.

activities.title: The Pineapple Cost
activities.prompt: How much did two pineapples cost altogether?
options: One hundred rupees
Forty-five rupees
Ninety rupees
Ten rupees
activities.explanation: Each pineapple cost forty-five rupees. So, two cost ninety rupees.

activities.title: Match the Story
activities.prompt: Match each item with its detail from the story.
activities.explanation: You matched the prices, amounts, and people from the story.

activities.title: The Seller’s Praise
activities.prompt: Why did the fruit seller praise Chinna?
options: He bought pineapples
He tied the bells
He showed honesty
He walked home
activities.explanation: The seller praised Chinna for being honest. You spotted the reason!

activities.title: Put the Events in Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Kamala gave the seller a hundred-rupee note
The seller gave Chinna two ten-rupee notes as change
Chinna paid ten rupees for the bells
activities.explanation: The story moves from buying fruit to noticing extra change and buying bells.

activities.prompt: Chinna hugged his mother and began crying. How did Chinna feel?
options: He felt very sad and upset.
He felt very calm and completely relaxed.
He felt happy and full of joy.
He felt angry and afraid of someone.

why.He felt very calm and completely relaxed: Calm and relaxed feelings do not usually cause such crying.
Nothing in the facts shows that Chinna felt happy or joyful.
Nothing in the facts shows that Chinna felt angry or afraid.

activities.explanation: Crying and hugging his mother show that Chinna felt upset.

activities.prompt: Kamala gently asked Chinna what had happened. Why did she ask gently?
options: She wanted Chinna to share what had happened.
She wanted Chinna to buy more pineapples.
She wanted the fruit seller to leave them.
She wanted Chinna to forget about his painful feelings.

why.She wanted Chinna to buy more pineapples: The question was about what happened, not buying fruit.
why.She wanted the fruit seller to leave the: The seller was not the person Chinna was talking to.
why.She wanted Chinna to forget about his pa: Gentle asking helps Chinna speak, not hide his feelings.

activities.explanation: Her gentle way showed that she cared about Chinna's feelings.

activities.prompt: Two pineapples cost forty-five rupees each. Kamala gave a hundred-rupee note. The seller gave two ten-rupee notes as change. What does the word change mean here?
options: The money left after paying for the pineapples.
The price of one extra pineapple.
The money for buying the bells later.
A gift from the seller for coming together.

The notes were left over, not the price of another fruit.
The bells were bought later, not paid for by the seller.
why.A gift from the seller for coming togeth: The notes were payment left over, not a gift from the seller.

activities.explanation: The notes were the money left after both pineapples were paid for.

activities.prompt: Chinna noticed ten extra rupees in the change. Why did Kamala call keeping it stealing?
options: The extra money belonged to the seller.
Chinna had already paid for two pineapples.
The bells had cost only ten rupees.
The seller had promised Chinna the money.

why.Chinna had already paid for two pineappl: Paying for pineapples does not make extra change Chinna's.
The bell cost was separate from the extra money.
why.The seller had promised Chinna the money: No fact says that the seller promised the extra money.

activities.explanation: The seller gave it by mistake, so it was not Chinna's.

activities.prompt: Chinna returned ten extra rupees from the seller. Why did the seller praise Chinna?
options: Chinna showed honesty by returning money that was not his.
Chinna showed kindness by buying two fresh pineapples.
Chinna showed wisdom by counting all his money.
Chinna showed courage by speaking to the seller.

why.Chinna showed kindness by buying two fre: Buying pineapples does not show honesty with extra money.
why.Chinna showed wisdom by counting all his: Counting money does not explain the seller's praise for honesty.
why.Chinna showed courage by speaking to the: Speaking to the seller does not show that he acted honestly.

activities.explanation: Returning money that was not his showed that Chinna was honest.

activities.prompt: Chinna paid ten rupees for the bells and tied them around Tara's neck. What does this suggest about Chinna?
options: He wanted to share the bells with Tara.
He wanted to keep the bells for himself.
He thought Tara should sell the bells again.
He planned to use the bells to buy fruit.

He tied the bells around Tara, not around his own neck.
why.He thought Tara should sell the bells ag: Nothing in the facts says that Chinna wanted Tara to sell them.
why.He planned to use the bells to buy fruit: Nothing in the facts says that he planned to buy more fruit.

activities.explanation: Tying the bells around Tara shows that he wanted to share them.

lessons.title: Comparing People and Things

activities.prompt: How can we compare people and things using special word endings?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How We Compare
activities.body: Comparisons use special adjective forms. Add -er when comparing two people or objects. Add -est when comparing a whole group. The word than helps compare two people or objects. The -est ending is added to the adjective. Aman is shorter than Jiya. February is the shortest month of the year. The lesson also asks for words with opposite meanings.
keyPoints: Use -er for two people or objects.
Use -est for a whole group.
Use than with a comparison of two.
activities.explanation: These endings and words help you make clear comparisons.

activities.prompt: How can Aman and Jiya be compared by height?
steps: Two people are compared, so -er is needed.
Adding -er to short makes shorter.
“Than” shows which person Aman is compared with.
Thus, Aman is shorter than Jiya.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which sentence compares two people correctly?
options: Aman is shorter than Jiya.
February is the shortest month.
The -er ending marks a group.
The -est ending marks two things.
activities.explanation: Aman is shorter than Jiya. This compares two people.

activities.prompt: The word than is used when comparing a whole group.
activities.explanation: Use than when comparing two people or objects.

activities.prompt: Aman is ______ than Jiya.
activities.hint: Choose the comparative word for Aman.
activities.explanation: Shorter tells us that Aman is less tall than Jiya.

activities.prompt: Match each word or part with its correct use.
activities.explanation: Shorter compares two, while shortest compares a whole group.

activities.prompt: Which pair has opposite meanings?
options: ugly and beautiful
punishment and purchase
short and reward
sell and ugly
activities.explanation: Ugly is the opposite of beautiful.

activities.prompt: Which sentence uses -er and than correctly?
options: Aman is shorter than Jiya.
Aman is shortest than Jiya.
February is short than the year.
Aman is more short than Jiya.
activities.explanation: Shorter has the -er ending. Than compares Aman with Jiya.

activities.prompt: Aman says, “I am shorter than Jiya.” What must be true?
options: Jiya is taller than Aman.
Jiya is shorter than Aman.
Both have exactly the same height.
Jiya is the shortest of all months.

This reverses the comparison and makes Jiya the shorter person.
This ignores “shorter,” which shows that their heights are different.
This mixes people with months and gives Jiya the wrong role.

activities.explanation: This is right because shorter than Jiya means Jiya is taller than Aman.

activities.prompt: Why is “than” needed in “Aman is shorter than Jiya”?
options: It shows the second person being compared.
It shows the first person is taller.
It shows a whole group is compared.
It shows both people have one height.

This mistakes the first person for the person compared with Aman.
This mistakes two people for a whole group.
This thinks “than” means both people have equal height.

activities.explanation: This is right because “than” introduces the person being compared.

activities.prompt: One pencil is longer than another. Which ending shows this comparison?
options: The ending -er, because two objects are compared.
The ending -est, because all objects are compared.
The ending than, because two objects are compared.
The ending -er, because one object is compared.

why.The ending -est, because all objects are: -est is for comparing a whole group, not two objects.
why.The ending than, because two objects are: “Than” links the comparison but does not show the adjective form.
why.The ending -er, because one object is co: -er fits two objects, but only one object is compared here.

activities.explanation: This is right because -er is used when comparing two objects.

activities.prompt: All months are being compared. Which ending shows the whole group?
options: The ending -est, because all months are compared.
The ending -er, because two months are compared.
The ending than, because all months are compared.
The ending -est, because one month is compared.

why.The ending -er, because two months are c: -er is used when only two months are compared.
why.The ending than, because all months are: “Than” links a comparison but does not mark a group.
why.The ending -est, because one month is co: -est fits a group, but this option compares only one month.

activities.explanation: This is right because -est compares the whole group of months.

lessons.title: Following the Story

activities.prompt: What happens when Chinna notices something is missing from his money?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Follow Chinna's Story
activities.body: Listen as your teacher reads ‘The Tinkling Bells’ aloud. Number the story’s sentences in order. Chinna found that his money was missing and felt sad. He went to the market with his mother. He hugged her and told her. The extra money came from the fruit seller’s mistake. Chinna returned it. After receiving some money, he bought the tinkling bells. He wanted bells for his pet at Chacha’s shop.
keyPoints: Chinna found that his money was missing.
He went to the market with his mother.
He returned the extra money to the fruit seller.
He bought tinkling bells for his pet.
activities.explanation: This helps you follow what happened in the story.

activities.prompt: What should Chinna do when he finds that his money is missing?
steps: His money is missing, so Chinna feels sad.
He hugs his mother and tells her, because she may help him.
He learns that the fruit seller made a mistake and gave extra money.
He returns the extra money, because it was not really his.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Chinna felt sad when he discovered that his money was missing.
activities.explanation: Chinna felt sad because his money was missing.

activities.prompt: What did Chinna discover about his money?
options: His money was missing.
His bells were missing.
His pet was missing.
His mother was missing.
activities.explanation: Chinna discovered that his money was missing.

activities.prompt: Chinna went to the market with his ______.
activities.hint: Who went with Chinna?
activities.explanation: Chinna went to the market with his mother.

activities.prompt: Why did the fruit seller give Chinna extra money?
options: The seller made a mistake.
The seller forgot his shop.
The market was too crowded.
Chinna lost his mother's money.
activities.explanation: The extra money came from the fruit seller’s mistake.

activities.prompt: Match each story part with its detail.
activities.explanation: Each detail matches the correct part of Chinna’s story.

activities.prompt: Chinna kept the extra money for himself.
activities.explanation: Chinna returned the extra money to the fruit seller.

activities.prompt: Put these story events in order.
items: Chinna told his mother about it.
activities.explanation: The events move from the missing money to the bell purchase.

activities.prompt: Why did Chinna want to buy the tinkling bells?
options: He wanted them for his pet.
He wanted them for his mother.
He wanted them for his teacher.
He wanted them for the seller.
activities.explanation: Chinna wanted to buy bells for his pet at Chacha’s shop.

activities.prompt: While following the story, what happens after Chinna finds his money missing?
options: He hugs his mother and tells her about the missing money.
He returns the extra money to the fruit seller.
He buys tinkling bells for his pet at Chacha’s shop.
He goes to the market with his mother.

why.He returns the extra money to the fruit: This mistake places a later event before telling his mother.
why.He buys tinkling bells for his pet at Ch: This mistake places a later shopping event before telling his mother.
This mistake places an earlier event before telling his mother.

activities.explanation: This is right because Chinna told his mother after finding the money missing.

lessons.title: Speaking and Writing

activities.prompt: How can you handle tricky moments with friends and write about what matters?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sharing ideas through speaking and writing
activities.body: Speaking and writing help you share ideas and show what you know. In this lesson, you practise speaking about borrowed pens, quiz answers, notebooks and snacks. You also frame sentences using story words. The story shows Chinna smiling when Kamala offers help. Chinna returns extra money, wins praise, and is told to be careful with money. Finally, you draw two national symbols.
keyPoints: Speak about practical school situations.
Frame sentences with story words.
Receive praise for returning money.
Draw two national symbols.
activities.explanation: These tasks help you express ideas clearly and confidently.

activities.prompt: Chinna receives extra money from the fruit seller. What should he do, and why?
steps: Chinna notices that the fruit seller gave him extra money.
He returns it because keeping money that is not his would be wrong.
The seller praises him, and Chinna is called honest.
Kamala tells him to be careful with money, so he learns from his mistake.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choosing a speaking task
activities.prompt: What does one speaking task ask you to discuss?
options: After breaking a borrowed pen
Before sharing a favourite snack
While drawing national symbols
After returning extra money
activities.explanation: The task asks what you should do after breaking a borrowed pen.

activities.title: Taking a notebook
activities.prompt: A classmate may take a notebook without the teacher’s ______.
activities.hint: Think about what the teacher needs to allow.
activities.explanation: The classmate may take the notebook without the teacher’s permission.

activities.title: Keeping a secret
activities.prompt: What does the classmate ask the learner to do?
options: Keep the matter secret
Return the extra money
Share a favourite snack
Frame story sentences now
activities.explanation: The classmate asks the learner to keep the matter secret.

activities.title: The extra-money problem
activities.prompt: What starts the fruit seller’s extra-money problem?
options: Seller gives Chinna extra money
Seller gives Chinna less money
Seller calls Chinna dishonest
Seller praises Chinna first
activities.explanation: The seller gives Chinna extra money. Chinna later returns it.

activities.title: Tasks in book order
activities.prompt: Put these tasks in the order they appear in your book.
items: What to do after breaking a borrowed pen
How to handle friends wanting quiz answers
Sharing a favourite snack with a classmate
activities.explanation: The pen task is on page 18. The quiz and snack tasks are on page 19. The symbol task is on page 20.

activities.title: Framing a story sentence
activities.prompt: Complete the sentence with a story word: The fruit seller gives Chinna extra ______.
activities.hint: Use the word connected with returning something extra.
activities.explanation: The story says the seller gives Chinna extra money. Your sentence uses a story word.

activities.prompt: You break a pen that you borrowed. What should you do next?
options: Tell the owner and offer to make it right.
Hide the broken pen and say nothing.
Keep the broken pen for another day.
Blame the owner for the broken pen.

This is wrong because it hides the mistake.
This is wrong because it puts off telling the owner.
This is wrong because Chinna broke the borrowed pen.

activities.explanation: This is right because telling the owner shows honesty.

activities.prompt: Two friends ask to see your quiz answers after the quiz. What should you do?
options: Keep the answers private and explain why.
Show every answer because they asked.
Give the quiz paper to both friends.
Read one answer aloud to the class.

This is wrong because friends asking does not make it right.
This is wrong because it gives away the whole quiz.
This is wrong because it shares answers with everyone.

activities.explanation: This is right because private answers help each friend learn.

activities.prompt: A classmate takes a notebook without permission. He asks you to keep it secret. What should you say?
options: I will tell the teacher what happened.
I will hide the notebook from the teacher.
I will take his notebook as well.
I will say nothing to anyone.

why.I will hide the notebook from the teache: This is wrong because it helps hide the wrong action.
This is wrong because it makes the wrong action worse.
This is wrong because it keeps the teacher’s permission rule secret.

activities.explanation: This is right because the teacher should know about the notebook.

activities.prompt: You have one favourite snack. Your classmate wants some. What is the kindest choice?
options: Keep it all so no one can have any.
Take some from the classmate instead.
Leave it where the classmate can take it.
Share some of it with your classmate.

This is wrong because it does not include the classmate.
This is wrong because taking is not sharing.
why.Leave it where the classmate can take it: This is wrong because hiding food is not sharing.

activities.explanation: This is right because sharing gives some to the classmate.

lessons.title: Making a Bell Craft

activities.prompt: What could we turn into a special bell to surprise a friend?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How to Make Your Bell
activities.body: Make a bell like the bells Chinna wanted for Tara. Use waste or recyclable items, which can be used again. Bottle caps or small tin cans can form the bells. Put pebbles, beans or beads inside for a tinkling sound. Thread string or yarn through the hole, then tie a knot. Add shiny aluminium foil and decorate a tag. Adjust the string so the bell can hang freely.
keyPoints: Use bottle caps or small tin cans.
Add pebbles, beans or beads for a tinkling sound.
Thread and tie the string, then adjust it.
activities.explanation: You now know the materials and steps for making a lovely bell.

activities.prompt: Chinna's bell keeps slipping and cannot dangle freely. How can he fix it?
steps: He threads string or yarn through the hole because the bell must hang from it.
He ties a knot at the end because this stops the string from slipping out.
He adjusts the string because this lets the bell dangle freely.
The bell can now hang securely and dangle freely, so it is ready for Tara.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Which Craft Should You Make?
activities.prompt: What should your craft resemble?
options: The bells Chinna wanted for Tara
The bags Chinna wanted for Tara
The drums Chinna wanted for Tara
The pots Chinna wanted for Tara
activities.explanation: The craft should resemble the bells Chinna wanted for Tara.

activities.title: Choose a Bell Material
activities.prompt: You can use bottle ______ or small tin cans.
activities.hint: Choose one word from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Bottle caps and small tin cans can both be used for the bells.

activities.title: Match Each Material
activities.prompt: Match each material or part to its use.
activities.explanation: Each material has a special job when you make your bell.

activities.title: Finish the String
activities.prompt: Put these string steps in order.
items: Thread string or yarn through the hole
Tie a knot at the end
Adjust the string so the bell hangs freely
activities.explanation: Thread first, secure with a knot, then adjust the string.

activities.title: Fix the Matchstick Puzzle
activities.prompt: How must the matchstick puzzle be fixed?
options: By adding some foil.
By moving one matchstick.
By tying a new knot.
By threading more yarn.
activities.explanation: You can fix the puzzle by moving one matchstick.

activities.title: Bells in India
activities.prompt: What can be found in India?
options: Only one type of bell
No bells at all
Different types of bells
No different types of bells
activities.explanation: Different types of bells can be found in India.

activities.prompt: Tara has a bottle cap, aluminium foil, string, and a pebble. What can Chinna use for the bell itself?
options: A bottle cap can form the bell.
A sheet of foil can form the bell.
A length of string can form the bell.
A small pebble can form the bell.

This mistake treats the shiny foil as the bell's main shape.
This mistake treats the hanging string as the bell's main shape.
This mistake treats a sound-making pebble as the bell's main shape.

activities.explanation: This is right because a bottle cap can be used to make the bell.

activities.prompt: Tara moves a finished bell. What sound should Chinna expect to hear?
options: A soft tinkling sound from the pieces inside.
A loud cracking sound from the foil outside.
A whistling sound from the string above.
A rustling sound from the coloured tag.

why.A loud cracking sound from the foil outs: This mistake thinks the shiny foil makes the sound when moved.
This mistake thinks the hanging string makes the sound.
This mistake thinks colouring the tag makes the sound.

activities.explanation: This is right because pebbles, beans or beads inside create a tinkling sound.

activities.prompt: Chinna threads string through the bell hole. The string slips and the bell cannot dangle. What should he do?
options: Tie a knot and adjust the string length.
Add pebbles and adjust the foil on top.
Tie a knot and add more beads inside.
Colour the tag and move one matchstick.

This mistake confuses adding sound with securing the hanging string.
This mistake secures the string but does not free the bell to dangle.
This mistake thinks decorating or solving a puzzle will fix the string.

activities.explanation: This is right because the knot secures the string and the adjustment lets it dangle freely.

activities.prompt: Tara wants the bell to look shiny and the tag to show her own work. What should Chinna do?
options: Add aluminium foil, then name or colour the tag.
Add pebbles outside, then tie up the string.
Cover the bell with string, then draw on it.
Fill the bell with foil, then knot the tag.

why.Add pebbles outside, then tie up the str: This mistake puts sound-making pieces on the outside and confuses the string.
why.Cover the bell with string, then draw on: This mistake uses string for decoration instead of foil.
why.Fill the bell with foil, then knot the t: This mistake puts foil inside and treats the tag like the string.

activities.explanation: This is right because foil gives a shiny look and the tag can be personalised.
