lessons.title: Riddles and Holiday Activities

activities.prompt: Can you uncover what the three riddles are describing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Three Riddles
activities.body: Three riddles describe unusual pictures. The first shows thirty white horses on a red hill. They can chomp, stomp, and stand still. The second shows a tall lady in a white frock. She has a yellow face and a red nose. As she grows taller, she becomes shorter. The third is hard and brown outside, but soft and white inside.
keyPoints: The first riddle shows thirty white horses on a red hill.
The second riddle shows a tall lady who becomes shorter.
The third riddle is hard and brown outside, but soft and white inside.
activities.explanation: Each riddle uses colours and changes to make a surprising picture.

activities.prompt: How can I make a holiday activity page that shows what I enjoy?
steps: I will draw activities I enjoy during holidays, because the lesson tells me to.
I may also paste pictures from old newspapers or magazines.
Both drawing and pasting are allowed ways to make the activity page.
My page will show my enjoyed activities, with pictures if I choose them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Holiday Activities
activities.body: During the holidays, you can make a special piece of work. Draw the activities that you enjoy doing. These pictures can show the holiday things you like. You may also paste pictures from old newspapers or magazines. These pictures come from old reading materials. You can add them to your work.
keyPoints: Draw activities that you enjoy during holidays.
You may paste pictures from old newspapers.
You may also paste pictures from old magazines.
activities.explanation: Your holiday work can include drawings and pictures from old reading materials.

activities.title: True or False?
activities.prompt: The thirty white horses stand on a red hill.
activities.explanation: The horses are on a red hill, as the first riddle says.

activities.title: Match Each Clue
activities.prompt: Match each riddle clue to its riddle number.
pairs: A tall lady in a white frock
activities.explanation: Each clue comes from a different riddle.

activities.title: Fill in the Colour
activities.prompt: The tall lady has a yellow face and a ______ nose.
activities.hint: The lady's nose has this colour.
activities.explanation: The tall lady has a yellow face and a red nose.

activities.title: What Happens Next?
activities.prompt: What happens when the tall lady stands taller?
options: She grows shorter.
She grows taller.
She starts chomping.
She turns brown.
activities.explanation: The riddle says that a taller lady becomes shorter.

activities.title: Check the Third Riddle
activities.prompt: The third riddle is soft and brown outside, but hard and white inside.
activities.explanation: The riddle says hard and brown outside, and soft and white inside.

activities.title: Choose the Holiday Idea
activities.prompt: Which sentence follows the lesson's holiday ideas?
options: Draw holiday activities and paste old pictures.
Draw classroom tests and paste blank pages.
Draw holiday chores and paste fresh adverts.
Make shopping lists and paste new covers.
activities.explanation: The lesson says to draw enjoyed activities and paste old pictures.

activities.prompt: In a riddle, white horses chomp, stomp, then stand still. What happens?
options: The horses change what they are doing.
The horses travel from far away to near.
The horses keep doing the same action.
The horses eat the red hill itself.

This mistake reads the changing actions as a journey.
This mistake overlooks the change between each action.
This mistake takes chomp literally and adds eating the hill.

activities.explanation: Each action is different, so the horses change what they do.

activities.prompt: A riddle says a taller lady grows shorter. What can readers understand?
options: Her size works in an opposite way.
Her size always changes the same way.
Her size never changes at all.
Her size depends only on her frock.

This mistake misses the opposite ideas in the clue.
This mistake ignores that her size does change.
This mistake connects her size to clothing instead of the clue.

activities.explanation: The clue links standing taller with growing shorter, which are opposites.

activities.prompt: Hard and soft are riddle clues. What do these words describe?
options: The texture of the outside and inside.
The colour of the outside and inside.
The size of the outside and inside.
The shape of the outside and inside.

This mistake confuses the colours with the textures.
This mistake confuses the size with the textures.
This mistake confuses the shape with the textures.

activities.explanation: Hard and soft describe texture, so they tell us how it feels.

activities.prompt: A reader is puzzled by the tall lady. What should they do?
options: Read the size clues and think about opposites.
Choose the colour clues before reading again.
Think about the frock and ignore her size.
Stop reading because the clues cannot work.

why.Choose the colour clues before reading a: This mistake focuses on colours instead of the puzzling size clue.
why.Think about the frock and ignore her siz: This mistake treats clothing as the key to the size change.
why.Stop reading because the clues cannot wo: This mistake gives up before checking the opposite size clue.

activities.explanation: The opposite size clue needs careful thought to understand.

activities.context: A child had some work to finish but could not stop playing. The child tried to paint a picture, put toys away, and sing all at once. Nothing was finished properly, and the child felt unhappy. An adult reminded the child to work while working and play while playing. The child chose the work first, gave it full attention, and then saved the game for the proper play time. The child felt useful and happy when everything was done.
activities.prompt: What would probably happen if the child continued trying to do everything at once?
options: The work would probably be done poorly.
The child would finish every task quickly and feel happy.
The child would find the work easier by changing tasks often.
The child would have more time to play and still finish the work properly.

why.The child would finish every task quickl: Trying to do everything at once does not help us work properly.
why.The child would find the work easier by: Changing tasks often does not make the work easier.
why.The child would have more time to play a: Doing several things together may spoil even the time saved for play.

activities.explanation: Dividing attention would prevent the work from being done right.

activities.context: A child had some work to finish but could not stop playing. The child tried to paint a picture, put toys away, and sing all at once. Nothing was finished properly, and the child felt unhappy. An adult reminded the child to work while working and play while playing. The child chose the work first, gave it full attention, and then saved the game for the proper play time. The child felt useful and happy when everything was done.
activities.prompt: If the child wanted to play before the work was finished, what should the child do?
options: Finish the work with full attention, then play at the right time.
Play first for a while, then finish the work carefully.
Alternate between work and play until both are done.
Leave the unfinished work and play without wasting any moments.

why.Play first for a while, then finish the: Playing first would stop the child from giving full attention to the work.
why.Alternate between work and play until bo: Alternating between activities would divide the child's attention.
why.Leave the unfinished work and play witho: Leaving the work unfinished would not make the child useful or happy.

activities.explanation: Doing one thing well helps the work be finished properly.

activities.prompt: Explain why doing one thing at a time is a good rule.
activities.answer: Doing one thing at a time helps us give the task our full attention. If we work while playing or keep changing between tasks, the work may not be done right. Finishing the work properly also makes us useful and keeps play at the right time.
points: Gives full attention to the task
Prevents work from being done carelessly
Helps finish work properly
Keeps work and play in the right order
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student wants to finish a school task quickly and make fewer mistakes. The student finds it difficult to concentrate, so progress is slow. Before continuing, the student does simple yoga asanas, including Pranayama and Tree Pose. The student notices that concentrating on the task becomes easier and returns to the work with steady attention.
activities.prompt: If the student continues without concentrating on the task, what will most likely happen?
options: The task will probably take longer and contain more mistakes.
The task will take less time but contain more mistakes.
The task will take longer but produce fewer mistakes.
The task will take less time and produce fewer mistakes.

why.The task will take less time but contain: Without focus, progress is likely to be slower.
why.The task will take longer but produce fe: Focus helps us reduce our mistakes.
why.The task will take less time and produce: The correct choice connects slower work with more mistakes.

activities.explanation: Focus helps us complete tasks faster and better.

activities.context: A student wants to finish a school task quickly and make fewer mistakes. The student finds it difficult to concentrate, so progress is slow. Before continuing, the student does simple yoga asanas, including Pranayama and Tree Pose. The student notices that concentrating on the task becomes easier and returns to the work with steady attention.
activities.prompt: If the student focuses during the task instead of working without attention, what should happen?
options: Learning should improve, and efficiency should increase.
Learning should improve, but efficiency should decrease.
Learning should decrease, but efficiency should increase.
Both learning and efficiency should decrease.

why.Learning should improve, but efficiency: Focus helps us increase our efficiency.
why.Learning should decrease, but efficiency: Improved learning does not mean efficiency will fall.
why.Both learning and efficiency should decr: Improved focus should not make learning worse.

activities.explanation: Focus helps us improve our learning.

activities.prompt: Explain how focus helps us improve our learning.
activities.answer: Focus helps us improve our learning because it helps us complete tasks faster and better. It also helps us reduce our mistakes and increase our efficiency. Together, these effects make learning more effective.
points: Focus helps tasks be completed faster.
Focus helps tasks be completed better.
Focus helps reduce mistakes.
Focus helps increase efficiency.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the Speaking and Listening activity, a speech table shows who is or are doing what action. Two girls are going to school, and a woman is typing on a computer. The example sentences describe both actions. Students use the given sentence structure to make their own sentences and describe the picture in English. They write at least seven sentences in their notebooks. The listening activity focuses on the missing l sound.
activities.prompt: After looking at the speech table and the example sentences, what should the students do next?
options: Create new sentences by following the shown pattern.
Copy only the headings from the speech table.
Make sentences without using an action word.
Describe the picture but ignore the given pattern.

why.Copy only the headings from the speech t: Copying headings does not practise making sentences.
why.Make sentences without using an action w: The speech sentences need an action word.
why.Describe the picture but ignore the give: The description should follow the given pattern.

activities.explanation: This follows the given sentence structure and makes new sentences.

activities.context: During the Speaking and Listening activity, a speech table shows who is or are doing what action. Two girls are going to school, and a woman is typing on a computer. The example sentences describe both actions. Students use the given sentence structure to make their own sentences and describe the picture in English. They write at least seven sentences in their notebooks. The listening activity focuses on the missing l sound.
activities.prompt: What is the best way for the students to practise listening for the missing l sound?
options: Read the given lines aloud.
Write the lines without reading them.
Study only the speech table.
Make sentences without listening.

Writing silently does not provide listening practice.
The table supports speaking, not the missing l sound activity.

activities.explanation: Reading aloud practises listening for the sound.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the speech table and the example sentences.
activities.answer: The speech table gives information about who is or are doing each action. The example sentences show how those actions are expressed using “is” or “are,” an action word, and “-ing.” So, the table guides what to describe, while the examples guide the sentence form.
points: The speech table identifies people and actions.
The example sentences show the actions in sentence form.
The sentences use “is” or “are.”
Each action word ends in “-ing.”
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Every school day, we begin our routine at an a.m. time. After one activity, we do another, and we are ready for the next thing by an a.m. time. Our mother helps us before we leave for school. School starts at an a.m. or p.m. time. We have some school periods before recess. At recess, we go to the playground and play many games together. School ends at a p.m. time.
activities.prompt: Which plan shows the correct order of the student's day?
options: Begin with the a.m. activities, receive mother's help, attend school, take recess, and finish when school ends.
Begin at recess, attend school, go home, do the activities, and then leave for school.
Receive mother's help, attend recess, return home, complete the activities, and then attend school.
Finish school, play at the playground, complete the activities, receive mother's help, and leave for school.

why.Begin at recess, attend school, go home,: This puts recess before school and home activities.
why.Receive mother's help, attend recess, re: This puts recess and home activities out of order.
why.Finish school, play at the playground, c: This puts the end of school before the morning activities.

activities.explanation: This follows the routine in the correct order.

activities.context: Every school day, we begin our routine at an a.m. time. After one activity, we do another, and we are ready for the next thing by an a.m. time. Our mother helps us before we leave for school. School starts at an a.m. or p.m. time. We have some school periods before recess. At recess, we go to the playground and play many games together. School ends at a p.m. time.
activities.prompt: Why should the teacher explain the meaning of a.m. and p.m.?
options: It helps the student understand the times written in the daily routine.
It helps the student decide which school games to play.
It explains how the student should help before leaving.
It shows which parts of the routine are work or play.

why.It helps the student decide which school: Games are not what these time labels mean.
why.It explains how the student should help: The labels do not explain the help given before leaving.
why.It shows which parts of the routine are: Work and play are shown in separate table columns.

activities.explanation: The explanation helps with understanding routine times.

activities.context: Every school day, we begin our routine at an a.m. time. After one activity, we do another, and we are ready for the next thing by an a.m. time. Our mother helps us before we leave for school. School starts at an a.m. or p.m. time. We have some school periods before recess. At recess, we go to the playground and play many games together. School ends at a p.m. time.
activities.prompt: What should the student do if school time arrives before mother has finished helping?
options: Wait for mother's help before leaving for school.
Go to the playground and play games before school.
Skip the first activities and leave immediately.
Start the school periods without taking recess.

why.Go to the playground and play games befo: The playground games happen during recess.
why.Skip the first activities and leave imme: The first activities should not be skipped.
why.Start the school periods without taking: Recess comes after some school periods.

activities.explanation: The student needs the help before leaving.

activities.prompt: How does the routine move from home to school?
activities.answer: The routine begins with one activity, followed by another, and the student is ready for the next thing by an a.m. time. Mother helps before the student leaves for school. At school, some periods come before recess. During recess, we go to the playground and play many games together before school ends.
points: The day begins with an a.m. activity.
Another activity follows, and the student is ready by an a.m. time.
Mother helps before the student leaves for school.
School periods come before recess and playground games.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a class display, one student showed a picture of thirty white horses on a red hill. As the picture was explained, the horses seemed to chomp, then stomp, and finally stand still. Another picture showed a tall lady wearing a white frock, with a yellow face and a red nose; when she stood taller, she seemed to grow shorter. The student also drew holiday activities and looked for pictures to add.
activities.prompt: If the student wants to show the horses' actions in the correct order, which sequence should be chosen?
options: First they use their mouths, next they stamp their feet, and at last they remain motionless.
First they stamp their feet, next they use their mouths, and at last they remain motionless.
First they remain motionless, next they use their mouths, and last they stamp their feet.
First they use their mouths, next they remain motionless, and last they stamp their feet.

why.First they stamp their feet, next they u: This swaps the first two actions.
why.First they remain motionless, next they: This puts standing still before the moving actions.
why.First they use their mouths, next they r: This places standing still between the two movements.

activities.explanation: This follows the stated order of the horses' actions.

activities.context: During a class display, one student showed a picture of thirty white horses on a red hill. As the picture was explained, the horses seemed to chomp, then stomp, and finally stand still. Another picture showed a tall lady wearing a white frock, with a yellow face and a red nose; when she stood taller, she seemed to grow shorter. The student also drew holiday activities and looked for pictures to add.
activities.prompt: The student has drawn holiday activities and wants suitable pictures for the display. What should the student do next according to the lesson?
options: Look through old newspapers or magazines and paste suitable pictures.
Draw the holiday activities again, but do not add any pictures.
Use the three riddle pictures instead of making holiday activity drawings.
Use blank paper instead of pictures or drawings for the holiday section.

why.Draw the holiday activities again, but d: The lesson allows pictures to be added, so redrawing is not necessary.
why.Use the three riddle pictures instead of: The riddle pictures cannot replace the required holiday activity drawings.
why.Use blank paper instead of pictures or d: The student should draw holiday activities or add pictures.

activities.explanation: This uses pictures from the sources allowed in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Explain how the first two riddles show a change.
activities.answer: The first riddle changes the horses by making them chomp and stomp before they stand still. The second riddle gives the lady an unusual height rule: the taller she stands, the shorter she seems to grow.
points: Mentions the horses chomping
Mentions the horses stomping
Mentions the horses finally standing still
Explains the taller-shorter rule
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

It raises our mistakes.

activities.prompt: We should work and play at the right times.

activities.explanation: Doing one thing well is a very good rule.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.

activities.prompt: Put the white horses' actions in order.

pairs: Shows who is or are doing each action

Use is or are with an action word and ing

chapters.title: The Old Stag
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the kind old stag; the stag falls ill; the friends become greedy; the animals make things right.

lessons.title: The Kind Old Stag

activities.prompt: What made the old stag so loved by everyone in the forest?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Kind Old Stag
activities.body: The old stag lived in a lush forest. Lush means full of green plants. He was famous for his kindness. Each day, he warmly greeted the animals and birds. The forest offered plenty of food. A hillock is raised land. He preferred staying there, where soft, green grass grew. He enjoyed the grass and came down each day to meet his friends. All the animals and birds loved him.
keyPoints: His home was a lush forest.
He greeted animals and birds warmly each day.
He enjoyed soft, green grass on a small hillock.
activities.explanation: The forest gave him food, friends, and a grassy hillock.

activities.prompt: Why do all the animals and birds love the old stag?
steps: The forest is lush, so the stag has plenty of food.
He greets animals and birds warmly, so he shows kindness.
He comes down to meet friends, so he cares for them.
So the animals and birds love him because he is kind.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Stag's Home
activities.prompt: Where did the old stag live?
options: A dry desert
A lush forest
A snowy mountain
A busy market
activities.explanation: He lived in a lush forest. The hillock was his favourite resting place.

activities.title: The Grassy Hillock
activities.prompt: The hillock was covered with soft, green ______.
activities.hint: This green plant covered the hillock.
activities.explanation: Soft, green grass covered the hillock where the stag liked staying.

activities.title: Food in the Forest
activities.prompt: What did the forest offer the old stag?
options: Plenty of food
Plenty of snow
Plenty of sand
Plenty of stones
activities.explanation: The forest offered plenty of food to the stag.

activities.title: Match the Details
activities.prompt: Match each part of the story with its detail.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a place or action with its matching detail.

activities.title: The Stag's Day
activities.prompt: Put the old stag's daily actions in order.
activities.explanation: He stayed on the hillock, enjoyed the grass, then came down to meet friends.

activities.title: Showing Kindness
activities.prompt: Which detail best shows that the old stag was kind?
options: He greeted the animals and birds warmly.
He stayed alone on the grassy hillock.
He kept all animals and birds away.
He welcomed only the loudest birds.
activities.explanation: Warmly greeting the animals and birds shows his kindness every day.

activities.prompt: The stag’s home is green and has plenty of food. What does “lush” mean here?
options: Full of green life.
Bare and dry ground.
Small and empty ground.
Hard and rocky ground.

This mistake reads lush as bare, dry land.
This mistake reads lush as small and empty.
This mistake reads lush as hard and rocky.

activities.explanation: Lush means full of rich, green growth.

activities.prompt: Each day, the stag greets the animals and birds warmly. How does he likely feel around them?
options: Happy and friendly.
Cross and unfriendly.
Afraid and alone.
Quiet and bored.

This mistake ignores his warm, kind greetings.
This mistake ignores his happy meetings with friends.
This mistake assumes silence means boredom.

activities.explanation: His warm greetings show that he feels happy and friendly.

activities.prompt: The stag is famous for his kindness and greets everyone warmly. Why do all the animals and birds love him?
options: His kindness makes him friendly.
He shares his soft green grass.
He keeps all the forest food.
He wants everyone far away.

This mistake thinks their love comes from sharing grass.
This mistake thinks their love comes from keeping food.
This mistake thinks his kind actions push others away.

activities.explanation: His famous kindness and warm greetings explain their love.

activities.prompt: The stag rests on the hillock but comes down to meet friends. What does this show?
options: He likes green grass and friends.
He likes grass but avoids friends.
He wants food and no friends.
He wants to leave the forest.

This mistake treats coming down as avoiding friends.
This mistake mistakes enjoying food for disliking friends.
This mistake treats meeting friends as wanting to leave.

activities.explanation: He enjoys the soft grass, but he also values his friends.

lessons.title: The Stag Falls Ill

activities.prompt: How could you show a sick friend that you care?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Stag and His Friends
activities.body: The stag became ill and struggled to reach the hillock, a small hill. He ate tender, soft grass and rested. He could not greet his friends. They worried when they learnt he was unwell and came to check on him. A deer asked how he was. The stag said he was too weak to meet everyone. The animals wished him a speedy recovery and left.
keyPoints: The stag became ill and rested.
His friends came to check on him.
They wished him a speedy recovery.
activities.explanation: This card explains the stag's illness and his friends' kind visit.

activities.prompt: How could the stag help himself after becoming ill, and why did his friends visit him?
steps: The stag was ill and struggled to the hillock, so healing mattered.
He ate tender grass because fresh, healthy food helps a sick animal.
He rested because proper rest also helps an ill animal heal.
His worried friends visited, so caring friends check on an ill friend.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the stag eat?
options: Dry leaves
Tender grass
Thick roots
Green fruit
activities.explanation: The stag ate tender grass and decided to rest for a while.

activities.prompt: The stag could go down the hillock to greet his friends.
activities.explanation: The stag was too unwell to go down and greet his friends.

activities.prompt: Fresh, healthy ______ and proper rest would help the stag get well.
activities.hint: Think of what the stag needs to eat.
activities.explanation: Fresh, healthy food and proper rest would help the stag get well.

activities.prompt: Match each action with its detail.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows what happened between the stag, the deer and his friends.

activities.prompt: Why did the worried friends come to the stag?
options: To meet a deer
To find a meal
To check on him
To climb up
activities.explanation: His friends worried when they learnt he was unwell, so they came to check on him.

activities.prompt: Put the main events in the order they happened.
items: He could not greet his friends.
His friends learnt he was unwell.
The friends came to check on him.
activities.explanation: The stag became ill and rested before his friends came to check on him.

activities.prompt: A deer feels ill. It eats tender grass. Then it rests for a while. What do these choices show?
options: He was trying to help himself get well.
He was trying to save his energy for friends.
He was trying to finish his daily work.
He was trying to keep his friends away.

why.He was trying to save his energy for fri: This mistake thinks resting was mainly for meeting friends.
This mistake treats resting as a way to finish work.
This mistake mistakes weakness for a wish to avoid friends.

activities.explanation: Eating fresh food and resting show that he tried to heal.

activities.prompt: You learn that a friend is unwell. You come to check on your friend. How do you likely feel?
options: You feel worried about your friend.
You feel excited about your friend.
You feel angry with your friend.
You feel bored by your friend.

This mistake treats a caring visit as happy news.
This mistake mixes illness with anger, although the visit shows concern.
This mistake thinks checking means having little interest.

activities.explanation: Coming to check after hearing the illness shows concern.

activities.prompt: You are ill. A deer asks how you are. You say you are too weak to meet everyone. Why do you say this?
options: Meeting everyone would use too much strength.
You are angry with the deer.
You want to frighten the deer.
You think the deer is unwell.

This mistake reads weakness as anger, but no anger is given.
This mistake thinks your answer was meant to scare the deer.
This mistake swaps who was unwell, but you were ill.

activities.explanation: Your weakness makes meeting everyone too hard.

activities.prompt: The stag became ill and had trouble reaching the hillock. What does “struggled” mean here?
options: He tried hard but had trouble.
He moved easily without effort.
He stayed still without trying.
He ate food and felt better.

This mistake treats struggle as easy movement, the opposite meaning.
This mistake thinks struggling means making no effort.
This mistake connects the word with eating, but it means trying with difficulty.

activities.explanation: The illness made reaching the hillock hard, and he still tried.

activities.prompt: Fresh, healthy food and proper rest would help the stag get well. What does “proper rest” mean here?
options: Enough rest to help him heal.
Rest for a very short time.
Rest without any healthy food.
Rest while doing extra work.

This mistake assumes proper rest must be brief, but the text gives no limit.
This mistake confuses food and rest, which are separate helpers.
This mistake confuses rest with more activity.

activities.explanation: The sentence says that proper rest helps the stag get well.

activities.prompt: A friend visits while you are ill. Your friend wishes you a speedy recovery, then leaves. What does the wish show?
options: Your friend hopes you will soon get well.
Your friend hopes you will stay ill longer.
Your friend hopes you will leave the hillock.
Your friend hopes you will stop taking rest.

why.Your friend hopes you will stay ill long: This mistake reverses the friendly wish for recovery.
why.Your friend hopes you will leave the hil: This mistake turns a recovery wish into a wish to leave.
why.Your friend hopes you will stop taking r: This mistake assumes rest was harmful, but it helps the stag heal.

activities.explanation: Wishing a speedy recovery means hoping that the illness ends quickly.

lessons.title: The Friends Become Greedy

activities.prompt: Why can wanting more food leave our friends with less?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: When Greed Makes Us Forget
activities.body: Before returning to the forest, the animals ate fresh green grass. The elephant called it tender and nice, while the giraffe loved its juicy leaves. News spread, and visiting animals feasted until little grass remained. The old stag grew weaker. His friends felt ashamed and realised their greed had made them forget him. They understood that he needed the remaining grass to eat and recover.
keyPoints: News about the tender grass brought many visiting animals.
The old stag was left with very little grass.
The friends realised that their greed had harmed their friend.
activities.explanation: This shows how greed can harm a friend.

activities.prompt: Why might a child grow weak after eating little at a picnic?
steps: The animals ate fresh grass because it was tender and nice.
News about the grass brought more animals to the stag.
Every visitor ate the grass, so very little remained for the stag.
Their greed left the stag without enough food, so he grew weaker.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Before the Return
activities.prompt: What did the animals do before returning to the forest?
options: They ate fresh green grass.
They left the forest at once.
They searched for the stag.
They hid beneath the trees.
activities.explanation: The animals ate fresh green grass before they returned to the forest.

activities.title: News About the Grass
activities.prompt: News soon spread about the ______ green grass.
activities.hint: The elephant said it was nice.
activities.explanation: News spread about the tender green grass.

activities.prompt: The elephant said that the grass was tender and nice.
activities.explanation: The elephant described the grass as tender and nice.

activities.title: The Visitors
activities.prompt: What did everyone who visited the stag do?
options: They ate the grass.
They sang together.
They found juicy leaves.
They left some grass.
activities.explanation: Everyone who visited the stag also ate the grass.

activities.title: What Happened Next?
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: The animals ate fresh green grass before returning to the forest.
News soon spread about the tender green grass.
Animals visited the stag and feasted on the grass.
Very little grass was left for the old stag.
The old stag began becoming weaker.
activities.explanation: The events move from eating and spreading news to the stag growing weaker.

activities.title: What Did the Friends Realise?
activities.prompt: What did the stag's friends finally understand?
options: They had eaten too many juicy leaves.
They wanted the stag to leave the forest.
They blamed the elephant for the news.
Their greed made them forget their friend.
activities.explanation: They realised that their greed made them forget about their friend.

activities.prompt: Greed made the animals forget their friend. At a snack, a child takes almost everything. The friend gets little. What kind of thinking does this show?
options: Greed, because the child wants more and forgets the friend.
Care, because the child wants more and forgets the friend.
Fear, because the child wants more and forgets the friend.
Pride, because the child wants more and forgets the friend.

why.Care, because the child wants more and f: This is wrong because care does not mean wanting more and forgetting.
why.Fear, because the child wants more and f: This is wrong because fear is not shown by wanting more food.
why.Pride, because the child wants more and: This is wrong because pride is not shown by wanting more food.

activities.explanation: This is right because the child wants more and forgets the friend.

activities.prompt: The elephant said the grass was tender and nice. At lunch, an apple feels soft and easy to bite. What does tender mean in the elephant's words?
options: Soft and nice to eat.
Hard and unpleasant to eat.
Old and not worth eating.
Dry and difficult to chew.

This is wrong because tender does not mean hard or unpleasant.
This is wrong because tender does not mean old or worthless.
This is wrong because tender does not mean dry or hard to chew.

activities.explanation: This is right because tender means soft and nice to eat.

activities.prompt: News spread about the tender green grass. At school, news spreads about a tasty snack. Why do the children come?
options: They come because they want to eat lots of snack.
They come because they want to help feed their friend.
They come because they want the snack left alone.
They come because they want their friend to leave.

why.They come because they want to help feed: This is wrong because helping is not why the animals visited.
why.They come because they want the snack le: This is wrong because leaving food alone is not what feasting means.
why.They come because they want their friend: This is wrong because the animals came for food, not to leave.

activities.explanation: This is right because the animals visited to feast on tender grass.

activities.prompt: Very little grass remained for the old stag, and he grew weaker. At a picnic, a friend gets very little food. What may happen?
options: The friend may become weaker because too little food remains.
The friend may become stronger because too little food remains.
The friend may find plenty of food after the picnic.
The friend may stay strong because very little food remains.

why.The friend may become stronger because t: This is wrong because too little food did not make the stag stronger.
why.The friend may find plenty of food after: This is wrong because plenty of grass was not left for the stag.
why.The friend may stay strong because very: This is wrong because the stag grew weaker, not stayed strong.

activities.explanation: This is right because the stag grew weaker with too little grass.

activities.prompt: Everyone who visited the stag also ate the grass. At a fruit table, a child visits. What must the child do?
options: The child must eat some of the shared fruit.
The child must leave all of the shared fruit.
The child must give the fruit to another child.
The child must take the fruit home without eating.

why.The child must leave all of the shared f: This is wrong because leaving the food does not match the fact.
why.The child must give the fruit to another: This is wrong because giving the food away is not stated.
why.The child must take the fruit home witho: This is wrong because taking food home is not the same as eating.

activities.explanation: This is right because every visitor ate the grass.

lessons.title: The Animals Make Things Right

activities.prompt: How did the animals help their sick friend feel better?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Caring for Nature
activities.body: When their friend was sick, the animals cared for him. Some brought fresh leaves, and it rained well that week. Soon, grass grew back on the hillock. The old stag found enough food and slowly recovered. The lesson teaches us that nature has enough for everybody, but we must use nature’s resources wisely.
keyPoints: Some animals brought fresh leaves for their sick friend.
Rain helped grass grow back on the hillock.
Nature has enough for everybody when its resources are used wisely.
activities.explanation: Caring for a friend and protecting nature can help things recover.

activities.prompt: How did caring for nature help the old stag recover?
steps: The old stag was ill, so some animals brought him fresh leaves.
It rained well, and they left the hillock undisturbed.
The grass grew back, so the old stag had enough food.
Thus, caring for nature wisely helped the old stag recover.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Kind Gift
activities.prompt: What did some animals bring for their sick friend?
options: fresh leaves
dry leaves
small stones
broken twigs
activities.explanation: The animals showed care by bringing fresh leaves for their sick friend.

activities.title: Grass Returns
activities.prompt: The grass soon grew back on the ______.
activities.hint: This was the place where the animals left the grass undisturbed.
activities.explanation: The grass grew back on the hillock because nobody disturbed it.

activities.title: What Happened Next?
activities.prompt: Match each event with what happened next.
pairs: They cared for their sick friend
It rained well during that week
The old stag had enough food
The old stag had enough food
He slowly recovered from his illness
activities.explanation: The caring actions, rain and new grass helped the old stag recover.

activities.title: Enough Food
activities.prompt: Why did the old stag have enough food once again?
options: Rain helped grass grow back.
Fresh leaves covered the ground.
Animals disturbed the hillock.
The old stag stopped eating.
activities.explanation: The grass grew back after the rain, so the old stag had enough food.

activities.title: The Recovery
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: It rained well during that week.
The grass soon grew back on the hillock.
The old stag had enough food once again.
The old stag slowly recovered from his illness.
activities.explanation: Rain came first, then grass grew and gave the old stag enough food.

activities.title: Use Nature Wisely
activities.prompt: What should people do with nature’s resources?
options: Use them wisely
Waste them daily
Take them carelessly
Leave them forever
activities.explanation: Nature has enough for everybody when people use its resources wisely.

activities.prompt: Some animals bring fresh leaves to their sick friend. Why do they do this?
options: They care about their sick friend.
They want their friend to go away.
They need the leaves for themselves.
They think the leaves can stop rain.

This wrongly treats their care as a wish to lose a friend.
This wrongly treats the leaves as food meant only for them.
This wrongly connects fresh leaves with stopping rain.

activities.explanation: This is right because they brought leaves to help their sick friend.

activities.prompt: Rain helps the grass grow back. The old stag has enough food. How does he likely feel?
options: He feels relieved and thankful.
He feels afraid and angry.
He feels bored and lonely.
He feels tired and upset.

This wrongly mistakes relief for anger.
This wrongly mistakes relief for loneliness.
This wrongly mistakes relief for tiredness.

activities.explanation: This is right because having enough food would ease his worry.

activities.prompt: Many animals need food from the same nature. What does the lesson advise people to do?
options: Use it fairly so every animal has enough.
Take as much as possible for themselves.
Keep all of it for one animal.
Stop all animals from getting food.

This wrongly takes more than the animals need.
This wrongly gives one animal all the resources.
This wrongly stops the animals from sharing.

activities.explanation: This is right because wise sharing lets everybody have enough.

activities.prompt: It rained well, and no one disturbed the hillock. Why did the grass soon grow back?
options: The rain and quiet helped it.
The animals took all the grass away.
The old stag stopped needing food.
The hillock was moved to another place.

This wrongly says taking the grass helped it grow back.
This wrongly says the old stag no longer needed food.
This wrongly thinks the hillock was moved.

activities.explanation: This is right because rain and no disturbance helped the grass return.

lessons.title: Descriptive Words and Adverbs

activities.prompt: How can you make a simple sentence feel vivid and show how something happens?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Descriptive Words and Adverbs
activities.body: Descriptive words give details about scenes, people and objects. An adverb can tell the way or manner of an action. Adverbs describe how something is done. “Warmly” is an adverb. The old stag slowly recovered from his illness, while the rabbit quickly ate the carrots.
keyPoints: Descriptive words give details.
Adverbs describe how something is done.
“Slowly” and “quickly” show manner.
activities.explanation: These examples show how descriptive words and adverbs make actions and scenes clearer.

activities.prompt: A child says “Thank you” warmly. Why does “warmly” make the sentence clearer?
steps: The sentence contains an action: saying “Thank you.”
“Warmly” is an adverb, so it describes that action.
An adverb can tell the way or manner of an action.
So, “warmly” shows how the child says “Thank you.”
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Describing a Forest
activities.prompt: Which pair of words describes a lush forest?
options: green and dense
delicate, young grass
cool resting place
nourishing and wholesome
activities.explanation: A lush forest is green and dense. This pair gives details about the forest.

activities.title: How Did the Rabbit Eat?
activities.prompt: The rabbit ______ ate the carrots.
activities.hint: This word tells how the rabbit ate.
activities.explanation: “Quickly” tells how the rabbit ate the carrots, so it is an adverb.

activities.title: What Descriptive Words Do
activities.prompt: Descriptive words give details about scenes, people and objects.
activities.explanation: Yes. Descriptive words add details to scenes, people and objects.

activities.title: Match Words with Meanings
activities.prompt: Match each thing with its description.
activities.explanation: Each description matches the meaning given in the lesson.

activities.title: What an Adverb Does
activities.prompt: What does an adverb describe?
options: how something is done
the colour of a forest
the age of a rabbit
the kind of food
activities.explanation: An adverb describes how something is done. It can tell the way or manner of an action.

activities.title: Speedy Recovery
activities.prompt: What does a speedy recovery mean?
options: quick healing
cool resting place
delicate young grass
green and dense
activities.explanation: A speedy recovery means quick healing. The other choices describe different things.

activities.prompt: Imagine a forest with green plants packed close together. Which words best describe it?
options: Lush and dense, because the plants fill the forest.
Tender and delicate, because the plants are young grass.
Shaded and cool, because the forest is a resting place.
Nourishing and wholesome, because the forest gives healthy food.

why.Tender and delicate, because the plants: This confuses young grass with a description of the whole forest.
why.Shaded and cool, because the forest is a: This confuses a resting place with a description of the forest.
why.Nourishing and wholesome, because the fo: This confuses healthy food with a description of the forest.

activities.explanation: A lush forest is green and dense, matching the crowded scene.

activities.prompt: Imagine young grass bending under a light touch. Which words best describe the grass?
options: Tender and delicate, because it is young grass.
Green and dense, because it fills a whole forest.
Shaded and cool, because it makes a resting place.
Nourishing and wholesome, because it is healthy food.

why.Green and dense, because it fills a whol: This mistakes young grass for a whole forest scene.
why.Shaded and cool, because it makes a rest: This mistakes grass for a shaded resting place.
why.Nourishing and wholesome, because it is: This mistakes grass for healthy food.

activities.explanation: Tender grass is delicate, young grass, which fits the light touch.

activities.prompt: Imagine a hot child choosing a shaded spot to sit. Why is that spot helpful?
options: It is cool and gives the child a place to rest.
It is nourishing because the child can eat healthy food there.
It makes the child’s recovery happen more quickly.
It shows the child that the forest is green and dense.

why.It is nourishing because the child can e: This thinks a shaded spot is healthy food.
why.It makes the child’s recovery happen mor: This confuses resting with quick healing.
why.It shows the child that the forest is gr: This confuses forest details with the purpose of shade.

activities.explanation: A shaded spot is a cool resting place.

activities.prompt: Imagine food that helps a child’s body stay strong. Which words best describe it?
options: Nourishing and wholesome, because it is healthy food.
Tender and delicate, because it is young grass.
Green and dense, because it comes from a forest.
Speedy, because the meal helps healing happen quickly.

why.Tender and delicate, because it is young: This mistakes healthy food for tender young grass.
why.Green and dense, because it comes from a: This mistakes healthy food for a forest scene.
why.Speedy, because the meal helps healing h: This mistakes healthy food for the speed of recovery.

activities.explanation: Healthy food is nourishing and wholesome.

activities.prompt: The old stag recovered from illness without much delay. Which word describes the recovery?
options: Speedy, because the healing happened very quickly.
Tender, because the healing was soft and gentle.
Shaded, because the stag recovered in a cool resting place.
Nourishing, because healthy food helped the healing.

why.Tender, because the healing was soft and: This applies tender, which describes young grass, to recovery.
why.Shaded, because the stag recovered in a: This confuses a shaded resting place with recovery.
why.Nourishing, because healthy food helped: This confuses nourishing food with the speed of recovery.

activities.explanation: A speedy recovery means quick healing.

lessons.title: Dialogues, Sharing and a Thank You Card

activities.prompt: How can sharing and a thoughtful card help someone feel better?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is the lesson about?
activities.body: Fasting means choosing not to eat. The monkey king is fasting. He asks all monkeys to fast too. The monkeys get no food till sunset. They learn fasting needs more self-control. The speaking activity imagines a large bowl of jalebis in the classroom. Friends enjoy sweets, but everyone keeps reaching for more. The card shows the stag and his friends. It shows how friends’ help made him feel better.
keyPoints: The monkey king asks every monkey to fast.
No food is available till sunset.
The card shows how his friends’ help made him feel better.
activities.explanation: The lesson links the monkey story, the speaking activity, and the card.

activities.prompt: You have collected food, but everyone must fast. How should you act?
steps: You know everyone must fast, so you choose not to eat.
You hold your collected food because holding it does no harm.
You wait because sunset will come soon.
So you show more self-control, because fasting needs it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The king’s request
activities.prompt: What does the monkey king ask all the monkeys to do?
options: Sing together
Fast with him
Run around
Plant trees
activities.explanation: The king is fasting and asks all the monkeys to fast too.

activities.title: What is the king doing?
activities.prompt: The monkey king is ______.
activities.hint: Choose not to eat for a time.
activities.explanation: The story says the monkey king is fasting. Fasting means choosing not to eat.

activities.title: Match each story part
activities.prompt: Match each part of the story to its detail.
activities.explanation: These details show the fasting, the speaking scene, and the card.

activities.title: Order the story
activities.prompt: Put the monkey story events in order.
items: He asks all the monkeys to fast too.
The monkeys get no food till sunset.
The monkeys peel their collected food.
activities.explanation: The story moves from fasting to peeling food and waiting for sunset.

activities.title: The tempting jalebis
activities.prompt: What happens because everyone loves the jalebis so much?
options: They stop enjoying the sweets
They leave the bowl untouched
They keep reaching for more
They share only one sweet
activities.explanation: Everyone loves the jalebis so much that they keep reaching for more.

activities.title: A lesson about self-control
activities.prompt: What do the monkeys learn about fasting?
options: It needs no self-control
It needs help from others
It needs more self-control
It needs less self-control
activities.explanation: The monkeys learn that fasting needs more self-control than they thought.

activities.prompt: The monkeys collected food before sunset. What must they learn to control?
options: Their wish to eat the food.
Their need to peel the food.
Their need to give food away.
Their need to find more food.

This confuses self-control with preparing food.
This confuses fasting with sharing food away.
This confuses fasting with finding more food.

activities.explanation: This is right because fasting needs self-control.

activities.prompt: Everyone must fast until sunset. Why might this be hard for them?
options: They have food, but cannot eat it.
They have food, but must give it.
They have food, but must peel it.
They have food, but must find more.

This confuses fasting with giving food away.
This confuses peeling food with controlling hunger.
This confuses fasting with getting more food.

activities.explanation: This is right because fasting asks for self-control.

activities.prompt: The monkeys want to eat their food. What does self-control mean here?
options: Stop themselves from eating the food.
Ask the monkey king for more.
Peel the food they collected.
Eat the food one by one.

This thinks self-control means asking for more.
This thinks self-control means preparing the food.
This thinks self-control means eating slowly.

activities.explanation: Self-control means stopping yourself from eating.

activities.prompt: Friends surround the stag in the picture. How does he likely feel?
options: He feels grateful for their help.
He feels worried about their help.
He feels lonely after their help.
He feels cross about their help.

This mistakes being surrounded by friends for worry.
This mistakes being surrounded by friends for loneliness.

activities.explanation: This is right because their help made the stag feel better.

lessons.sceneAlt: An alert stag stands in a green Indian forest at Kabini.
lessons.sceneCaption: An alert stag stands in a green forest at Kabini.

activities.context: The old stag lived in a lush forest, where plenty of food was available. He was famous for his kindness, and each day he warmly greeted the animals and birds around him. He preferred to stay on a small hillock covered with tender, soft, green grass, which he enjoyed. Every day, he came down to meet his friends. All the animals and birds loved him.
activities.prompt: The old stag is resting on his small hillock when his animal and bird friends arrive. What should he do next?
options: Come down and greet them warmly.
Stay on the hillock and wait for them to leave.
Greet only the animals and ignore the birds.
Enjoy the grass while the friends wait away from him.

why.Stay on the hillock and wait for them to: It continues his kind habit of welcoming everyone.
why.Greet only the animals and ignore the bi: He greeted both animals and birds each day.
why.Enjoy the grass while the friends wait a: Enjoying the grass should not make him ignore his friends.

activities.explanation: This follows his daily habit of meeting his friends.

activities.context: The old stag lived in a lush forest, where plenty of food was available. He was famous for his kindness, and each day he warmly greeted the animals and birds around him. He preferred to stay on a small hillock covered with tender, soft, green grass, which he enjoyed. Every day, he came down to meet his friends. All the animals and birds loved him.
activities.prompt: If the old stag stopped coming down from his hillock, what would most likely happen?
options: The animals and birds would have fewer chances to meet him and be greeted.
They would spend more time enjoying the tender grass on his hillock.
They would have to find food somewhere outside the lush forest.
They might love him less because he no longer met them.

why.They would spend more time enjoying the: They did not stop coming down to enjoy grass with him.
why.They would have to find food somewhere o: The forest still offered plenty of food.
why.They might love him less because he no l: Stopping one daily habit would not necessarily change their love.

activities.explanation: His daily visits gave them chances to meet him.

activities.prompt: Explain why the old stag preferred staying on the small hillock.
activities.answer: The old stag preferred the small hillock because it was covered with tender, soft, green grass, which he enjoyed. Although the forest offered plenty of food, he chose to stay on the hillock. This shows that he had a special place and kind of food he preferred.
points: The hillock had tender grass.
The grass was soft and green.
He enjoyed eating it.
He preferred it despite other available food.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The stag became ill and struggled to reach the hillock. Fresh, healthy food and proper rest would help him get well. He ate tender grass and rested for a while. He could not go down to greet his friends. When his friends learnt he was unwell, they worried and came to check on him. A deer asked how he was. The stag said that he was too weak to meet everyone. The animals wished him a speedy recovery and left.
activities.prompt: What should the stag do next to help himself get well?
options: Choose fresh, healthy food and give himself proper rest.
Try to greet all his friends before resting.
Eat only tender grass and give up resting.
Keep walking down the hillock even though he feels weak.

why.Try to greet all his friends before rest: He was too weak to meet everyone, so he should rest before trying to greet them.
why.Eat only tender grass and give up restin: He needed proper rest as well as tender grass to get well.
why.Keep walking down the hillock even thoug: He was struggling and weak, so continuing to walk did not follow the advice to rest.

activities.explanation: This follows the advice that fresh, healthy food and proper rest help him get well.

activities.context: The stag became ill and struggled to reach the hillock. Fresh, healthy food and proper rest would help him get well. He ate tender grass and rested for a while. He could not go down to greet his friends. When his friends learnt he was unwell, they worried and came to check on him. A deer asked how he was. The stag said that he was too weak to meet everyone. The animals wished him a speedy recovery and left.
activities.prompt: If the stag had not become ill, how would his friends' visit be different?
options: They might not have needed to check whether he was unwell.
They would certainly have come only to wish him a recovery.
The deer would certainly have asked whether he felt weak.
They would have asked him to stay on the hillock and rest.

why.They would certainly have come only to w: A wish for recovery would not be needed if the stag had not been unwell.
why.The deer would certainly have asked whet: The deer's question about his weakness was connected with his illness.
why.They would have asked him to stay on the: If he had not been ill, there would be no reason to ask him to rest on the hillock because of illness.

activities.explanation: Without his illness, the friends would not have needed to check on his health.

activities.prompt: Why did the stag rest after eating, and why could he not greet his friends?
activities.answer: Fresh, healthy food and proper rest would help the stag get well, so he ate tender grass and rested. He was too weak to go down the hillock and meet his friends. When his friends learnt that he was unwell, they worried and came to check on him.
points: Fresh, healthy food and proper rest help recovery.
The stag ate tender grass and rested.
He was too weak to go down the hillock.
His worried friends came to check on him.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Before the forest animals returned, they had eaten the fresh green grass. The elephant said it was tender and nice, while the giraffe said she had never eaten such juicy leaves. News spread, and animals visiting the stag feasted on the grass. Soon, very little was left for the old stag. As days passed, he grew weaker. His friends felt ashamed because their greed had made them forget about him.
activities.prompt: If the friends want to help the old stag recover, what should they do?
options: Leave the remaining grass for the old stag to eat.
Eat all the grass so that no other animal can have it.
Invite more animals to visit the stag.
Keep the grass away from the old stag.

why.Eat all the grass so that no other anima: Eating all the grass would leave him with even less.
More visitors would eat the little grass that remained.
Keeping it away would prevent him from eating it.

activities.explanation: Leaving grass gives the stag what he needs to eat and recover.

activities.context: Before the forest animals returned, they had eaten the fresh green grass. The elephant said it was tender and nice, while the giraffe said she had never eaten such juicy leaves. News spread, and animals visiting the stag feasted on the grass. Soon, very little was left for the old stag. As days passed, he grew weaker. His friends felt ashamed because their greed had made them forget about him.
activities.prompt: What would likely have happened if the news about the tender grass had not spread?
options: Fewer animals would visit, so more grass might remain for the stag.
More animals would visit, and they would eat all the grass.
The animals would become weaker instead of the stag.
The friends would not feel ashamed of their greed.

why.More animals would visit, and they would: Spreading the news caused animals to visit and feast.
why.The animals would become weaker instead: The stag was weakened because visitors ate the grass.
why.The friends would not feel ashamed of th: His friends' shame came from understanding their greed.

activities.explanation: Without the news, there would probably have been fewer visitors.

activities.prompt: Explain why the friends felt ashamed of their actions.
activities.answer: The friends felt ashamed because their greed had made them forget about their friend. By eating the tender grass, they left the old stag with very little to eat. As the days passed, he became weaker, and they understood that their own actions had harmed him.
points: They had allowed greed to make them forget their friend.
Their eating left very little grass for the stag.
The stag became weaker as the days passed.
They realised that their actions harmed him.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A hillock was disturbed, and a sick old stag could not find enough food. Some animals decided not to disturb it again. Others brought fresh leaves for their sick friend. During that week, it rained well, so the grass soon grew back. The old stag slowly recovered and had enough food once again. The case shows that nature can provide for everyone when people use its resources wisely.
activities.prompt: If it had not rained well during that week, what would probably have happened to the old stag?
options: The stag would probably have had less food, so his recovery could be slower.
The stag would still have recovered at the same speed because the leaves alone solved the problem.
The grass would have grown back faster because the hillock had more room.
The stag would have had plenty of food because nature never runs out for anyone.

why.The stag would still have recovered at t: The leaves helped, but they did not replace the need for grass.
why.The grass would have grown back faster b: Disturbing the hillock would not help its grass grow faster.
why.The stag would have had plenty of food b: Nature has enough only when its resources are used wisely.

activities.explanation: Without the rain, the grass might not have grown back so quickly.

activities.context: A hillock was disturbed, and a sick old stag could not find enough food. Some animals decided not to disturb it again. Others brought fresh leaves for their sick friend. During that week, it rained well, so the grass soon grew back. The old stag slowly recovered and had enough food once again. The case shows that nature can provide for everyone when people use its resources wisely.
activities.prompt: What should people do when they use nature’s resources?
options: They should use the resources wisely and avoid disturbing places that nature is restoring.
They should take everything they can because nature will always replace it.
They should keep disturbing the hillock because its grass grows back quickly.
They should collect all the fresh leaves so that no other animal can use them.

why.They should take everything they can bec: Taking everything can prevent other living things from receiving what they need.
why.They should keep disturbing the hillock: Constant disturbance can harm the returning grass.
why.They should collect all the fresh leaves: Taking all the leaves would not help the animals share nature’s resources.

activities.explanation: Wise use protects nature and helps it recover.

activities.prompt: Explain why the grass grew back on the hillock.
activities.answer: The grass grew back because it rained well during that week. The animals also decided not to disturb the hillock again. This gave the grass a chance to return. As the grass grew back, the old stag slowly recovered from his illness and had enough food once again.
points: It rained well during that week.
The animals left the hillock undisturbed.
The grass had a chance to grow back.
The old stag recovered and had enough food.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A lush forest is green and dense, and tender grass is delicate, young grass. A shaded spot is a cool resting place for an old stag after his illness. A speedy recovery means quick healing. The rabbit quickly ate the carrots, while the old stag slowly recovered from his illness. These descriptive details show the scene and how the actions happened.
activities.prompt: If the rabbit changed its quick eating to slower eating, which description would correctly show the manner of the action?
options: at a quick pace
at a slow pace
with a green appearance
as nourishing and wholesome food

why.at a quick pace: This means quick, but the action changed to slower.
why.with a green appearance: Green describes appearance, not the manner of eating.
why.as nourishing and wholesome food: Nourishing and wholesome describe food, not an action.

activities.explanation: This matches the slower manner of the changed action.

activities.context: A lush forest is green and dense, and tender grass is delicate, young grass. A shaded spot is a cool resting place for an old stag after his illness. A speedy recovery means quick healing. The rabbit quickly ate the carrots, while the old stag slowly recovered from his illness. These descriptive details show the scene and how the actions happened.
activities.prompt: In the case, what does the word “slowly” tell us about the stag’s recovery?
options: It shows the manner of the recovery.
It shows the age of the stag.
It shows the place of the recovery.
It shows the purpose of the recovery.

Age is not what this word describes.
Place is not what this word describes.
Purpose is not what this word describes.

activities.explanation: Slowly describes how the recovery happened.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between descriptive words and adverbs?
activities.answer: Descriptive words give details about scenes, people, and objects. Adverbs describe how an action is done. “Slowly” shows how the stag recovered, and “quickly” shows how the rabbit ate. “Warmly” is also an adverb because it tells the way or manner of an action.
points: Descriptive words give details.
Adverbs describe how actions are done.
“Slowly” describes the stag’s recovery.
“Warmly” is an adverb.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The monkey king decides to fast and asks all the monkeys to fast too. There is no food for them until sunset, although each monkey has collected some. They are told that keeping hold of the food will do them no harm. As they peel what they collected, they discover that fasting needs more self-control than they expected. The lesson then imagines friends enjoying jalebis from a large bowl, one by one, but everyone keeps reaching for more.
activities.prompt: What should a monkey do when holding collected food before sunset?
options: Keep waiting and leave the collected food uneaten.
Eat it now because the group has not reached sunset.
Give it to another monkey before sunset.
Peel it again and offer the pieces to the group.

why.Eat it now because the group has not rea: Eating early would break the group’s fast.
Giving away food would not help the monkey follow the request.
why.Peel it again and offer the pieces to th: Peeling and sharing it would still mean eating before sunset.

activities.explanation: This follows the king’s request to fast until sunset.

activities.context: The monkey king decides to fast and asks all the monkeys to fast too. There is no food for them until sunset, although each monkey has collected some. They are told that keeping hold of the food will do them no harm. As they peel what they collected, they discover that fasting needs more self-control than they expected. The lesson then imagines friends enjoying jalebis from a large bowl, one by one, but everyone keeps reaching for more.
activities.prompt: If the friends want to enjoy the jalebis without losing self-control, what should they do?
options: Take one sweet at a time and pause before reaching again.
Pass the bowl around without taking any sweets.
Save every sweet for after the activity.
Eat only the largest pieces of jalebi.

why.Pass the bowl around without taking any: Avoiding all the sweets would not include enjoying them one by one.
Waiting until after the activity would not explain enjoying them as the scene imagines.
Choosing only large pieces is not suggested by the situation.

activities.explanation: This allows them to enjoy the sweets one by one while exercising self-control.

activities.prompt: Explain why the monkeys need self-control even though they have collected food.
activities.answer: The monkeys have food, but the monkey king has asked everyone to fast. They must control the wish to eat and wait until sunset. Peeling the food they collected does not remove the temptation, so fasting takes more self-control than they first expected.
points: The monkeys have collected food.
The king asks everyone to fast.
They must wait until sunset.
Having food nearby makes self-control necessary.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Old Stag

activities.prompt: Where did the old stag prefer to stay?
options: On a small hillock
Inside a deep cave
Beside a noisy river
Under a rocky ledge
activities.explanation: He enjoyed the tender grass on the small hillock.

activities.prompt: Each day, the stag warmly greeted the animals and birds around him.
activities.explanation: The old stag greeted the animals and birds each day.

activities.prompt: The stag said that he was too ______ to meet everyone.
activities.hint: Use a word from the stag’s reply.
activities.explanation: His illness made him too weak to meet his friends.

activities.prompt: Match each animal with its words or action.
pairs: Called the grass tender and nice
Had never eaten such juicy leaves
activities.explanation: Each pair shows words or actions from the chapter.

activities.prompt: Why did the stag’s friends feel ashamed?
options: Their greed made them forget their friend.
Their kindness made them forget their friend.
Their hurry made them forget their friend.
Their anger made them forget their friend.
activities.explanation: Their greed made them forget the stag. They saw that little grass remained for him.

activities.prompt: Put the old stag’s recovery events in order.
items: The stag became ill and struggled to reach the hillock.
He ate the tender grass and decided to rest.
The grass soon grew back on the hillock.
The old stag had enough food once again.
The old stag slowly recovered from his illness.
activities.explanation: The order moves from illness and rest to food returning and recovery.

activities.prompt: People must use nature’s resources wisely.
activities.explanation: The lesson says nature has enough for everybody. Resources must be used wisely.

activities.prompt: Which sentence contains an adverb?
options: The hillock had soft green grass.
The forest was lush and dense.
The old stag slowly recovered.
The elephant said the grass was nice.
activities.explanation: “Slowly” is an adverb. It tells how the stag recovered.

activities.prompt: The monkeys fast, and the speaking scene has friends enjoying jalebis.
activities.explanation: The monkey king asks for fasting. The imagined friends enjoy jalebis one by one.

activities.prompt: Match each thank-you card part with its detail.
pairs: The stag surrounded by his friends
His friends’ help made him feel better
activities.explanation: The card is from the stag. It shows his friends and their helpful care.
