chapters.title: Let Us Read Braille
chapters.summary: In this chapter: louis braille’s childhood; how braille works; speaking, listening and writing braille; accidents and the past continuous.

lessons.title: Louis Braille’s Childhood

activities.prompt: What problem was young Louis Braille trying to solve?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Louis’s Early Life
activities.body: Louis Braille was a little boy in France long ago. His father was a blacksmith. A sharp tool pierced Louis’s eye. Within a few days, Louis became blind in that eye. His other eye was also affected, and he became totally blind. At ten, Louis joined the Royal Institute for Young Blind Persons in Paris. There, he learnt letters using wood, cloth or pins arranged in pincushions.
keyPoints: Louis’s father was a blacksmith.
A sharp tool pierced Louis’s eye.
His other eye was affected, and he became totally blind.
activities.explanation: These events shaped Louis Braille’s childhood.

activities.prompt: How can someone read raised dots and dashes without seeing them?
steps: Night Writing used raised dots and dashes because soldiers could read them with their fingers.
Touch works because the raised marks can be felt.
Night Writing was too difficult, so it was not a success.
Louis Braille became interested and simplified it, making the raised-dot system easier to use.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Night Writing
activities.body: Night Writing was invented by Captain Charles Barbier de la Serre. It used raised dots and dashes. Soldiers could read these marks with their fingers. It was too difficult, so it was not a success. Louis Braille became interested in Night Writing. He simplified it. At the institute, he had learnt letters using wood, cloth or pins arranged in pincushions.
keyPoints: Captain Charles Barbier de la Serre invented Night Writing.
Soldiers read raised dots and dashes with their fingers.
Louis Braille became interested and simplified Night Writing.
activities.explanation: Night Writing gave Louis Braille an idea that he simplified.

activities.prompt: What was Louis Braille’s father?
options: blacksmith
soldier
teacher
farmer
activities.explanation: Louis’s father worked as a blacksmith.

activities.prompt: Louis Braille was a little boy in France long ago.
activities.explanation: Louis lived in France during his childhood.

activities.prompt: Louis Braille was ______ years old in 1819.
activities.hint: Think about his age at the institute.
activities.explanation: Louis was ten years old in 1819.

activities.prompt: How could soldiers read Night Writing?
options: by feeling raised dots and dashes
by watching bright lights every night
by hearing spoken words outside
by following letters on paper
activities.explanation: Soldiers read the raised dots and dashes with their fingers.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the story to its matching detail.
pairs: Captain Charles Barbier de la Serre
activities.explanation: Each detail connects with the correct person or reading system.

activities.prompt: Put these events from Louis Braille’s childhood in order.
items: A sharp tool pierced his eye.
He became blind in one eye.
His other eye was also affected.
At ten, he joined the Royal Institute for Young Blind Persons in Paris.
activities.explanation: These events describe Louis’s childhood from the injury to his institute.

activities.prompt: Your class tries raised-dot messages. Many people give up. Why might Louis Braille want to simplify them?
options: He wants to make the raised-dot system easier to use.
He wants to make the raised-dot system harder to use.
He wants to remove every dot and every dash.
He wants only soldiers to learn the raised-dot system.

why.He wants to make the raised-dot system h: This mistakes simplifying for making a system more difficult.
why.He wants to remove every dot and every d: This mistakes simplifying for removing the raised marks.
why.He wants only soldiers to learn the rais: This mistakes simplifying for keeping a system for soldiers only.

activities.explanation: This matches Louis’s decision to simplify Night Writing.

activities.prompt: Soldiers cannot easily use Night Writing. How might Louis feel about it?
options: Interested, because he saw a way to simplify it.
Confused, because he thought soldiers never tried it.
Afraid, because he thought the raised marks hurt.
Proud, because he thought his father invented it.

why.Confused, because he thought soldiers ne: This confuses not succeeding with nobody having tried.
why.Afraid, because he thought the raised ma: This wrongly connects raised marks with pain.
why.Proud, because he thought his father inv: This wrongly links Night Writing to his blacksmith father.

activities.explanation: His interest in Night Writing supports this feeling and his later work.

activities.prompt: At school, wood and pins form letters. How can Louis learn them?
options: He can feel each letter and learn its shape.
He can see each letter and learn its colour.
He can hear each letter and learn its sound.
He can smell each letter and learn its smell.

why.He can see each letter and learn its col: This wrongly assumes that Louis could still see the letters.
why.He can hear each letter and learn its so: This confuses listening for sounds with learning letter shapes by touch.
why.He can smell each letter and learn its s: This wrongly connects learning letters with the sense of smell.

activities.explanation: He was blind, so he could learn the shapes by touching them.

activities.prompt: By 1819, ten-year-old Louis is totally blind. What learning would he need?
options: He needs to learn letters by touching raised shapes.
He needs to learn letters by looking at print.
He needs to learn letters by listening closely.
He needs to learn letters by watching tools.

why.He needs to learn letters by looking at: This wrongly assumes that he could still learn letters by sight.
why.He needs to learn letters by listening c: This confuses listening for words with learning letter shapes by touch.
why.He needs to learn letters by watching to: This wrongly connects his learning with blacksmith tools.

activities.explanation: He learned letters through touch, so raised shapes fitted his blindness.

lessons.title: How Braille Works

activities.prompt: How do tiny dots help someone read a whole book?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Braille Works
activities.body: Braille is a method of reading through touch. Each English letter has a Braille symbol. Braille letters need more space and cannot be written too close together. A Braille book is thicker than a printed book. Louis Braille gave the world this alphabet. People with sight can also learn Braille and write poems and stories in it. A blind person taught the world to see.
keyPoints: Braille is read through touch.
Each English letter has one Braille symbol.
People with sight can also learn Braille.
activities.explanation: Braille turns letters into symbols that can be read by touch.

activities.prompt: A child wants to read words without seeing them. How can touch make reading possible?
steps: Braille is read through touch, so raised marks can be read by touch.
Each English letter has one Braille symbol, so the marks can show alphabet letters.
Braille letters cannot be written too close together, so they need space around them.
Therefore, Braille books use more space and are thicker than regular printed books.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How is Braille read?
options: Through touch
Through sight
Through smell
Through movement
activities.explanation: Braille is a method of reading through touch.

activities.prompt: Braille is only for people with blindness.
activities.explanation: Braille can also be learned and used by people with sight.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with its Braille fact.
activities.explanation: Each clue matches a fact about Braille and its books.

activities.prompt: Who gave the world the Braille alphabet?
options: Louis Braille
A sighted reader
A blind writer
A printed book
activities.explanation: Louis Braille gave the world the Braille alphabet.

activities.prompt: Why is a Braille book thicker than a printed book?
options: Braille needs more space.
Braille letters stay close.
Printed books need more space.
Braille uses less space.
activities.explanation: Braille needs more space, and its letters cannot be written too close together.

activities.prompt: A sighted child writes a poem in Braille. What can we infer about Braille?
options: It can be used by people with sight.
It is only useful for reading poems.
It makes every book thicker than paper.
It cannot be used by people with blindness.

This mistake limits Braille to one kind of reading.
This mistake confuses using Braille with making books thicker.
why.It cannot be used by people with blindne: This mistake says Braille excludes blind people.

activities.explanation: This is right because people with sight can learn and use Braille.

activities.prompt: A book has many Braille pages. It is thicker than a printed book. Why?
options: Braille needs more space than ordinary writing.
Braille pages have fewer words than printed pages.
Braille letters can be written very close together.
Braille removes all spaces between its letters.

why.Braille pages have fewer words than prin: This mistake links thickness to fewer words.
why.Braille letters can be written very clos: This mistake says Braille letters can crowd together.
why.Braille removes all spaces between its l: This mistake says Braille has no spaces.

activities.explanation: This is right because Braille requires more space than ordinary writing.

activities.prompt: A reader touches raised symbols in order and understands a sentence. How are the symbols working?
options: They stand for English alphabet letters.
They stand for pictures of the objects.
They stand for sounds with no letters.
They stand for blank spaces between words.

This mistake confuses symbols with pictures.
This mistake confuses alphabet symbols with sounds.
why.They stand for blank spaces between word: This mistake confuses letter symbols with spaces.

activities.explanation: This is right because Braille symbols represent English alphabet letters.

lessons.sceneCaption: A blind student reads a Braille book at the Palestinian University of Bir Zeit.

lessons.title: Speaking, Listening and Writing Braille

activities.prompt: What secrets can your fingers discover when you cannot see?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How can you use words and Braille?
activities.body: Close your eyes, pick an object, and keep it back. Describe its shape, then add two more lines. Complete sentences and share them with the class. Listen as your teacher reads words. Give stress to ‘spl’, and repeat each word three or four times. Learners need time to learn the sound. Use the Braille alphabet. Paste bindis to make Braille words. You can write your own name in Braille.
keyPoints: Describe an object by its shape.
Listen for stress on ‘spl’ and repeat words.
Make Braille words with bindis.
activities.explanation: This lesson joins speaking, listening, and writing in clear steps.

activities.prompt: How can I describe an object without showing it to the class?
steps: Close your eyes because the class must not see the object.
Keep it back and describe its shape because shape gives the description.
Add two more lines because more details help the class understand.
Complete and share the sentences so the class hears the full description.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Add More Description
activities.prompt: Add ______ more lines to describe the object.
activities.hint: Think about the number of extra lines.
activities.explanation: The lesson asks you to add two more lines after describing the object.

activities.title: Repeat the Word
activities.prompt: Each word should be repeated only once.
activities.explanation: Each word should be repeated three or four times, not only once.

activities.title: Match the Lesson Parts
activities.prompt: Match each item with its partner from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a relationship described in the lesson. Check the listening and Braille pairs.

activities.title: Describe the Object
activities.prompt: Put the speaking steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: First follow the object activity. Then describe the shape and add two more lines.

activities.title: Make Braille Words
activities.prompt: How can you make Braille words?
options: Paste bindis
Say the words
Draw its shape
Share sentences
activities.explanation: Bindis can be pasted to make Braille words. This is the material used for writing them.

activities.prompt: A child closes their eyes and keeps an object back. Why?
options: To test how well classmates describe its shape
To find the object that someone has hidden
To show classmates the object's exact colour
To make the object disappear from the class

why.To find the object that someone has hidd: This mistakes the activity for finding a hidden object.
why.To show classmates the object's exact co: This confuses shape description with showing its colour.
why.To make the object disappear from the cl: This assumes keeping it back makes it disappear.

activities.explanation: Keeping it back lets classmates describe its shape.

activities.prompt: A child says, ‘It has a round shape.’ What should happen next?
options: Add two more lines about the object.
Choose another object for the class.
Show the object to everyone now.
Repeat the object's shape only once.

The child must keep describing the same object.
Showing it would stop the class from using words.
Repeating the shape adds no new describing lines.

activities.explanation: Two more lines add details after the shape description.

activities.prompt: A learner repeats the teacher's words three or four times. Why?
options: To become familiar with each word's sound.
To check whether the teacher can hear them.
To make the listening activity end sooner.
To stop the class from listening closely.

why.To check whether the teacher can hear th: Repetition is for learning sounds, not testing the teacher.
why.To make the listening activity end soone: Repeating does not mean trying to end the activity.
why.To stop the class from listening closely: The learner needs the class to listen closely.

activities.explanation: Repeating gives the learner time to know each sound.

activities.prompt: A learner writes their name in Braille. How might they feel?
options: Proud because they can write their name.
Worried because nobody can read their name.
Angry because the word needs more stress.
Unsure because Braille cannot show letters.

why.Worried because nobody can read their na: Writing their name does not mean it must stay hidden.
why.Angry because the word needs more stress: Braille writing does not involve spoken word stress.
why.Unsure because Braille cannot show lette: Braille is an alphabet, so it can show letters.

activities.explanation: A child can write their own name in Braille.

lessons.title: Accidents and the Past Continuous

activities.prompt: What were you doing when the accident happened?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Accidents and actions in the past
activities.body: Accidents can harm people, so precautions should be taken to protect eyes from harm. Louis Braille lost his eyesight in an accident. A newspaper reported this accident some time ago. The past continuous describes actions that started in the past and continued for some time. Use “was” for one subject and “were” for more than one.
keyPoints: Precautions protect eyes from harm.
Use was with one subject and were with more than one.
Past continuous actions started in the past and continued for some time.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand accidents and the past continuous.

activities.prompt: The students were writing in their notebooks. Why does this use 'were'?
steps: The students were writing in their notebooks.
Past continuous actions started earlier and continued for some time.
The word 'writing' ends in '-ing', so it needs 'was' or 'were'.
More than one student was writing, so 'were' is correct.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Louis Braille
activities.prompt: What happened to Louis Braille?
options: Lost his eyesight
Was writing in a notebook
Was lighting firecrackers
Was reading a newspaper
activities.explanation: Louis Braille lost his eyesight in an accident. This accident is described in the lesson.

activities.title: An accident
activities.prompt: Louis Braille ______ his eyesight in an accident.
activities.hint: Think about what happened in the accident.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that Louis Braille lost his eyesight in an accident.

activities.title: Protecting your eyes
activities.prompt: Precautions should be taken to protect eyes from harm.
activities.explanation: Yes. Precautions help protect eyes from harm.

activities.title: One student
activities.prompt: The student ______ writing in his notebook.
activities.hint: Use the helping word for one person.
activities.explanation: Use “was” with an action word ending in “ing” for one student.

activities.title: More than one student
activities.prompt: The students ______ writing in their notebooks.
activities.hint: Use the helping word for more than one person.
activities.explanation: Use “were” with an action word ending in “ing” for more than one student.

activities.title: Change an action into the past
activities.prompt: What does the exercise ask learners to do?
options: Match actions with people
Change present actions into the past
Find actions happening now
Write actions in a longer form
activities.explanation: The exercise asks learners to change present actions into the past.

activities.prompt: A child lost one eye while lighting firecrackers. How might that child feel?
options: Sad and afraid of another eye injury.
Happy and excited about the firecrackers.
Angry and sure that the eye is safe.
Bored and tired of hearing the news.

why.Happy and excited about the firecrackers: It mistakes a serious accident for a happy event.
It wrongly assumes that the eye is safe.
It ignores the serious harm in the accident.

activities.explanation: Loss of one eye can make a child sad and afraid.

activities.prompt: One child is sleeping now. How should this action be put in the past?
options: The child was sleeping.
The child were sleeping.
The children was sleeping.
The children were sleeping.

This uses 'were' with only one child.
This uses 'was' with the plural subject 'children'.
It changes one child into more than one child.

activities.explanation: 'Was' agrees with the one child, so it is correct.

activities.prompt: More than one dog is barking now. How should this action be put in the past?
options: The dogs were barking.
The dogs was barking.
The dog were barking.
The dog was barking.

'Was' does not agree with the plural 'dogs'.
'Were' needs more than one dog, not this one.
'Was' needs one dog, not these two.

activities.explanation: 'Were' agrees with more than one dog, so it is correct.

activities.prompt: The dogs were barking for some time. What does this tell us about the barking?
options: It began earlier and continued for some time.
It began later and ended at once.
It will only begin again in the future.
It was not happening during that time.

This reverses when the action began and how long it lasted.
This treats an action that already began as only future.
This denies that the barking was happening during that time.

activities.explanation: Past continuous started earlier and continued for some time.

activities.prompt: A newspaper reported Louis Braille's accident some time ago. When did the accident happen?
options: Before the newspaper made its report.
After the newspaper made its report.
At the same time as the report.
After another newspaper reported it again.

This reverses the order of the accident and the report.
This assumes the accident and report happened together.
why.After another newspaper reported it agai: This invents another report that the fact does not give.

activities.explanation: Reporting an accident means that the accident happened first.

activities.prompt: A child lost one eye while lighting firecrackers. A newspaper reported it. What should be done?
options: Take precautions to protect eyes from harm.
Take no precautions to protect eyes from harm.
Wait for another accident before taking precautions.
Read the newspaper report and take no action.

why.Take no precautions to protect eyes from: This wrongly assumes that eyes need no protection after harm.
why.Wait for another accident before taking: This waits for another accident instead of preventing harm.
why.Read the newspaper report and take no ac: This mistakes reading about an accident for preventing harm.

activities.explanation: The eye was harmed, so precautions should protect eyes.

lessons.title: Tarandeep’s Clothesline Story

activities.prompt: What wonderful surprise did Tarandeep’s animal friends give her?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Tarandeep’s Clothesline Story
activities.body: Tarandeep told her friend something interesting yesterday. Her friends were the squirrels and sparrows. Clothes dried on a clothesline when a strong wind began. Grandmother returned with pegs and saw the squirrels and sparrows on the clothes. They stayed there to stop the clothes falling. Grandmother put the pegs on the clothes. Tarandeep moved her hands with joy and set down water for her friends. The actions began in the past and continued for some time.
keyPoints: Tarandeep’s friends helped the clothes.
Grandmother used the clothes pegs.
Tarandeep set down water for her friends.
activities.explanation: The birds and squirrels worked together to save the clothes.

activities.prompt: Why did Tarandeep give her animal friends water after the windy day?
steps: The strong wind began while Grandmother was away, so the clothes needed help.
The sparrows and squirrels stayed on the clothes to prevent them from falling.
Grandmother returned and put on the pegs, so the clothes were held safely.
Tarandeep set down water because she cared for her helpful animal friends.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where were the clothes put out to dry?
options: In a bowl
On a clothesline
On a branch
In Grandmother’s hands
activities.explanation: The clothes were put out to dry on a clothesline.

activities.prompt: Grandmother returned with the clothes ______.
activities.hint: She used these to hold the clothes.
activities.explanation: Grandmother returned with the clothes pegs.

activities.prompt: Tarandeep’s friends were the squirrels and sparrows.
activities.explanation: Yes, the squirrels and sparrows were Tarandeep’s friends.

activities.prompt: What did Grandmother put on the clothes?
options: The sparrows
The squirrels
A bowl of water
The clothes pegs
activities.explanation: Grandmother put the clothes pegs on the clothes.

activities.prompt: Put the story events in order.
items: Put the clothes on the clothesline
Grandmother puts the pegs on the clothes
activities.explanation: The clothes were on the line before the wind began. Grandmother then returned and used the pegs.

activities.prompt: What did Tarandeep set down for her friends?
options: A bowl of water
The clothes pegs
A strong wind
A clothesline
activities.explanation: Tarandeep set down a bowl of water for her friends.

activities.prompt: Tarandeep moved her hands with joy. How did she feel?
options: She felt very happy.
She felt quite worried.
She felt very cross.
She felt quite sleepy.
activities.explanation: Joy shows that Tarandeep was happy.

activities.prompt: A strong wind blew while Grandmother was away. Why were the clothes pegs useful?
options: They helped hold the clothes.
They helped dry the clothes.
They helped feed the animals.
They helped make the wind.

This confuses holding clothes with drying them.
This confuses clothes pegs with animal food.
This wrongly thinks pegs can control the wind.

activities.explanation: Pegs help keep clothes in place on the line.

activities.prompt: Grandmother returned and saw the animals on the clothes. How did she most likely feel?
options: She felt pleased and surprised.
She felt bored and tired.
She felt cross and worried.
She felt scared and angry.

This ignores the wonderful scene she saw.
This confuses a wonderful scene with a bad one.
This thinks the helpful scene was frightening.

activities.explanation: A wonderful scene can please and surprise someone.

activities.prompt: Tarandeep set down water for the squirrels and sparrows. Why did she do this?
options: To care for her animal friends.
To make the clothes wetter.
To give it to Grandmother.
To make the wind stronger.

This confuses giving water with washing clothes.
This confuses Tarandeep's friends with Grandmother.
This wrongly thinks water can strengthen wind.

activities.explanation: The water was for her animal friends.

activities.prompt: The clothesline actions began in the past and continued for some time. What does this show?
options: The events were not all happening now.
The events were all happening together.
The events were only about the wind.
The events had no clear order.

This ignores that the events continued for some time.
This narrows a whole story to one event.
This mistakes a continuing story for a confused one.

activities.explanation: Starting in the past and continuing shows an earlier event.

lessons.title: Feeling Shapes and Helping Others

activities.prompt: How might your hands help you discover a shape without seeing it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Shapes you can feel
activities.body: Press hard with a matchstick or the back of a pencil. You can draw a circle, a plus sign or a letter. Close your eyes, turn the page over and run your finger over the paper. The raised shape can be felt. Try to make out the shape with a friend. You can check how you recite poems and think about the work you finished.
keyPoints: Press hard to draw a raised shape.
Close your eyes and feel the shape.
You can try with a friend and check your poems.
activities.explanation: Raised shapes can be felt, so you can play and learn with your fingers too.

activities.prompt: How can a child make a shape and work out what it is?
steps: Press a pencil back hard so you can feel the raised shape.
Close your eyes because you should feel the shape, not see it.
Turn the page, then use a finger because the shape is raised.
You can then make out the shape or its outline.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What can you use on the paper to draw a shape?
options: A thin metal cup
A small rubber ball
The back of a pencil
A soft green leaf
activities.explanation: The back of a pencil works well. Press it on the paper to make a raised shape.

activities.prompt: Pressing hard on the paper makes a raised shape that you can feel.
activities.explanation: Yes! Pressing hard makes the shape stand up, so your finger can feel it.

activities.prompt: Close your ______, turn the page over and run your finger over it.
activities.hint: You use these two to see.
activities.explanation: Closing your eyes helps your fingers do the seeing on this page.

activities.prompt: Your friend has turned the page over. What can your finger feel?
options: A cold wet page
The edge of the book
The raised shape
Nothing at all
activities.explanation: The raised shape can be felt. Then you can try to make out the shape or its outline.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the activity in order.
items: Press hard to draw a shape
Run your finger over the paper
Try to make out the shape
activities.explanation: You drew first, then felt. This order helps you find the hidden shape.

activities.prompt: Some children in the class have low vision. How can you help them read?
options: Read the lesson in a tiny print
Give a printout with large fonts
Take away their thick glasses
Hide their book from them
activities.explanation: A printout with large fonts helps them read. That is a kind way to help.

activities.prompt: A child wears thick glasses. They hold a book close to their eyes. What may be true?
options: The child may have low vision.
The child may not want to read.
The child may have lost a page.
The child may need a new pencil.

This mistakes a reading sign for a dislike of reading.
This mistakes thick glasses for a lost page.
This mistakes reading behaviour for a pencil problem.

activities.explanation: These may be signs of low vision.

activities.prompt: A child has low vision. They want to read a poem. Which choice may help most?
options: Use a printout with large fonts.
Use a page with very small fonts.
Use a page with no printed words.
Use a copy held very far away.

This mistakes small print for helpful reading support.
This mistakes a page without words for reading support.
This mistakes holding a book far away for easier reading.

activities.explanation: Large fonts can help children read.

activities.prompt: A child reads a poem from a large-font printout. They check how they recite it. What do these actions help with?
options: Reading and understanding a poem better.
Making a raised shape on paper.
Feeling a shape with closed eyes.
Trying the activity with a friend.

This mistakes poem reading for making a raised shape.
This mistakes poem reading for feeling a raised shape.
This mistakes poem reading for trying the activity with a friend.

activities.explanation: These actions help with reading and understanding the poem.

activities.context: Long ago in France, Louis Braille was a little boy whose father was a blacksmith. A sharp tool pierced Louis Braille’s eye. Within a few days, Louis became blind in that eye. His other eye was affected, and he became totally blind. In 1819, at ten years old, he joined the Royal Institute for Young Blind Persons in Paris. There he learnt letters using wood, cloth or pins in pincushions. He studied Night Writing and found it too difficult.
activities.prompt: If Captain Barbier wanted Night Writing to become more successful, what should he do?
options: Make the method easier for soldiers to use.
Make the raised dots and dashes smaller and more crowded.
Change the symbols so soldiers must use their eyes instead of their fingers.
Leave Night Writing unchanged because a difficult system can still succeed.

why.Make the raised dots and dashes smaller: Crowding the marks would probably make them harder to distinguish.
why.Change the symbols so soldiers must use: The system was designed to be read with the fingers.
why.Leave Night Writing unchanged because a: Difficulty was the reason it was not a success.

activities.explanation: Night Writing failed because it was too difficult to use.

activities.context: Long ago in France, Louis Braille was a little boy whose father was a blacksmith. A sharp tool pierced Louis Braille’s eye. Within a few days, Louis became blind in that eye. His other eye was affected, and he became totally blind. In 1819, at ten years old, he joined the Royal Institute for Young Blind Persons in Paris. There he learnt letters using wood, cloth or pins in pincushions. He studied Night Writing and found it too difficult.
activities.prompt: After finding Night Writing too difficult, what did Louis Braille do?
options: He became interested in it and made a simpler version.
He decided that Night Writing should remain difficult.
He stopped studying it and returned to his letters by touch.
He kept every symbol unchanged and asked soldiers to manage.

why.He decided that Night Writing should rem: The facts do not say that he wanted the method to remain difficult.
why.He stopped studying it and returned to h: Braille did not stop using the information in Night Writing.
why.He kept every symbol unchanged and asked: He changed the method by simplifying it.

activities.explanation: Braille became interested in Night Writing and simplified it.

activities.prompt: Explain why Night Writing was not successful and what Louis Braille did about it.
activities.answer: Night Writing was not successful because it was too difficult to use. Louis Braille became interested in it and simplified it. The raised dots and dashes were meant for soldiers to read with their fingers, but the system needed to become easier. Braille took the idea and made a simpler form.
points: Night Writing was too difficult.
It was not a success.
Louis Braille became interested in it.
Braille simplified the system.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Louis Braille gave the world the Braille alphabet. A sighted student is learning Braille at home. She can read each English letter by touching its one Braille symbol. She writes a poem in Braille and leaves enough room between the letters because they cannot be written too close together. She notices that her Braille book is thicker than a regular printed book. She also learns that Braille is not only for people with blindness.
activities.prompt: What is likely to happen if the student ignores the rule about how close Braille letters should be?
options: The letters will be too close together.
The Braille book will become thinner.
The poem will become easier to read by touch.
Each English letter will need several Braille symbols.

Braille still needs more space, so crowding the letters will not make the book thinner.
why.The poem will become easier to read by t: Letters that are too close will not become easier to read by touch.
why.Each English letter will need several Br: Each English letter has one Braille symbol, regardless of spacing.

activities.explanation: Braille letters cannot be written too close together.

activities.context: Louis Braille gave the world the Braille alphabet. A sighted student is learning Braille at home. She can read each English letter by touching its one Braille symbol. She writes a poem in Braille and leaves enough room between the letters because they cannot be written too close together. She notices that her Braille book is thicker than a regular printed book. She also learns that Braille is not only for people with blindness.
activities.prompt: A sighted person wants to write a story that can be read by touch. What should she do?
options: She can learn Braille and write the story in it.
She should wait until she cannot see.
She should put all the letters too close together.
She should use ordinary writing instead of Braille.

People with sight do not need to lose their sight to learn Braille.
why.She should put all the letters too close: Braille letters cannot be written too close together.
why.She should use ordinary writing instead: A story meant to be read by touch needs Braille symbols.

activities.explanation: People with sight can learn Braille and write stories in it.

activities.prompt: Explain why a Braille book is thicker than a regular printed book.
activities.answer: Braille requires more space than ordinary writing. Its letters also cannot be written too close together. Because each letter has a Braille symbol and the symbols need room, a Braille book takes up more space than a regular printed book.
points: Braille requires more space than ordinary writing.
Braille letters cannot be too close together.
Each English letter has a Braille symbol.
The extra space makes the Braille book thicker.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a speaking activity, a learner closed their eyes, picked an object, and kept it behind their back. They described it by its shape, completed sentences, and shared them with the class. The teacher read words for listening. Each word was repeated three or four times, and the learners noticed the stressed “spl” sound. Later, they wrote with the Braille alphabet and pasted bindis to make Braille words. One learner wrote their own name in Braille.
activities.prompt: After describing the hidden object by its shape, what should the learner do to add more detail?
options: Add two more lines describing the object.
Ask the teacher to describe the object.
Give the object to another learner.
Begin listening for the stressed word group.

The learner, not the teacher, should describe the object.
Passing the object would stop the speaking activity.
why.Begin listening for the stressed word gr: Listening is a separate part of the lesson.

activities.explanation: This follows the instruction to add two more lines.

activities.context: During a speaking activity, a learner closed their eyes, picked an object, and kept it behind their back. They described it by its shape, completed sentences, and shared them with the class. The teacher read words for listening. Each word was repeated three or four times, and the learners noticed the stressed “spl” sound. Later, they wrote with the Braille alphabet and pasted bindis to make Braille words. One learner wrote their own name in Braille.
activities.prompt: What should the class do after the teacher reads out the words?
options: Listen carefully for the stressed “spl” group.
Complete sentences about the hidden object.
Paste bindis to make Braille words.
Write their own names in Braille.

why.Complete sentences about the hidden obje: Sentence completion belongs to the earlier speaking activity.
Pasting bindis happens during the later Braille activity.
Writing a name comes later in the Braille activity.

activities.explanation: The class is listening for the stressed word group.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between describing an object aloud and making a Braille word?
activities.answer: Describing an object aloud uses speaking, while making a Braille word uses writing. The object can be described by its shape, and two more lines can be added. For Braille, words can be written using the Braille alphabet, and bindis can be pasted to make Braille words.
points: Speaking is used to describe the object.
The shape and two extra lines are used in the description.
Braille words use the Braille alphabet.
Bindis can be pasted to make Braille words.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Some time ago, a newspaper reported an accident. Louis Braille lost his eyesight in an accident. A child lost one eye while lighting firecrackers. Precautions should be taken to protect eyes from harm. The students were writing in their notebooks.
activities.prompt: What should people do when they use firecrackers?
options: Take precautions to protect the eyes while lighting firecrackers.
Take precautions only after an eye has been harmed.
Take no precautions because the accident was in the past.
Take precautions to protect the eyes only after the firecrackers are lit.

why.Take precautions only after an eye has b: Protecting eyes after an injury does not prevent the accident.
why.Take no precautions because the accident: An old accident still shows the need for safety.
why.Take precautions to protect the eyes onl: Precautions are most useful before lighting firecrackers.

activities.explanation: Precautions should be taken before harm happens.

activities.context: Some time ago, a newspaper reported an accident. Louis Braille lost his eyesight in an accident. A child lost one eye while lighting firecrackers. Precautions should be taken to protect eyes from harm. The students were writing in their notebooks.
activities.prompt: If the child had taken precautions while lighting firecrackers, what result would best fit the case?
options: The child’s eyes would have been less likely to be harmed.
The child’s eyes would have been more likely to be harmed.
The child would have needed to learn about safety after the accident.
The child would have needed no safety precautions at all.

why.The child’s eyes would have been more li: Taking precautions would not make harm more likely.
why.The child would have needed to learn abo: Safety learning should happen before an accident.
why.The child would have needed no safety pr: An accident does not remove the need for precautions.

activities.explanation: Precautions help protect eyes from harm.

activities.prompt: Explain how the past continuous describes what the students were doing.
activities.answer: Past continuous shows an action that began in the past and continued for some time. In “The students were writing in their notebooks,” “were” shows that there was more than one person, and “writing” ends in “-ing”. The sentence describes what the students were doing at that past time.
points: The action began in the past.
The action continued for some time.
“Were” agrees with more than one student.
“Writing” ends in “-ing”.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Yesterday, Tarandeep told her squirrel and sparrow friends something interesting. Clothes were put out to dry on a clothesline. While Grandmother was at the house, a strong wind began to blow. When Grandmother returned with the clothes pegs, she saw the sparrows and squirrels on the clothes, preventing them from falling. Tarandeep moved her hands with joy. Grandmother put the pegs on the clothes, and Tarandeep set down a bowl of water for her friends.
activities.prompt: Why did Tarandeep set down a bowl of water?
options: She wanted to provide water to the squirrels and sparrows.
She wanted to give Grandmother something to carry home.
She wanted to make the wet clothes dry sooner.
She wanted to keep the squirrels and sparrows away from the clothes.

why.She wanted to give Grandmother something: Grandmother had returned with the clothes pegs already.
why.She wanted to make the wet clothes dry s: Water would not help clothes dry more quickly on the line.
why.She wanted to keep the squirrels and spa: The bowl provided water rather than keeping the friends away.

activities.explanation: The bowl of water was meant for Tarandeep’s friends.

activities.context: Yesterday, Tarandeep told her squirrel and sparrow friends something interesting. Clothes were put out to dry on a clothesline. While Grandmother was at the house, a strong wind began to blow. When Grandmother returned with the clothes pegs, she saw the sparrows and squirrels on the clothes, preventing them from falling. Tarandeep moved her hands with joy. Grandmother put the pegs on the clothes, and Tarandeep set down a bowl of water for her friends.
activities.prompt: If Grandmother had been delayed, what should Tarandeep do?
options: Ask her friends to keep the clothes safe until Grandmother came back.
Ask her friends to leave the clothes and let the wind take them.
Ask Grandmother to bring more water instead of the clothes pegs.
Ask her friends to hold the bowl of water instead of the clothes.

why.Ask her friends to leave the clothes and: Leaving the clothes could allow them to fall.
why.Ask Grandmother to bring more water inst: Grandmother needed the pegs to secure the clothes.
why.Ask her friends to hold the bowl of wate: A bowl of water cannot hold clothes in place.

activities.explanation: Her friends had already prevented the clothes from falling in the wind.

activities.prompt: How did Tarandeep’s friends help the clothes, and what did Grandmother do when she returned?
activities.answer: The sparrows and squirrels were on the clothes and prevented them from falling while the strong wind blew. Grandmother returned with clothes pegs, saw the wonderful scene, and then put the pegs on the clothes to hold them in place.
points: The sparrows and squirrels helped prevent the clothes from falling.
A strong wind was blowing.
Grandmother returned with clothes pegs.
Grandmother put the pegs on the clothes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: One child in the class has low vision and wears thick glasses. The child reads a poem from a printout with large fonts, then checks how they recite it and whether they understand new words. For the next activity, the child presses the back of a pencil hard on paper to make a raised circle. The child closes their eyes, turns the page over, and runs a finger over it. A friend tries the activity too.
activities.prompt: What should the child do to check that the poem was recited and new words were understood?
options: Recite the poem and check whether the new words are understood.
Recite only the first word of the poem and stop there.
Draw a raised shape instead of checking the poem.
Read the poem silently without checking its meaning.

why.Recite only the first word of the poem a: One word does not check the whole poem.
why.Draw a raised shape instead of checking: Drawing a shape does not check the reading.
why.Read the poem silently without checking: Silent reading does not check recitation or understanding.

activities.explanation: This checks both recitation and understanding.

activities.context: One child in the class has low vision and wears thick glasses. The child reads a poem from a printout with large fonts, then checks how they recite it and whether they understand new words. For the next activity, the child presses the back of a pencil hard on paper to make a raised circle. The child closes their eyes, turns the page over, and runs a finger over it. A friend tries the activity too.
activities.prompt: If the printout has letters that are too small for the child to read, what is the better choice?
options: A printout with bigger lettering.
A sheet with a shape pressed into it.
White clay instead of paper.
The back of a pencil.

A raised shape is not meant for reading the poem.
White clay is another material for the shape activity.
The back of a pencil is used to press a shape onto paper.

activities.explanation: Larger lettering can help a child with low vision read.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Let Us Read Braille

activities.prompt: What did Louis Braille use to learn letters?
options: Wood and cloth
Wood, cloth or pins
Raised dots and dashes
Matchsticks and pencils
activities.explanation: He learnt letters using wood, cloth or pins. These were arranged in pincushions.

activities.prompt: Braille is a method of reading through ______.
activities.hint: Use your fingers to read.
activities.explanation: Braille is a method of reading through touch.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct detail.
pairs: Captain Charles Barbier de la Serre
gave the world the Braille alphabet
activities.explanation: These details show how Night Writing led to Braille and how reading can be helped.

activities.prompt: Which sentence uses ‘was’ correctly with one person?
options: The student was writing in his notebook.
The student were writing in his notebook.
The students was writing in their notebooks.
The student were reading in his notebook.
activities.explanation: Use ‘was’ with one person and an action word ending in ‘ing’.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for making and feeling a raised shape in order.
items: Use a matchstick or the back of a pencil.
Press hard to draw a circle, plus sign or letter.
Run your finger over the page.
activities.explanation: These steps make a raised shape on the paper. You can then feel its outline.

activities.prompt: People with sight can learn Braille too.
activities.explanation: People with sight can learn Braille. They can also write poems and stories in Braille.

activities.prompt: Grandmother returned with the clothes ______.
activities.hint: She used them to hold the clothes.
activities.explanation: Grandmother returned with the clothes pegs.

activities.prompt: Put Louis Braille’s eyesight events in the correct order.
items: A sharp tool pierced Louis Braille’s eye.
He became blind in one eye within a few days.
His other eye was also affected.
activities.explanation: He became blind in one eye within a few days. His other eye was also affected.

lessons.title: Children, Music and Games

activities.prompt: What can we learn from children who play, sing, and try their best?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Happy Children Play and Practise
activities.body: Anant is an active boy who plays hockey on rocky ground. Geeta is graceful and practises on her skates. She learns daily from her mistakes. Lhamo plays proudly on a guitar while his friend joins with a sitar. Shabana is swift and celebrates after winning a cycle race. Meena is musical and sings in rhythm. The playing children are cheerful, and playing is a joy for everyone.
keyPoints: Anant shows active play.
Geeta learns daily from her mistakes.
A fit body, a fit mind and the nation are linked.
activities.explanation: The lesson celebrates practice, music and cheerful play.

activities.prompt: The ground is rocky. How does Anant show he is active?
steps: Anant is active, because taking part in games shows this quality.
He plays on rocky ground, because hard ground does not stop him.
His play shows active means joining in, even when things are hard.
So Anant should keep playing and show an active spirit.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who plays hockey even when the ground is rocky?
options: Anant
Geeta
Lhamo
Shabana
activities.explanation: Anant plays hockey even when the ground is rocky.

activities.prompt: Geeta stops learning when she makes a mistake.
activities.explanation: Geeta learns daily from her mistakes. Keep practising and growing.

activities.prompt: Match each child with what the lesson says about their play.
activities.explanation: Each child enjoys a different kind of music, sport or game.

activities.prompt: Geeta practises on her ______.
activities.hint: She uses these while learning from her mistakes.
activities.explanation: Geeta practises on her skates and learns from her mistakes.

activities.prompt: Who plays a guitar while his friend joins with a sitar?
options: Anant
Lhamo
Geeta
Shabana
activities.explanation: Lhamo plays the guitar while his friend plays the sitar.

activities.prompt: Why is Geeta's skating practice a good example for you?
options: Mistakes can help you learn
Smooth ground is always needed
Only prizes make you learn
Practice should end after winning
activities.explanation: Geeta learns daily from her mistakes. You can learn from yours too.

activities.prompt: Anant is described as active. He plays hockey even when the ground is rocky. What does this show?
options: He gives up when the ground feels hard.
He keeps playing when the ground feels hard.
He waits until the ground feels easy.
He plays only when he can win.

This mistake thinks hard ground is a reason to give up.
This mistake thinks active children choose only easy games.
This mistake thinks taking part matters only when winning.

activities.explanation: This is right because Anant keeps playing on rocky ground.

activities.prompt: Lhamo is a little boy who plays proudly. He plays guitar while his friend joins with sitar. What does this show?
options: Music helps the friends play together.
Music makes the friends play separately.
Music stops the friends from joining.
Music makes the guitar louder than the sitar.

This mistake thinks their instruments keep them apart.
This mistake thinks joining ruins their music.
why.Music makes the guitar louder than the s: This mistake thinks playing together must be a competition.

activities.explanation: This is right because his friend joins his guitar playing.

activities.prompt: Shabana is described as swift. She celebrates happily after winning a cycle race. What does her celebration show?
options: She feels proud of her swift win.
She feels sorry that the race has ended.
She feels cross with her own speed.
She feels afraid to use her speed.

This mistake reads celebration as sadness.
This mistake thinks winning makes her angry with herself.
This mistake thinks a swift racer should fear her speed.

activities.explanation: This is right because she celebrates happily after her win.

lessons.title: Talking About Games and Us

activities.prompt: How can games and music show the special qualities of each of us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Games, Qualities and Music
activities.body: This lesson helps you talk about games, qualities, instruments and dances. A quality is a word that describes someone. A child can write a quality that starts with the same letter as their name. Anant plays hockey, while Geeta learns from her skating mistakes. Meena likes moving in rhythm. The poem mentions a guitar and a sitar. You will practise answering questions about games, instruments and dances.
keyPoints: Qualities describe people.
A quality can start with the same letter as a name.
Children discuss games, instruments and dances.
activities.explanation: These ideas will help you describe people and discuss games and music.

activities.prompt: What should Geeta do when she makes a mistake while skating?
steps: Geeta makes a mistake while skating.
She learns from the mistake every day.
Learning every day helps her improve.
So she treats mistakes as chances to learn.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Anant's Game
activities.prompt: Anant plays the game of hockey.
activities.explanation: Yes! Anant plays hockey.

activities.title: Learning While Skating
activities.prompt: Which child learns every day from mistakes she makes while skating?
options: Anant
Geeta
Meena
activities.explanation: Geeta learns every day from mistakes she makes while skating.

activities.title: A Missing Word
activities.prompt: Geeta learns every day from the ______ she makes while skating.
activities.hint: Think about what Geeta makes while skating.
activities.explanation: The missing word is 'mistakes'. Geeta learns from them while skating.

activities.title: Instruments in the Poem
activities.prompt: The poem mentions only a guitar.
activities.explanation: The poem mentions both a guitar and a sitar, not only a guitar.

activities.title: Moving in Rhythm
activities.prompt: Which child likes moving in rhythm?
options: Anant
Geeta
Meena
activities.explanation: Meena likes moving in rhythm, so she is the correct choice.

activities.title: Match the Children
activities.prompt: Match each child to the fact about them.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a child with the activity or quality described in the lesson.

activities.title: Dance Answers
activities.prompt: Which two dance ideas does the discussion request?
options: favourite and regional
favourite and school
school and famous
regional and school
activities.explanation: The discussion asks for a favourite dance and a famous dance from the region.

activities.title: Geeta's Learning Steps
activities.prompt: Put Geeta's learning steps in order.
activities.explanation: A mistake comes first. Geeta then learns from it every day.

lessons.title: Matching Words and Naming Words

activities.prompt: Can you find the perfect describing word for each naming word?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What are adjectives and naming words?
activities.body: An adjective is a word that tells more about a noun. The phrase blue sky shows an adjective with a noun. The phrase hardworking children gives another example. You must add descriptions or describing words to given words. Naming words can complete blanks with suitable first words.
keyPoints: An adjective tells more about a noun.
Blue sky and hardworking children show adjectives with nouns.
Add descriptions, and use naming words for suitable first words.
activities.explanation: These ideas will help you match words and complete blanks.

activities.prompt: An adjective tells more about a noun.
activities.explanation: Yes! That is exactly what an adjective does.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its given match.
activities.explanation: You matched all five word pairs correctly. Well done!

activities.prompt: Which word is matched with sky?
options: blue
hardworking
green
healthy
activities.explanation: Good choice! Hardworking is matched with sky.

activities.prompt: The ______ sky is an example of an adjective with a noun.
activities.hint: This word is also matched with leaves.
activities.explanation: Blue sky is an example of an adjective with a noun.

activities.prompt: The word blue is matched with children.
activities.explanation: Good check! Blue is matched with leaves, while green is matched with children.

activities.prompt: What does the phrase blue sky show?
options: A naming word with a noun
An adjective with a noun
A describing word alone
A blank with a first word
activities.explanation: Excellent! This phrase clearly shows an adjective joined to a noun.

activities.prompt: Blue is matched with leaves. Blue sky is an example of an adjective with a noun. A child sees both cards. What can the child learn?
options: One describing word can work with different nouns.
One naming word can work with different adjectives.
Each adjective can match only one noun.
Each noun must come before its adjective.

why.One naming word can work with different: This reverses the roles of describing and naming words.
This treats each match as the only possible choice.
why.Each noun must come before its adjective: This puts the naming word before the describing word.

activities.explanation: Both facts use blue as a description before a naming word.

activities.prompt: Hardworking is matched with sky. Hardworking children is an example of an adjective with a noun. A child sees both cards. What does this show?
options: A describing word can work with different nouns.
A naming word can work with different descriptions.
A describing word can name children and sky.
A naming word must match only one description.

why.A naming word can work with different de: This reverses the roles of describing and naming words.
why.A describing word can name children and: This mistakes a describing word for a naming word.
why.A naming word must match only one descri: This thinks one naming word can have only one match.

activities.explanation: The facts show hardworking with sky and with the noun children.

activities.prompt: Green is matched with children. A child adds green before children. What does green do in this phrase?
options: It gives more about children.
It names the children here.
It asks for a first word.
It points to blue sky.

This treats the description as the naming word.
This mistakes the first word for something that asks for an answer.
This uses the sky match instead of the children match.

activities.explanation: Green is matched with children and tells more about that noun.

activities.prompt: Naming words can complete blanks with suitable first words. Pebbled is matched with vegetables. A child sees “___ vegetables.” Why does pebbled fit?
options: It gives more information about vegetables.
It names vegetables for the first time.
It asks for a suitable first word.
It shows vegetables are green.

This treats the added description as the naming word.
This mistakes a suitable first word for a question.
This uses the green match instead of the vegetables match.

activities.explanation: Pebbled is matched with vegetables and gives them a description.

activities.prompt: Healthy is matched with road. A child must add a description to road. Why does healthy fit?
options: Healthy gives more about road.
Healthy names the road itself.
Healthy asks for a first word.
Healthy points to the sky.

This treats the description as the naming word.
This mistakes a describing word for something that asks for an answer.
This uses the hardworking-sky match instead of the healthy-road match.

activities.explanation: Healthy is matched with road and tells more about the noun.

activities.prompt: Naming words can complete blanks with suitable first words. Blue sky is an example of an adjective with a noun. A child sees “___ sky.” What should the child look for?
options: A word that describes the naming word.
A word that names the sky again.
A word that asks for another blank.
A word that matches leaves instead.

This treats the first word as another naming word.
This mistakes the blank for a question that needs another blank.
This follows the blue-leaves match even though the blank needs sky.

activities.explanation: The first word should describe sky, just as blue describes it.

lessons.title: Cooking and Double Letters

activities.prompt: What will we cook, and which hidden double letters will we spot together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Cooking and Double Letters
activities.body: Healthy and tasty food is liked by everyone. The class activity is called Preparing a Dish Without Fire. The teacher may help the children. The section asks whether children have cooked anything for anyone. The writing task uses words with double letters. Village has the double letters ll. The blanks name a pet, what the pet likes to eat, and the food's colour.
keyPoints: The class activity is called Preparing a Dish Without Fire.
The writing task uses words with double letters.
The blanks name a pet, its food and the food's colour.
activities.explanation: This card links the cooking activity with the double-letter writing task.

activities.prompt: How can our class find words for the double-letter writing task?
steps: We should look in the kitchen because the spelling hunt belongs there.
We need five words because the hunt asks for five double-letter things.
We can use Village because its spelling has the double letters ll.
We can use them because the writing task needs double-letter words.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Name the Activity
activities.prompt: What is the class activity called?
options: Preparing a Dish Without Fire
Preparing a Food Without Fire
Preparing a Meal Without Fire
Preparing a Dish With Fire
activities.explanation: This is the full name of the class activity.

activities.title: Healthy Food
activities.prompt: Healthy and tasty food is liked by everyone.
activities.explanation: Yes, the lesson says that everyone likes healthy and tasty food.

activities.title: Find the Double Letters
activities.prompt: The word ______ contains the double letters ll.
activities.hint: This is the example word in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Village is the example word, and its spelling has ll.

activities.title: Match the Blanks
activities.prompt: Match each blank to what it asks for.
pairs: What the pet likes to eat
activities.explanation: The lesson gives these three clues for the double-letter blanks.

activities.title: Order the Writing Tasks
activities.prompt: Put the writing tasks in the order given by the lesson.
items: Name what the pet likes to eat
activities.explanation: The lesson gives the pet name first, the pet's food next, and the food's colour after that.

activities.title: Plan the Spelling Hunt
activities.prompt: Where should the spelling hunt be done, and what should it find?
options: In the kitchen; five single-letter things.
In the kitchen; five double-letter things.
In the classroom; five double-letter things.
In the kitchen; five pet names.
activities.explanation: The hunt belongs in the kitchen and needs five double-letter things.

activities.prompt: A child pauses during the activity. The teacher walks closer. What is the teacher most likely doing?
options: Helping the child with the activity
Ending the class activity now
Starting some cooking with fire
Asking the class to stay silent

why.Ending the class activity now: Walking closer does not show that the teacher is ending it.
why.Starting some cooking with fire: This activity is called Preparing a Dish Without Fire.
why.Asking the class to stay silent: Walking closer suggests helping one child, not controlling noise.

activities.explanation: The teacher may help children with this class activity.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks, “Have you cooked anything for anyone?” What does “anyone” tell us?
options: The cooking was for another person
The cooking was only for themselves
The teacher cooked the food instead
The child must cook a second dish

why.The cooking was only for themselves: This mistake reads “anyone” as only the child.
why.The teacher cooked the food instead: This mistake swaps the roles of the child and teacher.
why.The child must cook a second dish: This mistake thinks the question gives a new cooking task.

activities.explanation: “For anyone” means the food was made for another person.

lessons.title: Rhymes and Word Meanings

activities.prompt: Which words rhyme, and what do they mean?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Find Rhymes and Learn Meanings
activities.body: Rhyming pairs include hockey and rocky. Skates rhymes with mistakes. Guitar rhymes with sitar. Race rhymes with pace. Joy rhymes with boy. The task asks you to find and write rhyming words from the poem. The lesson explains more words. Proudly matches feeling happy about something you did well. Rocky means uneven or full of difficulties. Delightful means very pleasing or enjoyable. Mistakes means errors or things done incorrectly.
keyPoints: Find and write rhyming words from the poem.
Rocky means uneven or full of difficulties.
Delightful means very pleasing or enjoyable.
activities.explanation: You matched the rhymes and meanings in this lesson.

activities.prompt: The skater made errors. What word can rhyme with 'skates' and mean those errors?
steps: The skater made errors, so the answer must mean errors.
The word must also rhyme with 'skates' because the poem asks for a rhyme.
'Mistakes' means errors and rhymes with 'skates'.
Therefore, 'mistakes' is the best word.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word rhymes with hockey?
options: race
skates
guitar
rocky
activities.explanation: Great choice! Rocky and hockey are a rhyming pair.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its rhyming partner.
activities.explanation: You matched every pair correctly. Each word has a rhyming partner.

activities.prompt: Skates rhymes with mistakes.
activities.explanation: That is right. Skates and mistakes are a rhyming pair.

activities.prompt: What does delightful mean?
options: very pleasing
very difficult
done incorrectly
happy about success
activities.explanation: Good choice! Delightful means very pleasing or enjoyable.

activities.prompt: Which word rhymes with hockey and means uneven or full of difficulties?
options: pace
sitar
rocky
boy
activities.explanation: Exactly! Rocky rhymes with hockey and means uneven or full of difficulties.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its correct meaning.
pairs: happy about something you did well
activities.explanation: You matched each word with its correct meaning. Strong work!

activities.prompt: The child did well and feels happy. Which word shows this feeling?
options: proudly
rocky
delightful
mistakes

why.rocky: Rocky is wrong because it describes uneven or difficult places.
why.delightful: Delightful is wrong because it describes something enjoyable, not this feeling.
why.mistakes: Mistakes is wrong because it names errors, not a feeling.

activities.explanation: Proudly is right because it matches happy feelings about something done well.

activities.prompt: A path has uneven ground and many difficulties. Which word describes it?
options: delightful
rocky
mistakes
proudly

why.delightful: Delightful is wrong because it means enjoyable, not uneven or difficult.
why.mistakes: Mistakes is wrong because it means errors, not a path condition.
why.proudly: Proudly is wrong because it describes a happy feeling about doing well.

activities.explanation: Rocky is right because it means uneven or full of difficulties.

activities.prompt: A game is very pleasing and enjoyable. Which word shows this meaning?
options: rocky
mistakes
proudly
delightful

why.rocky: Rocky is wrong because it means uneven or full of difficulties.
why.mistakes: Mistakes is wrong because it means errors, not an enjoyable thing.
why.proudly: Proudly is wrong because it shows feelings about something done well.

activities.explanation: Delightful is right because it means very pleasing or enjoyable.

activities.prompt: I did many things incorrectly. Which word shows this meaning?
options: mistakes
proudly
rocky
delightful

why.proudly: Proudly is wrong because it fits doing something well, not doing it incorrectly.
why.rocky: Rocky is wrong because it means uneven or full of difficulties.
why.delightful: Delightful is wrong because it means very pleasing or enjoyable.

activities.explanation: Mistakes is right because it means errors or things done incorrectly.

activities.prompt: The poem says, 'We watch the race.' Which word rhymes with 'race'?
options: hockey
sitar
pace
joy

why.hockey: Hockey is wrong because it does not rhyme with race.
why.sitar: Sitar is wrong because it does not rhyme with race.
why.joy: Joy is wrong because it does not rhyme with race.

activities.explanation: Pace is right because the lesson says race rhymes with pace.

activities.prompt: A skater made errors. Which word can rhyme with 'skates'?
options: hockey
guitar
mistakes
proudly

why.hockey: Hockey is wrong because it does not rhyme with skates.
why.guitar: Guitar is wrong because it does not rhyme with skates.
why.proudly: Proudly is wrong because it describes a feeling, not a rhyme for skates.

activities.explanation: Mistakes is right because it means errors and rhymes with skates.

activities.context: Anant, an active boy, played hockey on rocky ground without stopping. Geeta, a graceful girl, practised on her skates and learned daily from her mistakes. Lhamo, a little boy, played proudly on the guitar while his friend joined him with a sitar. Shabana, a swift girl, won a cycle race and celebrated happily. Meena, a musical girl, sang in rhythm. The playing children were cheerful, and play was a joy for every girl and boy.
activities.prompt: If Anant found another rocky place for hockey, what would he most likely do?
options: Keep playing and not let the rough ground stop him.
Stop immediately because the ground is rough.
Ask someone else to play while he watches.
Wait until the ground becomes smooth before playing.

why.Stop immediately because the ground is r: This contradicts the way Anant plays even on rocky ground.
why.Ask someone else to play while he watche: This does not fit Anant's own active participation in hockey.
why.Wait until the ground becomes smooth bef: This suggests that rough ground stops him, unlike the description.

activities.explanation: This matches Anant's active nature and his determination to play.

activities.context: Anant, an active boy, played hockey on rocky ground without stopping. Geeta, a graceful girl, practised on her skates and learned daily from her mistakes. Lhamo, a little boy, played proudly on the guitar while his friend joined him with a sitar. Shabana, a swift girl, won a cycle race and celebrated happily. Meena, a musical girl, sang in rhythm. The playing children were cheerful, and play was a joy for every girl and boy.
activities.prompt: After Shabana wins the cycle race, what would she most likely do?
options: Show happiness about her victory.
Become sad because the race is over.
Stop taking part in games.
Hide the race result from others.

The passage describes her reaction as joyful, not sorrowful.
The joyful play described does not suggest giving up games.
There is no reason in the case for her to hide the result.

activities.explanation: Shabana celebrates happily when she wins a cycle race.

activities.prompt: Explain how Geeta's response to mistakes helps her practise on her skates.
activities.answer: Geeta treats mistakes as part of learning. She practises on her skates and learns daily from what goes wrong. This helps her improve through regular practice. Her example connects physical activity with learning and shows how games can bring joy to children.
points: Geeta practises on her skates.
She learns from her mistakes every day.
Mistakes help her improve her practice.
Her example links activity, learning and joy.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In “Talking About Games and Us,” the children read a poem that shows them through qualities. A child can write a quality beginning with the same letter as their name. Anant plays hockey. Geeta learns every day from her skating mistakes. The poem mentions a guitar and a sitar, and Meena likes moving in rhythm. The class discusses school games, instruments children like to play, instruments they have seen, and favourite and famous regional dances.
activities.prompt: After Geeta makes a mistake while skating, what should she do next?
options: Use the mistake as something to learn from and keep skating.
Decide that skating is not for her and stop trying.
Repeat the mistake exactly without learning from it.
Blame the mistake instead of learning from it.

why.Decide that skating is not for her and s: Giving up after a mistake does not show that she learns from it.
why.Repeat the mistake exactly without learn: Repeating a mistake without learning does not match her approach.
why.Blame the mistake instead of learning fr: Blaming the mistake does not show that she learns from it.

activities.explanation: This matches Geeta's habit of learning every day from her skating mistakes.

activities.context: In “Talking About Games and Us,” the children read a poem that shows them through qualities. A child can write a quality beginning with the same letter as their name. Anant plays hockey. Geeta learns every day from her skating mistakes. The poem mentions a guitar and a sitar, and Meena likes moving in rhythm. The class discusses school games, instruments children like to play, instruments they have seen, and favourite and famous regional dances.
activities.prompt: A child wants to write a quality for the activity. What should the child do to follow the rule?
options: Choose a quality whose first letter matches the first letter of the child's name.
Choose a quality whose first letter is different from the child's name.
Choose a game whose first letter matches the child's name.
Choose an instrument and call it the child's quality.

why.Choose a quality whose first letter is d: A different first letter would not follow the stated rule.
why.Choose a game whose first letter matches: A game is not a quality.
why.Choose an instrument and call it the chi: An instrument is not a quality.

activities.explanation: The rule is to match the first letter of the quality with the first letter of the child's name.

activities.prompt: How does the poem show the children, and how can a child write a quality in the same way?
activities.answer: The poem shows children by describing qualities. A child can also write a quality whose first letter matches the first letter of their name. The examples of hockey, skating, and moving in rhythm help the reader understand the children through what they do and what they like.
points: Qualities are used to portray the children.
The quality's first letter should match the child's first letter.
Hockey, skating, and rhythm illustrate qualities.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner has word cards. The card “blue” is beside “leaves,” while “hardworking” is beside “sky.” The card “green” is beside “children,” and “pebbled” is beside “vegetables.” The learner also sees “healthy” beside “road.” The task is to match words and naming words. The learner must add descriptions or describing words to the given words. This activity shows that blue sky and hardworking children are examples of an adjective with a noun.
activities.prompt: The learner must keep the shown matching and add a suitable description before a naming word. Which action should the learner take?
options: Write healthy before road.
Write blue before road.
Write green before road.
Write hardworking before road.

Blue is matched with leaves, not road.
Green is matched with children, not road.
Hardworking is matched with sky, not road.

activities.explanation: Healthy is matched with road and describes it.

activities.context: A learner has word cards. The card “blue” is beside “leaves,” while “hardworking” is beside “sky.” The card “green” is beside “children,” and “pebbled” is beside “vegetables.” The learner also sees “healthy” beside “road.” The task is to match words and naming words. The learner must add descriptions or describing words to the given words. This activity shows that blue sky and hardworking children are examples of an adjective with a noun.
activities.prompt: A learner has a blank that ends with the naming word sky. The learner wants to complete it with a suitable first word. Which action should the learner take?
options: Put the describing word blue first and the naming word sky second.
Put the describing word sky first and the naming word blue second.
Put the naming word children first and the describing word green second.
Put the naming word leaves first and the describing word blue second.

why.Put the describing word sky first and th: Sky is the naming word, so it should come second.
why.Put the naming word children first and t: Green is matched with children, not sky.
why.Put the naming word leaves first and the: Blue is matched with leaves, not sky.

activities.explanation: Blue describes sky, and this order gives an adjective with a noun.

activities.prompt: Explain why blue sky and hardworking children are examples of an adjective with a noun.
activities.answer: An adjective tells more about a noun. In blue sky, blue describes sky; in hardworking children, hardworking describes children. Both are examples of an adjective with a noun. A describing word gives more information about the naming word that follows it.
points: An adjective tells more about a noun.
Blue describes sky.
Hardworking describes children.
A describing word comes before its naming word.

Ask the child to find kitchen items for the spelling hunt instead.

why.Complete all of the cooking work for the: This leaves the child out of the activity.
why.Stop the activity and move straight to t: The activity and the writing task are separate parts.
why.Ask the child to find kitchen items for: Finding spelling items would interrupt the cooking activity.

activities.explanation: Helping the children is part of the teacher's role.

Notes that the teacher may help.
Explains that the hunt finds five things with double letters.
States that the hunt belongs in the kitchen.

why.The ground had errors or things done inc: Errors describe mistakes, not the ground.
why.The ground made her feel happy about doi: Feeling happy about good work describes pride, not rocky.
