activities.title: Ravi Meets His Friends
activities.body: Ravi and Prakash went to the children’s park near their house. A few children were playing there. The children waved at Ravi, and Ravi waved back. Ravi introduced Prakash as his cousin. The next day, a Lagori match was planned. Guneet wanted Prakash because he was a good runner. Lagori is a game played with seven stones.
keyPoints: Ravi introduced Prakash as his cousin.
Guneet wanted Prakash because he was a good runner.
Lagori is a game played with seven stones.
activities.explanation: Great start! You know where the children met and what Lagori is.

activities.prompt: Why does Ravi bring Prakash to meet his friends at the park?
steps: Prakash is with Ravi at the park.
Ravi wants his friends to know who Prakash is.
Prakash can then meet Ravi’s friends too.
So Ravi introduces Prakash as his cousin.

To their classroom

activities.explanation: The children waved at Ravi, and Ravi waved back.

activities.title: Ravi’s Introduction
activities.prompt: Ravi introduced Prakash as his ______.
activities.hint: Think about how Ravi introduced Prakash.
activities.explanation: Well done! Ravi introduced Prakash as his cousin.

activities.prompt: Why did Guneet want Prakash in the team?
options: Because he was a good runner
Because he was a good painter
Because he knew every song
Because he liked Lagori
activities.explanation: Correct! Guneet wanted Prakash because he was a good runner.

activities.title: Know the Game
activities.prompt: Lagori is a game played with seven stones.
activities.explanation: Yes! Lagori is a game played with seven stones.

activities.title: Who Praised Prakash?
activities.prompt: Which two people praised Prakash’s running?
options: Guneet and Deepa
Ravi and Prakash
Ravi and Guneet
Prakash and Ravi

activities.prompt: At the park, Ravi tells his friends, “Prakash is my cousin.” What does this show?

He thinks Prakash can make less noise.

lessons.title: How Lagori Is Played

activities.prompt: Ready to discover how two teams play Lagori with teamwork and fun?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Lagori
activities.body: Lagori is a game played with seven flat stones. They are stacked one above the other. One team knocks them down by throwing a ball. The other team rebuilds the stack and avoids balls from the opposing team. The game is called Satoliya in Rajasthan. In Sundarpur village, people call it Lagori. The Sundarpur Tigers are led by captain Deepa, who runs very fast. Their opponents are the Green Warriors.
keyPoints: Seven flat stones are stacked one above the other.
One team knocks down the stones while the other rebuilds them.
The Sundarpur Tigers play the Green Warriors.
activities.explanation: This card explains the rules and teams in Lagori.

activities.prompt: How can Deepa help her team rebuild the stones safely?
steps: One team knocks down the stones by throwing a ball.
The other team rebuilds the stack and avoids thrown balls.
Deepa runs very fast, so she can move out of the way.
Therefore, she can help the Sundarpur Tigers rebuild safely.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How many flat stones are used in Lagori?
options: Seven
Six
Eight
Five
activities.explanation: Lagori uses seven flat stones.

activities.prompt: The game is called Satoliya in Rajasthan.
activities.explanation: Yes, Satoliya is the name used for the game in Rajasthan.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct answer.
pairs: What is the opposing team called?
What does the other team do?
activities.explanation: These pairs show the captain, teams, and their actions.

activities.prompt: Deepa is the captain of the ______ Tigers.
activities.hint: Name the village team.
activities.explanation: Deepa captains the Sundarpur Tigers.

activities.prompt: What does the rebuilding team do during Lagori?
options: It rebuilds the stack
It knocks down the stones
It throws the ball
It changes teams
activities.explanation: The rebuilding team puts the stones back into a stack.

activities.prompt: Put these Lagori steps in order.
items: The stones are stacked one above the other
One team throws a ball at the stones
The other team rebuilds the stack
activities.explanation: The stones are used, stacked, knocked down, and then rebuilt.

activities.prompt: Deepa is the captain of the Green Warriors.
activities.explanation: Deepa is the captain of the Sundarpur Tigers.

activities.prompt: Which team is called the Green Warriors?
options: The opposing team
The Sundarpur Tigers
The rebuilding team
The village people
activities.explanation: The Green Warriors are the opposing team.

activities.prompt: A ball is thrown toward the rebuilding team. What should Deepa do?
options: Move fast to avoid the thrown ball.
Stand still until the ball hits her.
Run away and leave the stones.
Throw the ball back at the other team.

This mistakes standing still for avoiding danger.
This mistakes leaving the game for doing her job.
This mixes up the two teams' roles.

activities.explanation: Deepa runs fast and must avoid the opposing team's balls.

activities.prompt: The ball hits the stack, and the stones fall down. What does "knocks down" mean here?
options: It makes the stones fall over.
It puts the stones into a stack.
It throws stones at another player.
It carries stones to another place.

This confuses falling down with building a stack.
This confuses knocking down with throwing.
This confuses knocking down with carrying.

activities.explanation: The falling stones show that the ball knocks them down.

activities.prompt: What will the children discover when the match begins?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Getting Ready for the Match
activities.body: The field has a marked boundary, and players must not go beyond it. Seven flat stones are stacked one over another at the centre. Lagori and Satoliya have the same rules. Everyone felt ready for the match. The next day, all the children gathered. The referee blows a whistle to begin the match. Deepa takes the first shot.
keyPoints: Players stay inside the marked boundary.
Seven stones form a stack in the centre.
The whistle begins the match, and Deepa takes the first shot.
activities.explanation: Great start! These are the key parts of the match.

activities.prompt: A ball rolls near the edge. Should the player chase it outside?
steps: The field has a marked boundary, so players know the edge.
Players must not cross it, because crossing it breaks the rule.
Reaching the ball does not change this rule for players.
So the player should not chase the ball beyond the boundary.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where was the stack placed?
options: Beside the boundary
In the centre
Outside the field
At one corner
activities.explanation: Good choice! The stack is placed in the centre of the field.

activities.prompt: Players must not cross the marked ______.
activities.hint: It marks the edge of the playing field.
activities.explanation: Well done! The boundary marks where players must stay.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct detail.
pairs: In the centre of the field
activities.explanation: Each clue matches a detail from the lesson. You found every pair!

activities.prompt: Which action began the match?
options: Blowing the whistle
Rebuilding the stack
Taking the first shot
Throwing the ball
activities.explanation: Good choice! The referee's whistle begins the match.

activities.prompt: Put the match events in the correct order.
items: Deepa throws the ball at the stack
activities.explanation: The whistle sounds first. Deepa throws, and the stones scatter.

activities.prompt: What happened when Deepa threw the ball at the stack?
options: The stones scattered
The stones stayed together
The stack moved outside
The stack grew taller
activities.explanation: Good choice! The ball hit the stack, and the stones scattered.

activities.prompt: All the children gathered for the match the next day. Everyone felt ready before the whistle. What did this show?
options: They were prepared to begin playing.
They were afraid to enter the field.
They were trying to avoid the match.
They were waiting for another game.

This mistakes readiness for fear of the field.
This mistakes readiness for wanting to avoid the match.
This mistakes readiness for waiting for another game.

activities.explanation: Feeling ready shows that the children were prepared to play.

activities.prompt: The field has a marked boundary. A ball rolls near it. What should the player do?
options: Stay inside the marked boundary.
Run beyond it to reach the ball.
Ask the referee to move it.
Push the ball outside the field.

Reaching a ball does not cancel the boundary rule.
Moving the boundary is not allowed by the stated rule.
This confuses the player's limit with the ball's movement.

activities.explanation: The rule says players must not go beyond the boundary.

activities.prompt: The Lagori and Satoliya games have the same rules. Which rule must apply in both?
options: Players stay inside the marked boundary.
Players may cross the marked boundary.
Stones stay outside the field centre.
Whistles blow only after the first shot.

This reverses the rule that players must not cross.
This moves the stack away from its stated place.
This reverses the order of the whistle and first shot.

activities.explanation: Same rules mean this boundary rule applies to both games.

activities.prompt: The Green Warriors take the ball and aim at the Tigers. Why do they aim there?
options: To knock down the Tigers' stone stack.
To move the Tigers beyond the boundary.
To help the Tigers rebuild the stones.
To place the ball beside the stones.

Moving a team beyond the boundary is not shown here.
Taking the ball and aiming is not helping the other team.
Placing the ball beside stones does not match aiming at Tigers.

activities.explanation: Their aim is at the stack the Tigers are rebuilding.

lessons.title: The Exciting Match

activities.prompt: How did teamwork and quick thinking shape this Lagori match?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Match Begins
activities.body: Ravi stacked two stones and ducked away from the ball. Deepa added another stone. A Green Warrior threw the ball towards Guneet and Deepa. Imran warned Deepa, and she dodged just in time. Nidhi placed the fourth and fifth stones, and Ravi placed the sixth. The Green Warriors tried once more to hit Ravi. Prakash placed the seventh stone before the final whistle. The Sundarpur Tigers won the Lagori match.
keyPoints: Stones were placed from Ravi's first stack to Prakash's seventh stone.
Warnings helped Deepa dodge the incoming ball.
The Sundarpur Tigers won the Lagori match.
activities.explanation: This card shows the important actions and the match result.

activities.prompt: What should a player do when only one stone is left near the final whistle?
steps: Only one stone was left, so one more placement was needed.
Prakash placed the seventh stone on top before the whistle.
He completed it in time because the placement came before play ended.
The final whistle blew, and the Sundarpur Tigers won the Lagori match.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who threw the ball towards Guneet and Deepa?
options: A Green Warrior
Imran
Prakash
Ravi
activities.explanation: A Green Warrior threw the ball towards Guneet and Deepa.

activities.prompt: Imran warned Deepa about the incoming ______.
activities.hint: What was coming towards Deepa?
activities.explanation: Good! Imran warned Deepa about the incoming ball.

activities.prompt: Ravi put the sixth stone in place.
activities.explanation: Yes! Ravi placed the sixth stone.

activities.prompt: Match each player with the correct action.
pairs: Warned Deepa about the incoming ball
Placed the fourth and fifth stones
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each player completed the correct action during the match.

activities.prompt: What remained after Ravi placed the sixth stone?
options: Only one
Two stones
The fourth and fifth
The sixth stone
activities.explanation: Only one stone was left to be placed.

activities.prompt: Which stone-placing action happened latest?
options: Deepa added another stone
Nidhi placed the fourth and fifth stones
Ravi put the sixth stone in place
Prakash placed the seventh stone
activities.explanation: The seventh stone came after the earlier stones. Prakash placed it.

activities.prompt: Imran warns Deepa about a coming ball. Deepa dodges it just in time. What did the warning help?
options: It gives Deepa time to dodge the ball.
It tells Deepa to place more stones.
It asks Deepa to leave the match.
It tells Deepa the ball has stopped.

This mistake thinks the warning is about stone work.
This mistake thinks Imran is ordering Deepa to leave.
This mistake thinks the warning says the ball has stopped.

activities.explanation: This is right because the warning lets Deepa move aside in time.

activities.prompt: Imran sees a ball coming toward Deepa and warns her. What does this show?
options: He watches closely and tries to help Deepa.
He wants the ball to hit Deepa instead.
He only thinks about placing the stones.
He hopes the Green Warriors will win.

This mistake thinks Imran wants Deepa to be hit.
This mistake thinks Imran only cares about stones.
This mistake thinks Imran wants the Green Warriors to win.

activities.explanation: This is right because warning Deepa shows that he wants to help.

activities.prompt: Deepa hears Imran's warning. She dodges the ball just in time. How might she feel?
options: Relieved that the ball did not hit her.
Angry that Imran spoke too loudly.
Sad that the ball came too close.
Afraid that Imran will warn her again.

This mistake uses loudness, but the story gives no loud words.
This mistake thinks Deepa was sad about the close ball.
This mistake adds a fear that the story does not give.

activities.explanation: This is right because dodging in time can leave Deepa feeling relieved.

activities.prompt: Prakash puts the seventh stone on top before the final whistle. What does “on top” show?
options: It goes above the stones already placed.
It goes beside the stones already placed.
It goes below the stones already placed.
It goes away from the stones already placed.

why.It goes beside the stones already placed: This mistake treats “on top” as being beside something.
This mistake treats “on top” as being below something.
why.It goes away from the stones already pla: This mistake treats “on top” as being far away.

activities.explanation: This is right because “on top” means above the other stones.

activities.prompt: The final whistle blows after Prakash places the seventh stone. What does this show about the Lagori match?
options: The stone task was finished before the match ended.
The stone task began after the match ended.
The final stone was removed before the whistle.
The match ended before any stone was placed.

why.The stone task began after the match end: This mistake reverses the order of the placement and whistle.
why.The final stone was removed before the w: This mistake imagines that the last stone was removed.
why.The match ended before any stone was pla: This mistake puts the whistle before every stone was placed.

activities.explanation: This is right because Prakash's placement came before the whistle.

lessons.title: The Winners Celebrate

activities.prompt: What did the players and villagers do after the Lagori match?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Match Full of Team Spirit
activities.body: After the Lagori match, players from both teams shook hands. The referee lifted both captains' hands. Everyone celebrated with laughter and joy. The match brought villagers together and reminded them about teamwork's simple joys. Deepa said the match was very fun. She enjoyed Lagori more than video games. Deepa and Ravi wanted to play traditional games more often.
keyPoints: Players showed appreciation and shook hands.
Everyone celebrated with laughter and joy.
The match reminded everyone about the simple joys of teamwork.
activities.explanation: You can see appreciation, joy and teamwork in this celebration.

activities.prompt: A match ends, and both teams shake hands. Why does everyone celebrate?
steps: The match is over, so players from both teams shake hands.
The handshake shows that they appreciate one another after the game.
Everyone agrees it was a good game, so they celebrate with laughter and joy.
Because Lagori brings villagers together and shows teamwork's simple joys, everyone celebrates the match.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happened when the match was over?
options: The teams started another game.
The players left the village.
The referee chose new captains.
The teams shook hands together.
activities.explanation: Both teams shook hands after the match ended.

activities.prompt: What did the referee do after the match?
options: He lifted both captains' hands.
He shook hands with the villagers.
He chose a new team captain.
He stopped the village game.
activities.explanation: The referee lifted the hands of both team captains.

activities.prompt: Deepa said that the Lagori match was very ______.
activities.hint: How did Deepa describe the match?
activities.explanation: Deepa called the Lagori match very fun.

activities.prompt: What did Deepa enjoy more than video games?
options: Handshakes
Lagori
Teamwork
Joy
activities.explanation: Deepa enjoyed playing Lagori more than video games.

activities.prompt: What did the match remind everyone about?
options: The end of all celebrations
The end of playing together
The simple joys of teamwork
The start of team arguments
activities.explanation: The match reminded everyone about the simple joys of teamwork.

activities.prompt: Put these moments in the order they happened.
items: The referee lifted the captains' hands
Everyone celebrated with laughter and joy
activities.explanation: The match ended first. Then came handshakes, lifted hands and joyful celebration.

activities.prompt: The match is over, and both teams shake hands. What does this show?
options: They appreciate one another after playing.
They want another game right away.
They are unhappy with the result.
They need to argue about the game.

This mistake thinks a handshake means wanting another game.
This mistake mistakes respect for being unhappy.
This mistake wrongly connects a handshake with arguing.

activities.explanation: The handshake shows that the players appreciate one another.

activities.prompt: Everyone agrees the game was good. How do they feel about it?
options: They feel pleased with the game.
They feel bored by the game.
They feel worried about the game.
They feel angry at the game.

This mistake confuses a good game with being bored.
This mistake confuses a good game with worry.
This mistake confuses a good game with anger.

activities.explanation: Calling the game good shows that everyone feels pleased.

activities.prompt: The referee lifts both captains' hands. Why might he do this?
options: To show that both teams deserve praise.
To show that only one team won.
To show that the game was difficult.
To show that the captains were tired.

This mistake thinks only one team was praised.
This mistake finds difficulty where the game was called good.
This mistake suggests tiredness instead of praise.

activities.explanation: Lifting both hands shows praise for both teams.

activities.prompt: The Lagori match brings villagers together. What does this suggest about teamwork?
options: Playing together can bring people closer.
Playing together can make people argue.
Playing together can make people forget others.
Playing together can make people stay apart.

This mistake treats coming together as causing arguments.
why.Playing together can make people forget: This mistake confuses being together with forgetting others.
why.Playing together can make people stay ap: This mistake reverses the meaning of bringing people together.

activities.explanation: Bringing villagers together shows that teamwork can make people feel connected.

activities.context: Ravi and Prakash went to the children’s park near their house. A few children were playing there. When they waved at Ravi, he waved back. Ravi then introduced Prakash as his cousin to all his friends. The Lagori match was to be held the next day. Guneet wanted Prakash in the team because he was a good runner, and Deepa said that Prakash was quick. Prakash asked what the Lagori match was about.
activities.prompt: If Prakash wanted to take part in the Lagori match the next day, what should he do first?
options: Find out what the game involves.
Wait for the children to introduce him to Guneet.
Look for seven stones in the park.
Ask Deepa to run in the match.

why.Wait for the children to introduce him t: Waiting for an introduction would not tell him about the game.
Looking for stones would not explain what the match is about.
Asking Deepa to run would not help him understand the game.

activities.explanation: He needs to learn what the Lagori match involves.

Guneet might not have wanted Prakash in the team.

why.Deepa might not have said that Prakash w: Deepa’s comment was about Prakash being quick.

activities.explanation: Ravi’s introduction told the children about Prakash and his cousin relationship.

He introduced him to all Ravi’s friends.
The children waved at Ravi.

activities.context: In Sundarpur village, people call the game Lagori, while people in Rajasthan call it Satoliya. The local team is the Sundarpur Tigers, and Deepa is its captain. Seven flat stones are stacked one above another. One team throws a ball to knock the stones down. The other team works to rebuild the stack while avoiding the opposing team's balls. The opposing side is the Green Warriors, and Imran is also a champion of the game.
activities.prompt: The Green Warriors knock down the stones. What should the Sundarpur Tigers do next?
options: They should put the seven flat stones back in a stack and stay clear of the ball.
They should keep throwing the ball until the fallen stones move.
They should leave the stones down and let the other side continue.
They should place the ball on top of the fallen stones.

why.They should keep throwing the ball until: This gives the rebuilding team the task of throwing the ball instead.
why.They should leave the stones down and le: This ignores the rebuilding team's responsibility.
why.They should place the ball on top of the: This treats the ball as part of the stone stack, although it is used to knock the stones down.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule that the other team rebuilds the stack while avoiding the opposing team's balls.

activities.context: In Sundarpur village, people call the game Lagori, while people in Rajasthan call it Satoliya. The local team is the Sundarpur Tigers, and Deepa is its captain. Seven flat stones are stacked one above another. One team throws a ball to knock the stones down. The other team works to rebuild the stack while avoiding the opposing team's balls. activities.prompt: A visitor hears people in Rajasthan call the game Satoliya. What should the visitor understand about the Lagori game?
options: It is the same game that people in Rajasthan call Satoliya.
It is a different game because the two places use different names.
It is only a name used by the Sundarpur Tigers.
It is the name of the ball used in the Sundarpur game.

why.It is a different game because the two p: Different names do not mean that the people are describing different games.
why.It is only a name used by the Sundarpur: The name Lagori is used by the people of Sundarpur village, not only by one team.
why.It is the name of the ball used in the S: Satoliya is another name for the game, while the ball is used to knock down the stones.

activities.explanation: People in Sundarpur call the game Lagori, while the same game is called Satoliya in Rajasthan.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the names Lagori and Satoliya?
activities.answer: Lagori is the name used by the people of Sundarpur village. Satoliya is the name used for the game in Rajasthan. Therefore, the two words refer to the same game in different places.
points: Sundarpur villagers call the game Lagori.
People in Rajasthan call the game Satoliya.
The names refer to the same game.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: All the children gathered for the match the next day. The field had a marked boundary, and the players were not allowed to go beyond it. Seven flat stones were stacked one over another and placed in the centre. Everyone felt ready. When the referee blew the whistle, Deepa took the first shot. Her throw scattered the stones. The Sundarpur Tigers began rebuilding the stack, while the Green Warriors took the ball and aimed at the Tigers.
activities.prompt: If the Green Warriors’ throw hits the rebuilt stack, what is most likely to happen?
options: The stones will be knocked out of their neat pile.
The stack will become taller than before.
The stones will remain perfectly stacked.
The marked boundary will move to another part of the field.

why.The stack will become taller than before: A thrown ball would not make the stack taller.
why.The stones will remain perfectly stacked: The force of the hit would disturb the stack.
why.The marked boundary will move to another: The boundary is marked on the field and would not move.

activities.explanation: A direct hit would knock the stones out of their stacked position.

activities.context: All the children gathered for the match the next day. The field had a marked boundary, and the players were not allowed to go beyond it. Seven flat stones were stacked one over another and placed in the centre. Everyone felt ready. When the referee blew the whistle, Deepa took the first shot. Her throw scattered the stones. The Sundarpur Tigers began rebuilding the stack, while the Green Warriors took the ball and aimed at the Tigers.
activities.prompt: Why can the same rule about staying inside the marked area guide players in both Lagori and Satoliya?
options: Both games have identical sets of rules.
Each game may make its own boundary rule.
The rule matters only in the game played first.
Players may ignore it when everyone feels ready.

why.Each game may make its own boundary rule: Identical rules mean the same boundary rule applies in both games.
why.The rule matters only in the game played: The rule does not depend on which game is played first.
why.Players may ignore it when everyone feel: Feeling ready does not cancel any game rule.

activities.explanation: Lagori and Satoliya follow exactly the same rules.

activities.prompt: Explain how the match began and what Deepa did.
activities.answer: The match began when the referee blew the whistle. Deepa took the first shot of the match. She threw the ball at the stack in the centre of the field, and the stones scattered. The Sundarpur Tigers then began rebuilding the stack.
points: The referee started the match with the whistle.
Deepa took the first shot.
She threw the ball at the central stack.
The stones scattered, and the Tigers rebuilt them.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ravi stacked two stones and ducked away from the ball. Deepa added another stone. A Green Warrior threw the ball towards Guneet and Deepa. Imran warned Deepa, and she dodged just in time. Nidhi placed the fourth and fifth stones. Ravi put in the sixth stone, leaving one stone to be placed. The Green Warriors tried again to hit Ravi. Before the final whistle, Prakash placed the seventh stone on top. The Sundarpur Tigers won the Lagori match.
activities.prompt: If Imran had not warned Deepa, what might have happened when the ball came towards Guneet and Deepa?
options: She might have been hit by the incoming ball.
The ball would have missed her anyway.
She would have caught the ball.
The Green Warrior would have stopped the throw.

The ball could miss her even without a warning.
Deepa dodged the ball rather than catching it.
why.The Green Warrior would have stopped the: The Green Warrior threw the ball and later tried again.

activities.explanation: Without the warning, Deepa might not have moved in time.

activities.prompt: The Green Warriors tried again to hit Ravi. What should Ravi do to stay safe?

Stay still and wait for the ball.
Walk towards the Green Warrior.
Remain beside the stone pile.

Standing still could allow the ball to hit him.
Walking towards the thrower could move him into danger.
Remaining beside the pile might not take him out of the ball's path.

activities.explanation: Ravi had already ducked away from an earlier throw.

activities.prompt: Explain how the stones were placed from Ravi's first turn to Prakash's final turn.
activities.answer: Ravi began with two stones, and Deepa added another. Nidhi placed the fourth and fifth stones. Ravi placed the sixth, so one stone was left. Prakash completed the pile by putting the seventh stone on top just before the final whistle. This left the pile ready when the match ended.
points: Ravi began with two stones, and Deepa added another.
Nidhi placed the fourth and fifth stones.
Ravi placed the sixth, leaving one stone.
Prakash placed the seventh before the final whistle.

activities.context: After the Lagori match was over, players from both teams shook hands. They appreciated one another, and everyone agreed that it had been a good game. The referee lifted the hands of both captains. Everyone celebrated with laughter and joy. The match brought the villagers together and reminded everyone about the simple joys of teamwork. Deepa said it was very fun. She enjoyed Lagori more than video games. Deepa and Ravi agreed that they should play traditional games more often.
activities.prompt: Why did the Lagori match help bring the villagers together?
options: Everyone could enjoy the same game and join in the friendly celebration.
The referee praised one captain over the other, so the villagers wanted to make a choice.
Deepa preferred Lagori to video games, so her choice alone brought everyone together.
The teams wanted to stay apart, so their disagreement attracted the village.

why.The referee praised one captain over the: The referee lifted both captains' hands; neither captain was singled out.
why.Deepa preferred Lagori to video games, s: Deepa's preference was personal, not the reason for the whole village joining.
why.The teams wanted to stay apart, so their: The match actually brought people together rather than keeping them apart.

activities.explanation: Everyone shared the game, appreciation, and celebration.

why.The match would never have brought the v: The village connection came from the whole match, not from that one gesture.

activities.explanation: Lifting both captains' hands was part of the shared celebration.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Lagori match mattered to the villagers as well as to the players.
activities.answer: Lagori did more than give the players fun. It brought the villagers together, and the handshakes and appreciation after the match showed respect between the teams. The shared celebration also reminded everyone about the simple joys of teamwork.
points: The match brought the villagers together.
Players from both teams shook hands and appreciated one another.
Everyone agreed that the game was good and celebrated together.
The match reminded everyone about the simple joys of teamwork.

chapters.title: Hekko: Challenging the Tiger
chapters.summary: In this chapter: let us read: the hekko story; let us read: the hekko game begins; let us read: how hekko ends; let us learn: words and past time.

lessons.title: Let us Read: The Hekko Story

activities.prompt: What might happen when someone challenges a tiger?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Hekko Story
activities.body: The Hekko story comes from Nagaland. “Hek” means to challenge a person or animal. “Ko” means a tiger. Together, “Hekko” means challenging the tiger. Aami is another name for the Man. Aakho is another name for the tiger. Once, humans and animals lived together. They disagreed about who was superior, meaning better or more important. The humans challenged Aakho, and the challenge became known as Hekko.
keyPoints: “Hek” means to challenge.
“Ko” means a tiger.
Hekko means challenging the tiger.
activities.explanation: This card explains the names and the main challenge in the story.

activities.prompt: A class learns that people once challenged a tiger. How do the two parts of “Hekko” explain this?
steps: “Hek” means challenge, and “ko” means tiger.
This fits because the humans challenged Aakho, another name for the tiger.
Therefore, “Hekko” means challenging the tiger.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Does Ko Mean?
activities.prompt: What does “Ko” mean in the Nagaland folk story?
options: the Man
a tiger
a challenge
a human
activities.explanation: “Ko” means a tiger in the Nagaland folk story.

activities.title: Complete the Meaning
activities.prompt: “Hek” means to ______ a person or animal.
activities.hint: Think about what Hekko means.
activities.explanation: “Hek” means to challenge a person or an animal.

activities.title: Match the Words
activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning in the story.
activities.explanation: Hek means challenge, Ko means tiger, and Aami names the Man.

activities.title: The Main Challenge
activities.prompt: What did the humans challenge in the story?
options: Aami
Ko
Hekko
Aakho
activities.explanation: The humans challenged Aakho, who was the tiger.

activities.title: Order the Story
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct story order.
items: They disagreed about who was superior.
The challenge became known as Hekko.
activities.explanation: The disagreement led to the challenge, and the challenge became known as Hekko.

activities.title: Build the Name
activities.prompt: Which two words make the name Hekko?
options: Aami and Ko
Aakho and Hek
Hek and Ko
Ko and Aakho
activities.explanation: Hek means challenge, and Ko means tiger. Together, they mean challenging the tiger.

activities.prompt: A boy says, “I challenge you to jump.” What does “challenge” mean?
options: To ask a person or animal to act
To help a person or animal act
To stop a person or animal acting
To teach a person or animal tricks

why.To help a person or animal act: This confuses challenging someone with helping them.
why.To stop a person or animal acting: This confuses challenging someone with stopping them.
why.To teach a person or animal tricks: This confuses challenging someone with teaching them.

activities.explanation: He challenges someone by asking that person to act.

activities.prompt: Humans and animals disagree about who is better. Why do humans challenge Aakho?
options: They want to settle who is better.
They want Aakho to leave this place.
They want to give Aakho some food.
They want Aakho to learn some tricks

Leaving is not mentioned anywhere in the story.
Giving food is not the reason for the challenge.
why.They want Aakho to learn some tricks: Teaching tricks is not part of the challenge.

activities.explanation: The challenge comes from their disagreement about who is better.

activities.prompt: The humans say they are better. How might the animals feel?
options: They may feel upset and angry.
They may feel happy and proud.
They may feel sleepy and calm.
They may feel sorry and safe

Nothing in the story shows the animals are happy.
Nothing connects the disagreement with sleep or calm.
why.They may feel sorry and safe: Nothing connects the disagreement with pity or safety.

activities.explanation: Their disagreement and the challenge can make the animals upset.

lessons.title: Let us Read: The Hekko Game Begins

activities.prompt: How do two teams play the exciting Hekko game?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Hekko Teams
activities.body: People in Mokokchung district play Hekko, now a well-known sport. It finds the strongest people in the village. The two teams are Aakho and Aami. A toss decides which team is called Aami, while the other is called Aakho. Before play, a circle is drawn. Aami players form a human chain inside it. Aakho players stay outside, enter the circle, and try to push Aami players out.
keyPoints: People in Mokokchung district play Hekko.
The teams are called Aakho and Aami.
Aami players stay inside a circle while Aakho players push them.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the teams, the circle and the main action.

activities.prompt: Why do Aami players hold hands while Aakho players push them?
steps: The toss chooses the Aami team, which will play inside.
Aami players join hands because they must make a human chain.
The other team is Aakho, so it waits outside the circle.
Two Aakho players enter and push, so Aami stays together inside.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which teams play Hekko?
options: Aakho and Aakho
Aakho and Aami
Aami and Aami
activities.explanation: Hekko has two teams. They are called Aakho and Aami.

activities.prompt: What does the toss decide?
options: the number of players
the human chain
the name Aami
whether a circle is drawn
activities.explanation: The toss decides which team will be called Aami.

activities.prompt: Each Hekko team has ______ players.
activities.hint: Think about the number of players in one team.
activities.explanation: Each team has 11 players.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct detail.
pairs: the strongest people in the village
activities.explanation: People in Mokokchung district play Hekko. The toss names Aami and Aakho. The game finds the strongest people in the village.

activities.prompt: Where do the Aami players stay?
options: inside the circle
outside the circle
beside the circle
above the circle
activities.explanation: Aami players stay inside the circle by making a human chain.

activities.prompt: Why do the Aami players make a human chain?
options: To draw the circle before play
To call the teams Aakho and Aami
To find the strongest people
To stay inside the circle
activities.explanation: The human chain helps the Aami players stay inside the circle.

activities.prompt: The Aami players make a human chain inside the circle. Two Aakho players enter and try to push them outside. What will the Aami players most likely do?
options: Try to keep their team inside the circle.
Try to leave the circle and join Aakho.
Try to stop the game before the toss.
Try to choose a new team name.

This mistake mixes up the pushing team with the team being pushed.
This mistake thinks the toss happens during the pushing.
This mistake thinks the players choose new names during play.

activities.explanation: Keeping Aami inside is the best way to meet the push.

activities.prompt: The toss chooses one team as Aami. The other team becomes Aakho. Why do players need to hear the toss?
options: To learn which team has eleven players.
To learn which team stays inside the circle.
To learn who has drawn the circle.
To learn when the game will end.

Aami is the inside team, so players need their team's name.
This mistake thinks the toss chooses who draws the circle.
This mistake thinks the toss sets the ending time.

activities.explanation: This mistake thinks the toss changes the number of players.

activities.prompt: The village chooses the strongest people to play Hekko. What difficulty might these players face?
options: They may need to draw a smaller circle.
They may need to choose a different game.
They may need to play without a toss.
They may need to push a strong human chain.

Strong Aami players can resist when Aakho pushes them.
why.They may need to choose a different game: This mistake thinks strength changes the size of the circle.
This mistake thinks strength means choosing another game.

activities.explanation: This mistake thinks strength lets the game skip the toss.

activities.prompt: Two Aakho players step inside the circle. They face the Aami human chain. How might they feel?
options: Ready to push the Aami players outside.
Ready to hold hands with the Aami team.
Ready to take the Aami team's place.
Ready to stop playing before a push.

This mistake mixes up pushing with joining hands.
This mistake thinks entering means taking the other team's place.
This mistake thinks feeling ready means stopping the game.

activities.explanation: The Aakho players' aim is to push, so they may feel ready.

lessons.title: Let us Read: How Hekko Ends

activities.prompt: How does the game end, and who earns the special titles?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Game Ends
activities.body: Aami catch Aakho players. Aakho players pushed outside the circle are out and cannot enter again. A caught Aakho player must say “Joko” before release. Surrender means agreeing to be caught. Another Aakho player enters when one surrenders. The game ends when every Aakho player is caught or time runs out. The team with the most points wins. The fastest Aami player is “Khozuba”. The strongest Aakho player is “Khotiba”.
keyPoints: An Aakho player pushed outside the circle cannot enter again.
The game ends when every Aakho player is caught or time runs out.
The team with the most points wins.
activities.explanation: This card explains the main rules, the winning condition, and the player titles.

activities.prompt: An Aami player is pushed outside while two teams play. What happens during the game and at the end?
steps: The pushed Aami player is out and cannot enter again.
Aami surrounds Aakho players to catch them and gain points.
The game ends when all Aakho players are caught or time runs out.
The team with the most points wins the game.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens when an Aami player is pushed outside the circle?
options: The player is out
The player is safe
The player can enter again
The player wins the game
activities.explanation: An Aami player pushed outside the circle is out.

activities.prompt: An Aami player who is out can enter the game again.
activities.explanation: Once an Aami player is out, that player cannot enter again.

activities.prompt: A caught Aakho player must say ______ before being released.
activities.hint: This is the special word said before release.
activities.explanation: A caught Aakho player must say “Joko” before being released.

activities.prompt: What happens when the time runs out?
options: The game ends
The players change teams
A new round begins
Every player goes out
activities.explanation: The game also ends when the time runs out.

activities.prompt: Put the catching events in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The caught player must say “Joko” before being released.

activities.prompt: Which title does the fastest Aami player receive?
options: Khozuba
Khotiba
Joko
Aami
activities.explanation: The fastest Aami player receives the title “Khozuba”.

activities.prompt: An Aami player is pushed outside the circle. How does that player feel?
options: They know they cannot play again.
They think they can enter again.
They hope the circle will move.
They feel ready to catch someone.

This wrongly believes an out player may return.
This wrongly believes moving the circle can change the rule.
This wrongly believes being out still allows catching opponents.

activities.explanation: An out player cannot enter the game again.

activities.prompt: An Aami team surrounds Aakho players. Why does the Aami team do this?
options: To catch Aakho players and gain points.
To help Aakho players gain more points.
To push Aakho players outside the circle.
To make Aakho players say “Joko”.

This wrongly says Aami helps its opponents gain points.
why.To push Aakho players outside the circle: This wrongly thinks the circle pushes Aakho players out.
This wrongly says “Joko” is Aami’s main reason for surrounding.

activities.explanation: Surrounding Aakho players helps Aami catch them and gain points.

activities.prompt: All Aakho players are caught, and the Aami team has more points. Which team wins the game?
options: The Aami team wins.
The Aakho team wins.
Both teams win the same amount.
The game must start again.

This ignores that Aami has more points than Aakho.
The rules give the win to one team with the most points.
The game ends, but it does not start again.

activities.explanation: The game has ended, and the team with more points wins.

lessons.title: Let us Learn: Words and Past Time

activities.prompt: How can we talk about yesterday and choose the right past-time verbs?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words from the Past
activities.body: Spelling examples can describe a park, a poster competition, a bowler and batsman, or ice cream at night. Another example asks a road user to look right and left while crossing. Underlined words show that something happened some time ago. In past simple tense, many verbs add -ed. Some verbs do not add -ed. These are irregular verbs. Came, drank, drove and saw are examples.
keyPoints: Underlined words show events from some time ago.
Many past simple verbs add -ed.
Some verbs do not add -ed and are irregular.
activities.explanation: Underlined words and verb endings help us spot events from the past.

activities.prompt: A child reads an underlined word like saw. What does the underline mean, and why is saw different?
steps: Some words are underlined because the events happened some time ago.
Many verbs add -ed because this marks a past action.
Some verbs do not add -ed, like came, drank, drove, and saw.
They change because they are irregular verbs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which spelling example is about friends making a poster?
options: Friends joining a poster competition
A beautiful park in a neighbourhood
A bowler sending the ball towards a batsman
A mother catching someone eating ice cream
activities.explanation: This example is about friends joining a poster-making competition.

activities.prompt: Match each topic to its detail.
pairs: Sends the ball towards a batsman
Catches someone eating ice cream at night
activities.explanation: Each detail matches the spelling example about the same topic.

activities.prompt: In past simple tense, many verbs add ______ to show past time.
activities.hint: This ending is used with many verbs.
activities.explanation: Many verbs use -ed to show that an event happened some time ago.

activities.prompt: Which statement about came, drank, drove and saw is correct?
options: Only came and drank are irregular verbs.
None of the four are irregular verbs.
All four are irregular verbs.
Only drove and saw are irregular verbs.
activities.explanation: Came, drank, drove and saw are all irregular verbs.

activities.prompt: What do underlined words tell you?
options: They happened some time ago.
They are happening now.
They will happen later.
They show how to spell a word.
activities.explanation: Underlined words show that the events happened some time ago.

activities.prompt: Verbs that do not add -ed are called ______ verbs.
activities.hint: These verbs have past forms that are not made by adding -ed.
activities.explanation: Verbs that do not add -ed are called irregular verbs.

activities.prompt: A bowler sends the ball towards a batsman. What may the batsman do next?
options: The batsman may try to hit the ball.
The bowler may try to hit the same ball.
The mother may try to stop the player.
The friends may try to make a poster.

This mistake gives the bowler the batsman's job.
This mistake mixes the ball scene with the ice-cream scene.
This mistake mixes the ball scene with the poster scene.

activities.explanation: This is right because the ball is sent towards the batsman.

activities.prompt: A mother catches her child eating ice cream at night. How does the child most likely feel?
options: The child feels worried about being caught.
The child feels happy about the ice cream.
The child feels calm after being caught.
The child feels excited to see the mother.

why.The child feels happy about the ice crea: This mistake ignores that the child was caught at night.
This mistake thinks being caught leaves the child calm.
why.The child feels excited to see the mothe: This mistake treats seeing the mother as a happy surprise.

activities.explanation: This is right because the mother has caught the child.

activities.prompt: A road user looks right and left while crossing. Why does the person do this?
options: To check the road is safe before crossing.
To choose a poster for the competition.
To find some ice cream before eating.
To show a bowler how to send a ball.

This mistake mixes crossing the road with poster-making.
This mistake mixes looking for ice cream with crossing safely.
This mistake mixes the road scene with the bowler's action.

activities.explanation: This is right because looking both ways helps check safety.

activities.prompt: Friends join a poster-making competition. Why do they join together?
options: They want to make a poster together.
They want to admire a beautiful park nearby.
They need to catch a moving ball together.
They must look both ways while crossing together.

why.They want to admire a beautiful park nea: This mistake mixes poster-making with the beautiful park example.
why.They need to catch a moving ball togethe: This mistake mixes poster-making with the bowler's action.
why.They must look both ways while crossing: This mistake mixes poster-making with crossing the road.

activities.explanation: This is right because the friends are making posters for the competition.

lessons.title: Let us Learn and Listen: Adding -ed and Traditional Games

activities.prompt: How can we use -ed while talking about traditional games?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Past actions and a team game
activities.body: Adding -ed helps you show actions that happened. In this lesson, you will meet words such as played, muddied, and decided. The park scene includes kabbadi, a puddle, and fish in a pond. A traditional game has two teams. One team throws a ball at seven stacked stones and rearranges them. The other team catches the ball and tries to hit players.
keyPoints: Some action words use the ending -ed.
A traditional game is played with two teams.
A player who is hit by the ball is out.
activities.explanation: These clues help you spot -ed words and understand the game.

activities.prompt: Some children were playing kabbadi in the park. How can we show this past action with -ed?
steps: The children were playing in the park, so this action happened in the past.
Past actions need -ed here, so we add -ed to play.
Adding -ed makes played, so that is the correct word.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find an -ed word
activities.prompt: Which word has the ending -ed?
options: played
kabbadi
pond
children
activities.explanation: Played has the ending -ed. It tells us what the children were doing.

activities.title: Children at the park
activities.prompt: Some children were playing kabbadi.
activities.explanation: Yes, some children were playing kabbadi in the park.

activities.title: Complete the grammar clue
activities.prompt: The grammar practice asks learners to fill blanks using ____.
activities.hint: It is the ending used in played and decided.
activities.explanation: Good spotting! The ending is -ed.

activities.title: After the stones fall
activities.prompt: What did the first team do after the stones fell?
options: It caught the ball.
It rearranged the stones.
It watched kabbadi.
It entered the pond.
activities.explanation: The first team rearranged the stones after they fell.

activities.title: Order the stone game steps
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The team throws the ball, knocks the stones down, and then rearranges them.

activities.title: A player is hit
activities.prompt: What happens when a player is hit by the ball?
options: The player is out.
The player catches it.
The player rearranges it.
The player joins the pond.
activities.explanation: A player who is hit by the ball is out.

activities.prompt: Some children were playing kabbadi. Which sentence shows this past action with -ed?
options: The children played kabbadi.
The children play kabbadi.
The children plays kabbadi.
The children playing kabbadi.

This uses the present form and misses -ed.
This uses the wrong form with children and misses -ed.
This leaves -ing without the helping word were.

activities.explanation: Adding -ed to play shows the past action.

activities.prompt: The writer decided to stay and watch kabbadi. What does this choice show?
options: It interested the writer.
It made the writer leave.
It made the writer muddy.
It made the writer sleep.

This forgets that the writer chose to stay, not leave.
This mixes up kabbadi with the muddy puddle event.
This adds an action that the choice does not suggest.

activities.explanation: Choosing to stay and watch shows that kabbadi interested the writer.

activities.prompt: Many fish were in the pond. Imagine the children watching them. Which sentence uses -ed?
options: The children watched the fish.
The children watch the fish.
The children watches the fish.
The children watching the fish.

Watch has no -ed ending for the past action.
Watches has no -ed ending and does not fit children.
This leaves -ing without the helping word were.

activities.explanation: Watched has -ed and shows the children’s past action.

activities.prompt: The opposing team caught the ball and aimed at a player. Why do they try to hit the player?
options: To make the player be out.
To make the stones stand up.
To make the writer go home.
To make the pond fish swim.

The game knocks stones down and does not make them stand.
The writer chose to stay and watch the kabbadi game.
The fish belong to the pond, not to the teams.

activities.explanation: A player who is hit is out, so hitting can make that player leave.

lessons.title: Let us Listen, Speak, Write and Explore

activities.prompt: What fun things can we discover by playing, listening, speaking, and writing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Explore traditional games
activities.body: Traditional games need physical and mental strength. One game uses a short wooden stick and a longer stick. The shorter stick is hit into the air, and players measure how far it travels. A caught player gives the other team a score. Two children make an arch with their arms. Another game uses a glass object. Skipping is jumping that can build bone density. You will describe a new game.
keyPoints: Traditional games need physical and mental strength.
The writing task asks you to describe a new game.
Nagaland is described as a land of festivals.
activities.explanation: Great start—these ideas will help you explore the traditional games.

activities.prompt: A child jumps well but finds measuring hard. Can the child play a traditional game well?
steps: The jumping stick game needs physical strength because the stick is hit.
Measuring its travel needs mental strength because players learn the distance.
Skipping also uses the body because it is linked with jumping.
So a child needs both strengths to play traditional games well.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Hit the shorter stick
activities.prompt: What do players do with the shorter wooden stick?
options: Forms an arch with arms
Hits it so it jumps
Flicks a glass object
Uses two arms
activities.explanation: The shorter stick is hit so that it jumps into the air.

activities.title: Flick the glass object
activities.prompt: How is the small round glass object flicked?
options: With the players’ fingers
Using a wooden stick
Using two arms
Using a jumping foot
activities.explanation: The glass object is flicked with the players’ fingers.

activities.title: Your writing task
activities.prompt: The writing task asks you to describe a ______ game.
activities.hint: It is the kind of game you will explain.
activities.explanation: You are asked to describe a new game.

activities.title: Match the game clues
activities.prompt: Match each clue to its correct detail.
pairs: Form an arch with their arms
activities.explanation: You matched each game clue with its correct detail. Good job noticing the different actions.

activities.title: A land of festivals
activities.prompt: How does the lesson describe Nagaland?
options: A place for writing games
A land of glass games
A land of festivals
A land of wooden sticks
activities.explanation: The lesson describes Nagaland as a land of festivals.

activities.title: Order the stick game
activities.prompt: Put the stick game steps in the correct order.
items: Watch it jump into the air
activities.explanation: First, the shorter stick is hit. Then it jumps, and players measure how far it travels.

activities.prompt: One game uses two wooden sticks. Another game has two children form an arm arch. What do both games show?
options: Both games need physical strength because players use their bodies.
Both games need mental strength because players never move.
Both games need no strength because players only stay still.
Both games need writing strength because players write the rules.

why.Both games need mental strength because: This is wrong because forming an arch and hitting sticks need body strength.
why.Both games need no strength because play: This is wrong because the players act with sticks and their arms.
why.Both games need writing strength because: This is wrong because these examples show body actions, not writing.

activities.explanation: This is right because hitting sticks and forming arches use the body.

activities.prompt: Skipping is linked with jumping. It can build bone density. What may happen if a child skips?
options: The child's bones may gain more density.
The child's bones may lose more density.
The child's bones will gain no density.
The child's bones will lose all density.

This is wrong because skipping can build density, not reduce it.
This is wrong because skipping may build bone density.
This is wrong because skipping can build density, not remove all of it.

activities.explanation: This is right because skipping can build bone density.

activities.prompt: Nagaland is described as a land of festivals. The learner must describe a new game. Why might writing about this game fit the lesson?
options: It connects a new game with a land known for festivals.
It avoids festivals because the learner must describe a game.
It changes the task into a list of places and festivals.
It relies on a caught player instead of describing a game.

why.It avoids festivals because the learner: This is wrong because describing a game does not need to avoid festivals.
why.It changes the task into a list of place: This is wrong because the task asks for a described game.
why.It relies on a caught player instead of: This is wrong because catching is not part of the writing task.

activities.explanation: This is right because it connects the game task with festival life.

activities.context: During a classroom folk-story activity, children retell a story that comes from Nagaland. Humans and animals once lived together, but they disagreed about who was superior. The humans challenged Aakho, the tiger. The Man in the story is also called Aami. The challenge came to be known as Hekko, and the tiger is called Hekko too. The children explain that “Hek” means to challenge and “Ko” means a tiger.
activities.prompt: If the humans and animals had agreed about who was superior, what should they have done before challenging Aakho?
options: They should have discussed their disagreement without challenging the tiger.
They should have asked Aakho to accept the humans’ claim of superiority.
They should have let Aakho make the first challenge.
They should have challenged another animal to settle the disagreement.

why.They should have asked Aakho to accept t: This reverses the challenge and assumes the humans were superior.
why.They should have let Aakho make the firs: The facts say that the humans made the challenge.
why.They should have challenged another anim: This changes the challenge from Aakho to another animal.

activities.explanation: This avoids the challenge because there was no disagreement.

activities.context: During a classroom folk-story activity, children retell a story that comes from Nagaland. Humans and animals once lived together, but they disagreed about who was superior. The humans challenged Aakho, the tiger. The Man in the story is also called Aami. The challenge came to be known as Hekko, and the tiger is called Hekko too. The children explain that “Hek” means to challenge and “Ko” means a tiger.
activities.prompt: A child says that “Hekko” is only the name of the tiger. Which reply correctly explains what the whole word shows?
options: It links the act of challenging with the tiger.
It shows that the tiger made the challenge.
It shows that the challenge was directed at a human.
It shows that the challenge had nothing to do with the tiger.

why.It shows that the tiger made the challen: The humans, not the tiger, made the challenge.
why.It shows that the challenge was directed: Aakho was the tiger who was challenged.
why.It shows that the challenge had nothing: Hekko directly refers to challenging the tiger.

activities.explanation: The word combines challenging with tiger.

activities.context: During a classroom folk-story activity, children retell a story that comes from Nagaland. Humans and animals once lived together, but they disagreed about who was superior. The humans challenged Aakho, the tiger. The Man in the story is also called Aami. The challenge came to be known as Hekko, and the tiger is called Hekko too. The children explain that “Hek” means to challenge and “Ko” means a tiger.
activities.prompt: Suppose a listener says that the story is called Hekko because Aami is another name for the Man. How should the class correct the listener?
options: It describes challenging the tiger; Aami is only the Man’s alternative name.
It is the Man’s name; Aakho is the name of the challenge.
It is the tiger’s challenge to the Man; Aami names that challenge.
It means that the Man and tiger became one character.

why.It is the Man’s name; Aakho is the name: This swaps the meanings of Aakho and Hekko.
why.It is the tiger’s challenge to the Man;: The challenge was made by the humans against the tiger.
why.It means that the Man and tiger became o: The Man and the tiger are named separately.

activities.explanation: Hekko refers to the challenge, while Aami names the Man.

activities.prompt: Explain how the meanings of “Hek” and “Ko” help a reader understand the word “Hekko.”
activities.answer: The word Hekko can be understood in two parts. Hek means to challenge, and Ko means a tiger. Together, they describe challenging the tiger. This fits the story because the humans challenged Aakho, and the challenge came to be known as Hekko.
points: Explains that Hek means to challenge.
Explains that Ko means a tiger.
Connects the two meanings to Hekko.
Links the meaning to the challenge against Aakho.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In Mokokchung district, people play the game Hekko, which is now a well-known sport. Before the game, a circle is drawn and a toss decides which team will be called Aami. The Aami team has 11 players who stay inside the circle, making a human chain. The other team, Aakho, also has 11 players and stays outside. Two Aakho players enter the circle first and try to push the Aami players outside.
activities.prompt: After the toss names one team Aami, what should the teams do next?
options: The Aami side should link up within the circle, while the Aakho side should wait beyond its boundary.
The Aakho side should link up within the circle, while the Aami side should wait beyond its boundary.
Both sides should form human chains within the circle before anyone pushes.
The Aami side should wait beyond the circle, and the Aakho players should remain outside without entering.

why.The Aakho side should link up within the: This reverses the correct positions of the teams.
why.Both sides should form human chains with: The Aakho team should begin outside the circle.
why.The Aami side should wait beyond the cir: Only two Aakho players enter the circle first.

activities.explanation: This places Aami inside and Aakho outside, as required.

activities.context: In Mokokchung district, people play the game Hekko, which is now a well-known sport. Before the game, a circle is drawn and a toss decides which team will be called Aami. The Aami team has 11 players who stay inside the circle, making a human chain. The other team, Aakho, also has 11 players and stays outside. Two Aakho players enter the circle first and try to push the Aami players outside.
activities.prompt: Suppose the game is about to begin, but no circle has been drawn. What should happen first?
options: A circle should be marked before the teams take their places.
Another toss should be held to choose both team names.
Both teams should be named before a circle is needed.
Two Aakho players should begin pushing without a circle.

why.Another toss should be held to choose bo: The toss chooses only which team is Aami.
why.Both teams should be named before a circ: Both team names are settled by the same toss.
why.Two Aakho players should begin pushing w: The pushing starts after two Aakho players enter the circle.

activities.explanation: A circle is drawn before the game begins.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the Aami and Aakho teams.
activities.answer: Aami and Aakho are the two sides, but their positions are different. After the toss, Aami has 11 players inside the circle, joined as a human chain. Aakho has 11 players outside, and two of them enter first to try pushing Aami players out.
points: Aami is chosen by the toss.
Aami players stay inside the circle.
Aami players make a human chain.
Aakho players begin outside the circle.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a game between Aami and Aakho, Aami players pushed players outside the circle while Aakho players tried to escape. One Aakho player was surrounded and surrendered. The teams gained points by putting opponents out. The game would finish when every Aakho player was caught or when the time ran out.
activities.prompt: One Aami player is pushed outside the circle. What must be true of that player?
options: The player is out and cannot enter again.
The player is out but may enter again.
The player may enter again if Aakho gains points.
The player receives the title “Khozuba”.

A player who is out cannot enter again.
why.The player may enter again if Aakho gain: Gaining points does not cancel the rule against re-entering.
“Khozuba” is awarded to the fastest Aami player.

activities.explanation: Being pushed outside the circle makes a player out.

activities.context: In a game between Aami and Aakho, Aami players pushed players outside the circle while Aakho players tried to escape. One Aakho player was surrounded and surrendered. The teams gained points by putting opponents out. The game would finish when every Aakho player was caught or when the time ran out.
activities.prompt: If the time runs out and Aami has more points than Aakho, which team wins?
options: Aami wins.
Aakho wins.
Neither team wins.
The team with a “Khozuba” player wins.

Aakho does not have the most points in this situation.
The ending of time does not cancel the result.
The title “Khozuba” does not replace the points rule.

activities.explanation: The team with the most points wins.

activities.prompt: How is a player who is out different from a player who has been caught but not yet released?
activities.answer: An out player has been pushed outside the circle and cannot enter the game again. A caught player must say “Joko” before being released. Thus, an out player cannot return, while a caught player must follow the speaking rule before release can happen.
points: Identifies that an out player cannot enter again.
Explains that being pushed outside the circle makes a player out.
States that a caught player must say “Joko”.
Distinguishes the two rules clearly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A pupil reads a spelling exercise. One example describes a beautiful park in a neighbourhood. Another is about friends joining a poster-making competition. It also shows a bowler sending the ball towards a batsman and a mother catching someone eating ice cream at night. A sentence tells a road user to look right and left while crossing. Some words are underlined because the events happened some time ago. The pupil checks came, drank, drove and saw.
activities.prompt: The road user is ready to cross in the spelling example. What should the person do first?
options: Check both sides before crossing
Check only one side before crossing
Check both sides after crossing
Cross without checking either side

why.Check only one side before crossing: Wrong: checking only one side leaves out the other part of the instruction.
why.Check both sides after crossing: Wrong: checking after crossing does not follow the instruction to look before crossing.
why.Cross without checking either side: Wrong: crossing without looking ignores the instruction about crossing.

activities.explanation: Correct: this follows the instruction to look right and left before crossing.

activities.context: A pupil reads a spelling exercise. One example describes a beautiful park in a neighbourhood. Another is about friends joining a poster-making competition. It also shows a bowler sending the ball towards a batsman and a mother catching someone eating ice cream at night. A sentence tells a road user to look right and left while crossing. Some words are underlined because the events happened some time ago. The pupil checks came, drank, drove and saw.
activities.prompt: The pupil finds that came, drank, drove and saw do not take -ed. What should the pupil do with these verbs?
options: Use each verb's irregular past form
Add -ed to each verb
Use the -ing form of each verb
Leave each verb unchanged

why.Add -ed to each verb: Wrong: adding -ed would not give the correct past forms.
why.Use the -ing form of each verb: Wrong: -ing does not make the past simple form.
why.Leave each verb unchanged: Wrong: leaving them unchanged would not show that the events happened some time ago.

activities.explanation: Correct: verbs that do not add -ed are called irregular verbs.

activities.prompt: Explain why some words in the spelling examples are underlined.
activities.answer: Underlined words show events that happened some time ago. They tell us that the actions are over, not happening now. The words came, drank, drove and saw are past simple forms. They are irregular verbs because they do not simply add -ed to make the past form.
points: Explains that underlining shows an event happened some time ago
Explains that the actions are not happening now
Identifies came, drank, drove and saw as past simple forms
Explains that these verbs are irregular
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Learners filled grammar blanks by adding -ed to verbs. Many children were playing in the park. Some children were playing kabbadi, while a sister jumped in a puddle and muddied everyone’s clothes. The writer stayed to watch kabbadi beside a pond with many fish. One game used two teams and seven stacked stones. The first team threw a ball to knock them down and later rearranged them. The opposing team caught the ball and tried to hit the players.
activities.prompt: After the first team rearranges the stones, what does the opposing side do next?
options: Receive the ball and try to hit players on the first team.
Knock the stones over again before taking the ball.
Leave the game because the stones are standing again.
Become the first team and throw the next ball.

why.Knock the stones over again before takin: The opposing team does not knock down the stones again.
why.Leave the game because the stones are st: Leaving the game is not stated in the case.
why.Become the first team and throw the next: The teams do not change their sides in the case.

activities.explanation: This follows the opposing team's role in the game.

activities.context: Learners filled grammar blanks by adding -ed to verbs. Many children were playing in the park. Some children were playing kabbadi, while a sister jumped in a puddle and muddied everyone’s clothes. The writer stayed to watch kabbadi beside a pond with many fish. One game used two teams and seven stacked stones. The first team threw a ball to knock them down and later rearranged them. The opposing team caught the ball and tried to hit the players.
activities.prompt: Why does the opposing team need to catch the ball?
options: So it can try to hit the players.
So it can rearrange the stones.
So it can make the hit player leave.
So it can start a third team.

Rearranging the stones is the first team's action.
Leaving the game results from a player being hit, not from catching.
The game is played with two teams, not three.

activities.explanation: Catching the ball allows the opposing team to try to hit players.

activities.prompt: How does adding -ed help show that an action happened?
activities.answer: Adding -ed helps show completed actions. For example, “play” becomes “played,” “jump” becomes “jumped,” and “stack” becomes “stacked.” The case includes these action words because the grammar practice asks learners to fill blanks using -ed.
points: Identifies -ed as showing a completed action
Gives the example play becoming played
Gives the examples jump and stack
Connects the forms to the grammar blanks
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a festival in Nagaland, children show traditional games to a learner. In one game, a short wooden stick is hit so it jumps, and the players measure how far it travels. Two children make an arch with their arms while another game is played. Nearby, children flick a small round glass object to knock out other glass objects. The other team scores when a player is caught. The learner is asked to describe a new game in writing.
activities.prompt: After the shorter stick jumps into the air, what should the players find out?
options: How far the jumping stick has travelled
How far the longer wooden stick has moved
How far the arch made by the children reaches
How far the flicked glass object has moved

why.How far the longer wooden stick has move: The longer stick is not the object that jumps.
why.How far the arch made by the children re: The arch belongs to a different game.
why.How far the flicked glass object has mov: The glass object belongs to a different game.

activities.explanation: This follows the measuring step in the stick game.

activities.context: During a festival in Nagaland, children show traditional games to a learner. In one game, a short wooden stick is hit so it jumps, and the players measure how far it travels. Two children make an arch with their arms while another game is played. Nearby, children flick a small round glass object to knock out other glass objects. The other team scores when a player is caught. The learner is asked to describe a new game in writing.
activities.prompt: The learner wants another child to understand the new game from the description. What should the learner do?
options: Explain the actions and rules of the game
List only the objects used in the game
Give only the name of the game
Describe a festival without explaining the game

why.List only the objects used in the game: A list of objects does not explain how the game works.
why.Give only the name of the game: A name alone does not describe the game.
why.Describe a festival without explaining t: Festival details do not explain how the game is played.

activities.explanation: A clear explanation helps the reader understand the game.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Hekko: Challenging the Tiger

activities.prompt: In the folk story, what does Hekko mean?
options: the tiger's name
the Man's name
challenging the tiger
the folk story
activities.explanation: Hekko means challenging the tiger. It comes from the words Hek and Ko.

activities.prompt: Aakho is another name for the Man in the story.
activities.explanation: Aami is another name for the Man. Aakho is another name for the tiger.

activities.prompt: Put the story events in the correct order.
items: They disagree about who is superior
The challenge becomes known as Hekko
activities.explanation: The challenge came first, and its name later became Hekko.

activities.prompt: An Aami player who is out can enter the circle again.
activities.explanation: An Aami player who is out cannot enter the game again.

activities.prompt: Yesterday, the player ______ the whole game.
activities.hint: This verb does not add -ed in the past form.
activities.explanation: Saw is an irregular verb. Some verbs do not add -ed to make the past form.

activities.prompt: Match each spelling example with its detail.
pairs: sending the ball towards a batsman
looking right and left while crossing
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a detail from one spelling example.

activities.prompt: What does the writing task ask you to do?
options: Describe a new game
Name the strongest player
Match past-tense verbs
List the Hekko players
activities.explanation: The writing task asks you to describe a new game.
