chapters.title: Unit 4: Up High
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the swing and the wide view; longer sentences and two meanings of swing; verbs and nouns in sentences; tongue twisters and rhyming words.

lessons.title: The Swing and the Wide View

activities.prompt: What does a child discover when the swing carries him up high?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A High View
activities.body: The poet plays on a swing and rises high in the blue air. Going over the wall lifts the swing even higher. From up there, he sees a wide view with rivers, trees and cattle. He looks down at a green garden and a brown roof. Then he says that he flies up again. The swing carries him upward and downward, and he calls it the most pleasant thing. A child can enjoy this too.
keyPoints: The swing rises high in the blue air.
The wide view includes rivers, trees and cattle.
The poet looks down on a garden and a brown roof.
activities.explanation: The swing lifts the poet high, where he can enjoy a wide view.

activities.prompt: What will a child see after the swing goes over a wall?
steps: The swing carries the child up and down because it moves in both directions.
When the child goes over the wall, the swing rises even higher.
From that height, the child can see a very wide view.
So going over the wall lets the child rise higher and see more.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens while the poet plays on the swing?
options: He rises high in blue air.
He rides through a wide view.
He looks down from a roof.
He plays beside the cattle.
activities.explanation: The poet goes high in the blue air while playing on the swing.

activities.prompt: When the swing goes over the wall, it rises even ______.
activities.hint: The swing goes up more.
activities.explanation: Going over the wall makes the swing rise even higher.

activities.prompt: Match each thing to the poet's view of it.
activities.explanation: The poet sees these things from different places around the swing.

activities.prompt: What does the poet say after looking down?
options: He says that he flies up now.
He says that he stays below.
He says that the roof moves.
He says that the garden flies.
activities.explanation: After looking down, the poet says that he flies up again.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: Rises high in the blue air
activities.explanation: The poet looks down before he says that he flies up again.

activities.prompt: Which group belongs to the wide view?
options: Rivers, trees and cattle
Wall, garden and roof
Swing, air and cattle
Roof, garden and wall
activities.explanation: The wide view includes rivers, trees and cattle.

activities.prompt: A child rides over a wall and sees a wide view. How might the child feel?
options: The child feels very pleased.
The child feels quite bored.
The child feels very cross.
The child feels slightly tired.

The child thinks a wide view causes boredom.
The child has confused pleasure with anger.
The child has confused pleasure with tiredness.

activities.explanation: The poet calls the swing pleasant, so the child is likely pleased.

activities.prompt: The poet looks down on a garden and sees a roof below. Where is the poet?
options: High above the garden and roof.
Low below the garden and roof.
Far inside the garden and roof.
Close beside the garden and roof.

The child has mixed up above and below.
The child has mistaken seeing from above for being inside.
The child has mistaken being beside for being above.

activities.explanation: Looking down means the garden and roof are below the poet.

activities.prompt: The poet calls the swing the most pleasant thing. What does “pleasant” mean here?
options: Enjoyable to spend time on
Hard for the swing to move
Impossible for the poet to see
Difficult for the child to ride

why.Hard for the swing to move: The child thinks pleasant describes difficulty of movement.
why.Impossible for the poet to see: The child thinks pleasant means the swing cannot be seen.
why.Difficult for the child to ride: The child thinks pleasant describes difficulty of riding again.

activities.explanation: Pleasant means enjoyable, and the poet likes the swing most.

activities.prompt: The poet looks down at a garden and a roof below. Why might he fly up again?
options: To enjoy the swing and its view.
To leave the garden behind him.
To hide the roof from his view.
To make the swing stay lower.

The child thinks the poet is trying to leave the garden.
The child thinks the poet wants to hide what he saw.
The child thinks the poet wants less movement.

activities.explanation: The swing is pleasant, so the poet wants more of its wide view.

lessons.title: Longer Sentences and Two Meanings of Swing

activities.prompt: Why might “swing” make you think of two different things?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Longer Sentences and Swing
activities.body: Longer sentences can add details. “Jeevan waited for the bus” is shorter. “Jeevan waited for the bus all morning” tells us more. “Jeevan waited for the bus in the rain” also adds details. The writer is asked to read a sentence aloud. The word “swing” has two meanings here. It can be an action word and a verb. It can also refer to an object.
keyPoints: Each new sentence must be longer than the sentence before it.
Adding “all morning” or “in the rain” makes the sentence longer.
The first swing is an action word and a verb; the second means an object.
activities.explanation: Longer sentences add details, while swing has two meanings.

activities.prompt: Jeevan waited for the bus. How can each new sentence be longer and show more?
steps: Start with “Jeevan waited for the bus.”
Add “all morning” because it shows how long he waited.
Add “in the rain” because it shows where he waited.
Add the scooter reason because it explains why, so the sentence grows longer.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Did Jeevan Wait For?
activities.prompt: Which thing did Jeevan wait for?
options: the bus
the rain
the garage
the scooter
activities.explanation: Jeevan waited for the bus, so “the bus” is correct.

activities.title: Waiting All Morning
activities.prompt: Jeevan waited for the bus all morning.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that Jeevan waited for the bus all morning.

activities.title: Match the Meanings
activities.prompt: Match each word or phrase to its meaning.
activities.explanation: The first swing is an action word, the second is an object, and swing means moving forward and backward.

activities.title: The First Swing
activities.prompt: What does the first swing show?
options: an action
a place
a number
a sound
activities.explanation: The first swing is an action word and also a verb.

activities.title: From Shortest to Longest
activities.prompt: Put these sentences in order from shortest to longest.
items: Jeevan waited for the bus all morning.
Jeevan waited for the bus in the rain.
activities.explanation: Each sentence has more words than the one before it.

activities.prompt: Jeevan waited for the bus all morning. How might Jeevan feel now?
options: He may feel tired of waiting.
He may feel excited about waiting.
He may feel happy about waiting.
He may feel worried about waiting.

Nothing in the facts shows excitement about waiting.
Nothing in the facts shows happiness about waiting.
Nothing in the facts shows worry about waiting.

activities.explanation: Waiting all morning can make a person feel tired.

activities.prompt: Jeevan waited for the bus in the rain. What can we infer about his wait?
options: Jeevan stayed where rain could reach him.
Jeevan stayed where rain could not reach him.
Jeevan waited until all the rain had gone.
Jeevan waited before any rain began.

why.Jeevan stayed where rain could not reach: This suggests shelter, but the fact says in the rain.
why.Jeevan waited until all the rain had gon: The fact does not say the rain had stopped.
The fact does not say the wait began before rain.

activities.explanation: Being in the rain means rain could reach Jeevan.

activities.prompt: Jeevan waited for the bus in the rain. Each new sentence must be longer. Which sentence can come next?
options: Jeevan waited for the bus in the rain all morning.
Jeevan waited for the bus as rain fell.
Jeevan waited for the bus after rain stopped.
Jeevan waited for the bus until rain began.

It has the same number of words as the first sentence.
why.Jeevan waited for the bus after rain sto: This changes the detail but does not add any words.
why.Jeevan waited for the bus until rain beg: This changes the detail but does not add any words.

activities.explanation: It adds “all morning,” so the sentence is longer.

lessons.title: Verbs and Nouns in Sentences

activities.prompt: How can one word be both a verb and a noun?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The same word can change its job
activities.body: Sometimes one word changes its job in a sentence. “Dance” names an activity in one sentence, but it shows an action in another. “Play” can also be a noun or a verb. “Answer,” “fly,” and “waves” can change too. Notice how each word works before you decide what it is. The exercise asks you to circle verbs and underline nouns.
keyPoints: A word can be a noun in one sentence and a verb in another.
The words dance, play, answer, fly, and waves can change their jobs.
Circle verbs and underline nouns.
activities.explanation: Look closely at how each word works in its sentence.

activities.prompt: Can the word dance be both a noun and a verb?
steps: When friends dance, it is a verb because it shows an action.
The dance begins, so dance names the event and is a noun.
The same word needs different marks in these two lines.
Circle the verb and underline the noun.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the word “dance” in the sentence about the dance beginning?
options: A verb
A noun
A place
A person
activities.explanation: Here, “dance” names the activity, so it is a noun.

activities.prompt: The word “dance” is a verb when the friends dance.
activities.explanation: Correct. The word shows what the friends do, so it is a verb.

activities.prompt: What is the word “fly” when it names the fly on the wall?
options: A noun
A verb
An action
A sentence
activities.explanation: Correct. Here, “fly” names the fly on the wall, so it is a noun.

activities.prompt: Which sentence uses “waves” as a verb?
options: The girl waves to her siblings.
The waves are near the sandcastle.
The waves sing with the sand.
The sandcastle has waves.
activities.explanation: Correct. “Waves” shows what the girl does when she waves to her siblings.

activities.prompt: The word “play” is a noun in the sentence about watching a play.
activities.explanation: Correct. The word “play” names what is being watched in that sentence.

activities.prompt: Which choice uses “answer” correctly as a verb?
options: Someone answers questions.
The answer is on the page.
She knows the answer.
The answer was easy.
activities.explanation: Correct. “Answers” shows what someone does with questions, so it is a verb.

activities.prompt: Someone answers questions. What does answer show in this line?
options: An action they perform
A thing that they know
A thing that they watch
Something on the wall

why.A thing that they know: It confuses the answer given with the thing being known.
why.A thing that they watch: It confuses answering with watching a play.
why.Something on the wall: It confuses answering with naming the fly on a wall.

activities.explanation: Answering questions shows an action, so answer is a verb.

activities.prompt: A sentence mentions waves and a sandcastle. The girl waves to her siblings. What does waves show in the second line?
options: An action she performs
A thing she watches
A thing she knows
Something on the wall

why.A thing she watches: It uses the noun meaning of waves from the sandcastle.
why.A thing she knows: It confuses the girl's action with knowing an answer.
why.Something on the wall: It confuses the girl's action with the fly on the wall.

activities.explanation: Waving shows what she does, so waves is a verb.

lessons.title: Tongue Twisters and Rhyming Words

activities.prompt: Can your tongue twist tricky words and discover perfect rhymes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Practise Sounds and Rhymes
activities.body: The poem is called ‘The Swing’. The tongue twister asks how much wood a woodchuck could chuck. While saying the W sound, make an O shape with your lips. Repeat the tongue twister four or five times. Read the practice words aloud. Then listen while your teacher reads the poem again. Finally, make a list of rhyming words. Focus on heard sounds, not spellings.
keyPoints: ‘The Swing’ is the poem’s title.
A woodchuck could chuck wood in the tongue twister.
Make an O shape for the W sound and focus on heard rhymes.
activities.explanation: You will practise clear sounds and rhyming words.

activities.prompt: A child finds the W sound difficult in the tongue twister. How can the child practise it?
steps: Make an O shape with the lips, because the W sound needs this mouth shape.
Read the practice words aloud, because the child must hear the sounds.
Say the full tongue twister about a woodchuck chucking wood, because it includes the W sound.
Repeat it four or five times, so the mouth can practise the sound clearly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the tongue twister say the woodchuck could do?
options: Read the poem.
Count the words.
Chuck the wood.
Make a list.
activities.explanation: The tongue twister says that a woodchuck could chuck wood.

activities.prompt: The poem is called ‘The ______’.
activities.hint: Check the poem title in your book.
activities.explanation: The poem in your book is called ‘The Swing’.

activities.prompt: What should you do while saying the W sound?
options: Keep both lips completely still.
Make an A shape with your lips.
Make an O shape with your lips.
Make a C shape with your lips.
activities.explanation: Make an O shape with your lips while saying the W sound.

activities.prompt: Match each action to the right instruction.
pairs: Do it four or five times
activities.explanation: These pairs match the speaking and rhyming instructions in the lesson.

activities.prompt: What may you add to the list of rhyming words?
options: No words for the list.
Only the poem’s title.
Only words with odd spellings.
Two words of your own.
activities.explanation: You may add two words of your own to the list.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: Listen while your teacher reads the poem again.
Focus on heard sounds instead of spellings.
Make a list of the words that rhyme.
Add two words of your own to the list.
activities.explanation: Listen, check heard sounds, list the rhymes, then add two words.

activities.prompt: In the tongue twister, which two words rhyme?
options: wood and would
wood and much
chuck and how
wood and chew

why.wood and much: This mistake comes from focusing on one ending sound instead of the whole rhyme.
why.chuck and how: This mistake comes from noticing similar letters instead of matching sounds.
why.wood and chew: This mistake comes from treating the shared w letter as the rhyme sound.

activities.explanation: This is right because both words have the same heard sound.

activities.prompt: A child says the tongue twister five times. Why?
options: Practising the tongue twister.
Making a list of rhyming words.
Choosing two extra words to rhyme.
Checking the poem by its spelling.

This mistake comes from confusing speaking practice with making a list.
This mistake comes from confusing practice with adding extra rhyme words.
This mistake comes from confusing speaking practice with checking spellings.

activities.explanation: This is right because repeating it is how the child practises the sound.

activities.prompt: A child listens as the teacher reads ‘The Swing’ again. What can the child notice?
options: Words that rhyme with each other.
Words that begin with the same letter.
Words that have the longest spelling.
Words that end with the same letter.

This mistake comes from noticing first letters instead of heard sounds.
This mistake comes from confusing spelling length with rhyming sounds.
This mistake comes from thinking matching final letters always prove a rhyme.

activities.explanation: This is right because listening helps the child hear the rhyming words.

lessons.sceneCaption: A woodchuck, the animal featured in the tongue twister.

lessons.title: Writing, Prepositions and Magical Swings

activities.prompt: Where would your magical swing take you if it could fly anywhere?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Enjoyable Activities and Magical Writing
activities.body: The word “pleasantest” means “most enjoyable”. Many things can be enjoyable for people. In your free time, write about activities you enjoy. You are encouraged to share your hobbies in class. A preposition shows place, time and direction. Examples include on, beside, between, above, in front of, behind and under. Draw a magical swing that can take you anywhere, then write about its adventure.
keyPoints: Pleasantest means most enjoyable.
A preposition shows place, time and direction.
Draw a magical swing, then write about its adventure.
activities.explanation: This card helps you write about enjoyable activities and a magical adventure.

activities.prompt: How can a writer clearly show where a magical swing is?
steps: Because prepositions show place, time and direction, they help show location.
Use on, beside, between or above, because these show where the swing is.
Use infront of, behind or under, because these also show where it is.
Choose the word that fits the picture, because that makes the writing clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Meaning of Pleasantest
activities.prompt: Which word has the same meaning as “pleasantest”?
options: magical
enjoyable
possible
hobby
activities.explanation: “Pleasantest” means “most enjoyable”, so “enjoyable” is correct.

activities.title: What Prepositions Show
activities.prompt: A preposition can show place, time and direction.
activities.explanation: Yes. A preposition shows place, time and direction.

activities.title: Complete the Word
activities.prompt: The word ______ means enjoyable.
activities.hint: Use the word from your book that describes the most enjoyable thing.
activities.explanation: “Pleasantest” means “most enjoyable”. You have found the right word.

activities.title: Match the Lesson Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each group or instruction with its description.
pairs: outer space, a jungle and a book world
activities.explanation: You matched the preposition groups, possible places and writing steps.

activities.title: Order the Adventure Steps
activities.prompt: Put the magical adventure steps in order.
items: Draw a magical swing that can take the writer anywhere.
Take the magical swing to a possible place.
Write a short paragraph about the adventure.
activities.explanation: First draw the swing, then choose its place, and finally write the adventure.

activities.title: What Comes Next?
activities.prompt: The writer has chosen a possible place for the magical swing. What should the writer write next?
options: A list of possible swing places.
A set of enjoyable class hobbies.
A short paragraph about adventure.
A group of simple prepositions.
activities.explanation: The writing task asks for a short paragraph about the adventure.

activities.prompt: At free time, a child calls an adventure the pleasantest part. What does pleasantest mean here?
options: a very enjoyable experience
a slow and difficult journey
a place that has no fun
a hobby that is kept alone

why.a slow and difficult journey: The child mistakes an enjoyable time for a difficult journey.
why.a place that has no fun: The child thinks pleasantest means a place without fun.
why.a hobby that is kept alone: The child thinks pleasantest means doing a hobby alone.

activities.explanation: The word means enjoyable in this sentence.

activities.prompt: In class, learners are asked to share their hobbies. A learner smiles and talks about a drawing. How does this learner most likely feel?
options: excited and happy to share
bored and wanting to leave
angry that the class asked
afraid of sharing with others

why.bored and wanting to leave: The child mistakes a polite smile for boredom.
why.angry that the class asked: The child mistakes speaking for anger at the class.
why.afraid of sharing with others: The child thinks sharing means being afraid of others.

activities.explanation: The smile and talk show that the learner wants to share.

activities.prompt: A child draws a magical swing high over jungle trees. The seat is not level with the trees. Where is the seat in relation to the trees?
options: above the jungle trees
beside the jungle trees
between the jungle trees
under the jungle trees

why.beside the jungle trees: Beside means at the side, not high over.
why.between the jungle trees: Between means in the middle, not high over.
why.under the jungle trees: Under means below, the opposite of high over.

activities.explanation: High over the trees shows that the seat is above them.

activities.prompt: A middle shape has another shape on each side. Where is the middle shape?
options: between the two outer shapes
beside the two outer shapes
above the two outer shapes
behind the two outer shapes

why.beside the two outer shapes: Beside means at one side, not in the middle.
why.above the two outer shapes: Above means higher, not in the middle.
why.behind the two outer shapes: Behind means hidden from view, not in the middle.

activities.explanation: A middle shape with shapes on both sides is between them.

activities.prompt: A child stands between another child and the front wall. Where is this child in relation to the other child?
options: infront of the other child
behind the other child
beside the other child
above the other child

why.behind the other child: Behind would put the child farther from the front wall.
why.beside the other child: Beside means at one side, not toward the front.
why.above the other child: Above means higher, not farther forward.

activities.explanation: Standing between the child and the front wall puts the child infront.

activities.prompt: A writer finishes drawing a magical swing that can travel anywhere. The swing can take the writer to outer space. It can also go to a jungle or a book world. What should the writer do next?
options: write a short paragraph about the adventure
choose the word pleasantest for the title
fill every blank with the same preposition
draw another swing without any adventure

why.choose the word pleasantest for the titl: Pleasantest means enjoyable, but it is not the next task.
why.fill every blank with the same prepositi: Each blank needs a suitable preposition, not the same one.
why.draw another swing without any adventure: The task asks for a paragraph after the drawing.

activities.explanation: The writer should describe the adventure in a short paragraph.

activities.context: A child enjoys playing on a swing. It lifts the child high in the blue air. Going over the wall makes it rise even higher. From up high, the child sees a wide view with rivers, trees and cattle. The child looks down on a green garden and sees a brown roof below. After looking down, the child says he flies up again. The swing moves upward and downward, and the child calls the swing the most pleasant thing.
activities.prompt: If the child's swing goes over the wall, what should the child expect next?
options: It will reach a greater height.
It will begin moving lower.
It will stay at the same height.
It will lose the wide view.

Going over the wall causes a rise, not an immediate fall.
The rule says that the swing rises higher instead of remaining level.
The child remains high enough to see the wide view.

activities.explanation: Going over the wall makes the swing rise even higher.

activities.context: A child enjoys playing on a swing. It lifts the child high in the blue air. Going over the wall makes it rise even higher. From up high, the child sees a wide view with rivers, trees and cattle. The child looks down on a green garden and sees a brown roof below. After looking down, the child says he flies up again. The swing moves upward and downward, and the child calls the swing the most pleasant thing.
activities.prompt: After the child looks down at the garden and roof, what happens next?
options: The swing lifts the child upward once more.
The swing stays at the same height.
The child sees only the garden and roof.
The child stops moving.

The swing rises again instead of staying at one height.
The wide view also includes rivers, trees and cattle.
The swing moves the child both upward and downward.

activities.explanation: After looking down, the child says that he flies up again.

activities.prompt: How does going over the wall change the child's view and the swing's movement?
activities.answer: Going over the wall makes the swing rise even higher. This lifts the child higher into the blue air, where the view becomes very wide. The child can see rivers, trees and cattle, and can look down on a green garden and a brown roof below.
points: Going over the wall makes the swing rise.
The child is lifted higher into the blue air.
The higher position gives a very wide view.
The child can see the garden and roof below.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Jeevan waited for the bus. Jeevan waited for the bus all morning. Jeevan waited for the bus in the rain. Jeevan was waiting because his scooter was in the garage. The writer was asked to read the new longer sentence aloud. The first swing in the lesson is an action word and also a verb. The second swing in the lesson refers to an object, while the verb swing means moving forward and backward.
activities.prompt: Why is Jeevan waiting for the bus instead of using his scooter?
options: His scooter is unavailable because it is in the garage.
His scooter is available to him while it is in the garage.
The bus is unavailable to him because his scooter is in the garage.
The garage is unavailable to him because his scooter is in the garage.

why.His scooter is available to him while it: Mistake: being in the garage does not make the scooter available.
why.The bus is unavailable to him because hi: Mistake: this wrongly says that the bus is unavailable.
why.The garage is unavailable to him because: Mistake: this wrongly says that the garage is unavailable.

activities.explanation: Correct: the scooter cannot be used while it is in the garage.

activities.context: Jeevan waited for the bus. Jeevan waited for the bus all morning. Jeevan waited for the bus in the rain. Jeevan was waiting because his scooter was in the garage. The writer was asked to read the new longer sentence aloud. The first swing in the lesson is an action word and also a verb. The second swing in the lesson refers to an object, while the verb swing means moving forward and backward.
activities.prompt: What should the writer explain when reading a sentence that uses “swing” twice?
options: The first use names an action, while the second use names a thing.
The first use names a thing, while the second use names an action.
Both uses name actions that mean moving forward and backward.
Both uses name objects, and neither use is a verb.

why.The first use names a thing, while the s: Mistake: this reverses the two meanings.
why.Both uses name actions that mean moving: Mistake: only the first use means moving forward and backward.
why.Both uses name objects, and neither use: Mistake: the first use is an action and also a verb.

activities.explanation: Correct: the first use is a verb and the second use names an object.

activities.context: A girl and her friends watch the waves beside a sandcastle. The dance begins, and soon the friends dance. They play kho-kho before they watch a play. There is a fly on the wall while the friends fly kites. The girl waves to her siblings.
activities.prompt: If the dance begins and then the friends dance, how should the word “dance” be classified in the two parts?
options: It is a noun when the dance begins and a verb when the friends dance.
It is a noun in both parts because it refers to the dance.
It is a verb in both parts because it shows what the friends do.
It is a verb when the dance begins and a noun when the friends dance.

why.It is a noun in both parts because it re: The first use names the dance, so it is a noun.
why.It is a verb in both parts because it sh: The second use shows the friends dancing, so it is a verb.
why.It is a verb when the dance begins and a: This reverses the correct noun and verb uses.

activities.explanation: This matches the two uses of “dance” in the case.

activities.context: A girl and her friends watch the waves beside a sandcastle. The dance begins, and soon the friends dance. They play kho-kho before they watch a play. There is a fly on the wall while the friends fly kites. The girl waves to her siblings.
activities.prompt: If the friends first play kho-kho and later watch a play, how should the word “play” be classified?
options: It is a verb when they play kho-kho and a noun when they watch a play.
It is a noun when they play kho-kho and a verb when they watch a play.
It is a noun in both parts because it names an activity.
It is a verb in both parts because it shows what the friends do.

why.It is a noun when they play kho-kho and: Playing kho-kho needs the verb use.
why.It is a noun in both parts because it na: Watching a play needs the noun use.
why.It is a verb in both parts because it sh: This reverses the correct verb and noun uses.

activities.explanation: This correctly identifies the two uses of “play” in the case.

activities.context: A girl and her friends watch the waves beside a sandcastle. The dance begins, and soon the friends dance. They play kho-kho before they watch a play. There is a fly on the wall while the friends fly kites. The girl waves to her siblings.
activities.prompt: If the waves are first shown with the sandcastle and later the girl waves to her siblings, how should the word “waves” be classified?
options: It is a noun with the sandcastle and a verb when the girl waves to her siblings.
It is a verb with the sandcastle and a noun when the girl waves to her siblings.
It is a noun in both parts because it always names water.
It is a verb in both parts because it shows an action.

why.It is a verb with the sandcastle and a n: The waves with the sandcastle need the noun use.
why.It is a noun in both parts because it al: The girl waving to her siblings needs the verb use.
why.It is a verb in both parts because it sh: This reverses the correct noun and verb uses.

activities.explanation: This matches the two uses of “waves” in the case.

activities.prompt: Explain why the word “dance” can be a noun in one sentence and a verb in another.
activities.answer: In the sentence about the dance beginning, “dance” names the event, so it is a noun. In the sentence about the friends dance, “dance” shows what the friends do, so it is a verb. The word stays the same, but its job in the sentence is different.
points: Identifies the noun use with the dance beginning.
Identifies the verb use with the friends dancing.
Explains that the word’s job changes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In class, a learner works with ‘The Swing’ and a tongue twister about how much wood a woodchuck would chuck. The twister says a woodchuck could chuck wood. To practise the W sound, the learner makes an O shape with their lips and repeats the twister four or five times. The teacher reads the poem again as the learner lists rhymes. They read the words aloud, add two of their own, and check rhymes by heard sounds, not spellings.
activities.prompt: When the learner checks the rhyme list, which rule should they use?
options: Choose words whose spellings must be exactly the same.
Trust words that look alike even when their spoken sounds differ.
Listen for matching sounds instead of comparing how words are written.
Choose words by their length rather than by how they sound.

why.Choose words whose spellings must be exa: This focuses on spelling instead of sound.
why.Trust words that look alike even when th: This trusts spelling over heard sounds.
why.Choose words by their length rather than: This ignores how the words sound.

activities.explanation: This follows the lesson’s rule for checking rhymes.

activities.context: In class, a learner works with ‘The Swing’ and a tongue twister about how much wood a woodchuck would chuck. The twister says a woodchuck could chuck wood. To practise the W sound, the learner makes an O shape with their lips and repeats the twister four or five times. The teacher reads the poem again as the learner lists rhymes. They read the words aloud, add two of their own, and check rhymes by heard sounds, not spellings.
activities.prompt: After reading the practice words aloud, what can the learner do to extend the rhyme list?
options: Add one new word and stop.
Add two new words even if they do not rhyme.
Add two words whose spellings look alike but whose sounds differ.
Add two words of their own that rhyme with the words on the list.

The learner may add two words, not only one.
why.Add two new words even if they do not rh: The added words should fit the rhyme list.
why.Add two words whose spellings look alike: Similar spellings do not necessarily give matching sounds.

activities.explanation: This adds two original rhyming words as allowed.

activities.prompt: How should the learner practise the W sound and the tongue twister?
activities.answer: The learner should make an O shape with their lips while saying the W sound. Repeating the tongue twister four or five times gives more speaking practice. This follows the lesson’s instructions for practising the sound and saying the tongue twister aloud.
points: Makes an O shape with the lips
Says the W sound while doing this
Repeats the tongue twister four or five times
Practises the tongue twister aloud
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During free time, a learner drew a magical swing and planned a short adventure without choosing its destination yet. At school, the learner shared a hobby because the class encouraged learners to share their hobbies. The learner explained that drawing and writing were enjoyable activities and prepared to tell classmates about the adventure.
activities.prompt: What should the learner do after drawing the magical swing?
options: Write a short paragraph describing the swing's journey.
Choose a different activity because the drawing is already finished.
Draw the destination and leave out the adventure.
Keep the drawing private and do not share the hobby.

why.Choose a different activity because the: The drawing is only part of the task.
why.Draw the destination and leave out the a: The learner must also write a short paragraph.
why.Keep the drawing private and do not shar: Learners are encouraged to share their hobbies.

activities.explanation: This completes the task by writing about the adventure.

activities.context: During free time, a learner drew a magical swing and planned a short adventure without choosing its destination yet. At school, the learner shared a hobby because the class encouraged learners to share their hobbies. The learner explained that drawing and writing were enjoyable activities and prepared to tell classmates about the adventure.
activities.prompt: Why did the learner share the hobby in class?
options: To help classmates hear about an enjoyable interest.
To show that drawing is the only free-time activity.
To make classmates enjoy every hobby they have.
To stop learners from sharing different hobbies.

why.To show that drawing is the only free-ti: Many activities are enjoyable, not only drawing.
why.To make classmates enjoy every hobby the: The learner cannot make others feel or enjoy something.

activities.explanation: Sharing helps classmates learn about an enjoyable hobby.

activities.prompt: How does a preposition show meaning in this lesson?
activities.answer: The words on, beside, between and above are in the first group. The other words are infront of, behind and under. All of them can describe place, while prepositions can also show time and direction.
points: Identifies the first group of prepositions.
Identifies the other prepositions.
Explains that prepositions show place.
Also mentions time and direction.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Unit 4: Up High

activities.title: A Higher Swing
activities.prompt: Which thing makes the swing rise even higher?
options: Going over the wall
Playing in the garden
Looking at a roof
Waiting for the bus
activities.explanation: Going over the wall makes the swing rise even higher.

activities.prompt: The poet sees a brown roof above him.
activities.explanation: The poet looks down and sees the brown roof below.

activities.title: The Swing's Movement
activities.prompt: The swing moves the poet upward and ______.
activities.hint: The swing moves in two directions.
activities.explanation: The swing carries the poet upward and downward.

activities.title: Jeevan's Wait
activities.prompt: What was Jeevan waiting for?
options: the bus
the scooter
the garage
the rain
activities.explanation: Jeevan waited for the bus because his scooter was in the garage.

activities.title: Growing Sentences
activities.prompt: Each new sentence must be longer than the sentence before it.
activities.explanation: This rule helps you build a longer and longer sentence.

activities.title: Nouns and Verbs
activities.prompt: Match each word with its correct use.
pairs: a noun when the dance begins
a verb when friends play kho-kho
a verb when someone answers questions
a noun when it names the fly on the wall
a verb when the girl waves to her siblings
activities.explanation: A word can name a thing or show an action, depending on the sentence.

activities.title: Say the W Sound
activities.prompt: Which lip shape should you make while saying the W sound?
options: An O shape
A triangle shape
A square shape
A line shape
activities.explanation: Make an O shape, then repeat the tongue twister four or five times.

activities.title: A Pleasant Word
activities.prompt: The word pleasantest means ______.
activities.hint: It describes something that gives you joy.
activities.explanation: Pleasantest means enjoyable, and many things can give people joy.

chapters.title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
chapters.summary: In this chapter: minam and the special journey; lunch by the river and yaks; snow, a snowman and mount everest; the journey home and a promise.

lessons.title: Minam and the Special Journey

activities.prompt: What will Minam discover on her journey with her grandfather?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey to the Mountains
activities.body: The Himalayas are great mountains. Minam lived in a village at their foot. She loved listening to her grandfather’s mountain stories. He had once been a Sherpa, and they often walked together. Her grandfather said Minam had become strong. He promised her a special journey. Minam packed food and water. Minam saw beautiful flowers and tall trees. She heard new bird sounds. The fresh, cool air made her very happy.
keyPoints: Minam lives in a village at the foot of the Himalayas.
Her grandfather was once a Sherpa.
The journey brings flowers, trees, bird sounds and cool air.
activities.explanation: These details introduce Minam’s home, her grandfather and their mountain journey.

activities.prompt: How did Minam get ready for the special mountain journey?
steps: The promised mountain journey means Minam must prepare her bag.
She packs rotis with achaar and two water bottles for the long walk.
She gets ready early because their journey begins in the morning.
Therefore, Minam is ready to see the Himalayas with her grandfather.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where did Minam live?
options: At the foot of the Himalayas
Far away from the mountains
Inside a busy city centre
On a wide sandy beach
activities.explanation: Minam lived in a small village at the foot of the mighty Himalayas.

activities.prompt: Minam packed rotis with ______ in her bag.
activities.hint: Minam packed it with her rotis.
activities.explanation: She packed rotis with achaar and two water bottles.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the story to its detail.
pairs: A small village at the foot of the Himalayas
He had once been a Sherpa
They often went on long walks together
activities.explanation: Each detail belongs to a person or place in Minam’s story.

activities.prompt: What made Minam feel very happy during the walk?
options: The warm wind made her happy.
She enjoyed the fresh, cool air.
The dry heat made her happy.
The noisy market made her happy.
activities.explanation: The fresh, cool air made Minam feel very happy.

activities.prompt: Put the journey events in the correct order.
items: Her grandfather promised a special journey.
Minam packed rotis, achaar and water.
They began the journey early in the morning.
Minam saw flowers and tall trees during the walk.
activities.explanation: The promise came first, followed by packing, the early start and the sights during the walk.

activities.prompt: Which set includes only things Minam noticed during the walk?
options: Rotis, water bottles and apples
Stories, Sherpa work and strength
Flowers, trees and bird sounds
Journeys, promises and early mornings
activities.explanation: During the walk, Minam saw flowers and tall trees and heard new bird sounds.

activities.prompt: Before a special journey, Minam's grandfather says, “You have become strong.” What does this show?
options: He believes Minam is ready for the mountain journey.
He wants Minam to stop walking with him.
He thinks Minam is afraid of the mountains.
He has forgotten how Minam became strong.

This mistake reads praise as a wish to separate.
why.He thinks Minam is afraid of the mountai: This mistake reads praise as fear.
why.He has forgotten how Minam became strong: This mistake treats praise as forgetting.

activities.explanation: He praises her strength before their promised journey.

activities.prompt: Minam's grandfather promises a special journey to the mountains. What does his promise show?
options: He wants to share the beauty of the Himalayas with Minam.
He wants Minam to stay inside her small village.
He thinks the mountains are not worth seeing.
He plans to see the mountains without Minam.

why.He wants Minam to stay inside her small: This mistake reverses his wish to take Minam along.
why.He thinks the mountains are not worth se: This mistake turns an exciting promise into dislike.
why.He plans to see the mountains without Mi: This mistake ignores that Minam will join him.

activities.explanation: The promise includes seeing the Himalayas up close together.

activities.prompt: The mountains will be seen up close on Minam's special journey. What does “special” suggest?
options: The journey is different from their usual walks together.
The journey is less exciting than their usual walks.
The journey is shorter than their usual walks together.
The journey is another ordinary walk near home.

why.The journey is less exciting than their: This mistake assumes special means less exciting.
why.The journey is shorter than their usual: This mistake assumes special means shorter.
why.The journey is another ordinary walk nea: This mistake treats a promised mountain journey as ordinary.

activities.explanation: A promised mountain journey sounds different from ordinary walks.

activities.prompt: Minam loves apples, but she packs rotis with achaar. What can you understand?
options: Her favourite fruit need not be the food she packs.
Her packed food must be her least favourite food.
She must never eat apples at any time.
Her bag must contain only her favourite foods.

why.Her packed food must be her least favour: This mistake confuses her favourite fruit with her packed food.
This mistake turns a favourite fruit into one she avoids.
why.Her bag must contain only her favourite: This mistake assumes a bag holds only favourite foods.

activities.explanation: Liking apples does not mean she must pack them.

activities.prompt: During the walk, Minam hears bird sounds she has not heard before. How might she feel?
options: Curious, because the new sounds interest her.
Bored, because she has heard the sounds before.
Angry, because the birds interrupt her walk.
Afraid, because the sounds are completely new.

why.Bored, because she has heard the sounds: This mistake forgets that the sounds are new to Minam.
why.Angry, because the birds interrupt her w: This mistake assumes she dislikes hearing birds.
why.Afraid, because the sounds are completel: This mistake treats new sounds as a reason for fear.

activities.explanation: New bird sounds can make a walker feel curious.

lessons.sceneCaption: Lachung village and its river valley are surrounded by the magnificent Himalayas.

lessons.title: Lunch by the River and Yaks

activities.prompt: What might Minam and her grandfather discover on their journey together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lunch by the River
activities.body: Minam and her grandfather reached a small river with clear water. Her grandfather said they would have lunch there. They enjoyed rotis and watched fish swim. Minam put her feet in the cool water and laughed with joy. She ate an apple. After lunch, they continued their journey. They climbed higher and saw yaks. Yaks gave mountain people milk and wool and helped carry heavy loads.
keyPoints: Minam and her grandfather had lunch by a small river.
Minam enjoyed the cool water and watched fish swim.
Yaks gave milk and wool and helped carry heavy loads.
activities.explanation: This story shows a happy river lunch and the useful yaks they met.

activities.prompt: After lunch by a clear river, why do Minam and her grandfather keep climbing, and why are yaks useful?
steps: They keep going because their journey continues after the meal.
They climb because they are moving onward on that journey.
The yaks help because they give milk and wool and carry heavy loads.
So the yaks make mountain life easier, and the journey continues.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where did Minam and her grandfather have lunch?
options: By a small river
At the top of a mountain
Inside a house
Near a busy market
activities.explanation: Her grandfather said they would have lunch at the small river.

activities.prompt: Minam and her grandfather enjoyed their ______ and watched the fish swim.
activities.hint: This food came with their lunch.
activities.explanation: They enjoyed their rotis while sitting beside the river.

activities.prompt: Minam and her grandfather watched fish swim in the river.
activities.explanation: They enjoyed their rotis and watched the fish swim.

activities.prompt: Match each word with the correct action or description.
pairs: put her feet in the cool water
activities.explanation: Each pair shows something that happened in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
activities.explanation: They first reached the river, ate lunch, and then continued climbing.

activities.prompt: Which two things did yaks give people?
options: Milk and wool
Milk and fruit
Wool and bread
Milk and flowers
activities.explanation: Yaks gave people milk and wool. They also helped carry heavy loads.

activities.prompt: A child dips their feet into cool river water. The child laughs with joy. How does the child feel?
options: The child feels very happy and excited.
The child feels afraid of the water.
The child feels bored by the river.
The child feels tired of laughing.

The child may think cool water is scary, but the story says joy.
Boredom does not match the child's joyful laughter.
The child's laughter shows energy, not tiredness.

activities.explanation: Laughing with joy shows that the child feels happy and excited.

activities.prompt: A grandfather and child reach a small river with clear water. The grandfather says, "We will eat here." Why might they choose this place?
options: They must finish their whole journey before eating.
They are waiting to buy lunch at a shop.
They can enjoy lunch beside the clear water.
They need clear water to cook their lunch.

why.They must finish their whole journey bef: Enjoying lunch beside clear water matches what they do at the river.
This choice wrongly assumes lunch comes only at the journey's end.
why.They need clear water to cook their lunc: This choice confuses clear river water with a place for cooking.

activities.explanation: This choice wrongly assumes they need a shop to find lunch.

activities.prompt: One animal gives people milk and wool. It also carries heavy bags for them. Why would mountain people value this animal?
options: It gives toys and games to the children.
It gives needed supplies and helps with work.
It gives fish and helps people swim.
It gives clear water and helps them rest.

This mistake treats milk and wool as toys for children.
This mistake mixes up the mountain animal with river animals.
why.It gives clear water and helps them rest: This mistake mixes up the useful animal with the clear river.

activities.explanation: Milk, wool, and carrying help give useful supplies and work support.

lessons.sceneAlt: Local herders and their grazing yaks appear among lush alpine meadows and arid slopes near Chota Baldar in Spiti.
lessons.sceneCaption: Herding yaks graze beside green alpine meadows in the high-altitude Spiti region.

lessons.title: Snow, a Snowman and Mount Everest

activities.prompt: What did Minam and her grandfather find on their snowy mountain adventure?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A snowy mountain day
activities.body: Minam and her grandfather reached a place where the ground was covered with snow. Minam had never seen so much snow before. They made a small snowman. They laughed and played and made memories that Minam would value forever. At the top of a hill, she saw huge Himalayan peaks, or high mountain tops, shining in the sun. Her grandfather said Mount Everest was the tallest mountain in the world.
keyPoints: Minam and her grandfather made a small snowman.
Minam saw huge Himalayan peaks shining in the sun.
Her grandfather said Mount Everest was the tallest mountain in the world.
activities.explanation: This lesson follows Minam's snowy day and her mountain view.

activities.prompt: Minam and her grandfather are visiting a snowy place. How can they make the day special?
steps: They can make a small snowman, because the ground is covered with snow.
They can laugh and play, because this happy time becomes a lasting memory.
They can climb the hill, because the top lets Minam see the huge Himalayan peaks.
The day will stay special, because Minam will value these shared memories forever.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Minam and her grandfather make together?
options: a small snowman
a small snow tree
a small snow boat
a small snow cake
activities.explanation: They made a small snowman together.

activities.prompt: Minam was surprised because she had never seen so much ______ before.
activities.hint: This white thing covered the ground.
activities.explanation: The ground was covered with snow, and Minam had never seen so much before.

activities.prompt: Match each person or pair to what happened.
pairs: said Mount Everest was the tallest mountain
made memories Minam would value forever
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an action or feeling from the story.

activities.prompt: What could Minam see after they reached the top of the hill?
options: a forest growing beside the hill
the small snowman beside the path
huge Himalayan peaks shining in the sun
a town resting under the hills
activities.explanation: At the hilltop, Minam saw the huge Himalayan peaks shining in the sun.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: reached a place covered with snow
reached the top of a hill
finished sightseeing as the sun began to set
activities.explanation: The snow came first, then the snowman, the hilltop and the sunset.

activities.prompt: Why did Minam enjoy living near the mountains?
options: The mountains were wonderful.
The mountains were crowded.
The mountains were very low.
The mountains stood close together.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that Minam felt happy near such wonderful mountains.

activities.prompt: Minam reaches a place where the ground is covered with snow. She has never seen so much snow before. How does she most likely feel?
options: She feels amazed because the snow was so unexpected.
She feels cross because the snow covered the ground.
She feels afraid because her grandfather stood nearby.
She feels bored because the snowy place was quiet.

why.She feels cross because the snow covered: This mistake treats covered ground as a reason to be cross.
why.She feels afraid because her grandfather: This mistake treats another person's presence as a reason to fear.
why.She feels bored because the snowy place: This mistake treats a snowy place as boring without evidence.

activities.explanation: The huge amount of snow makes amazement the most likely feeling.

activities.prompt: Minam and her grandfather laugh and play while making a small snowman. Why will Minam value these memories forever?
options: They laughed and played together on that snowy day.
They saw the tallest mountain in the world that day.
They reached the top of a snowy hill that day.
They watched the sun begin to set that day.

why.They saw the tallest mountain in the wor: This mistake chooses a mountain sight instead of their happy shared time.
why.They reached the top of a snowy hill tha: This mistake chooses the hill climb instead of their happy shared time.
why.They watched the sun begin to set that d: This mistake chooses the sunset instead of their happy shared time.

activities.explanation: They laughed and played together, and those memories became forever.

activities.prompt: The story says, “Minam had never seen so much snow before.” What does this line tell us about her?
options: The snow gave her a surprising new sight.
The snow made her feel extremely disappointed.
The snow made her feel extremely frightened.
The snow made her feel extremely bored today.

why.The snow made her feel extremely disappo: The line shows surprise, but it does not show disappointment.
why.The snow made her feel extremely frighte: The line shows surprise, but it does not show fear.
why.The snow made her feel extremely bored t: The line shows surprise, but it does not show boredom.

activities.explanation: Never seeing so much snow before shows that the sight surprised her.

activities.prompt: The sun begins to set, and Minam's sightseeing with her grandfather ends. What should they do now?
options: They should stop sightseeing because the sun is beginning to set.
They should make a snowman because the snowy ground is still there.
They should climb Everest because the shining peaks look close.
They should wait there because their visit is not over.

why.They should make a snowman because the s: This assumes the snow calls for more play after the visit ends.
why.They should climb Everest because the sh: This mistakes seeing tall peaks for a chance to climb them.
why.They should wait there because their vis: This assumes the visit continues although the story says it ended.

activities.explanation: The story says their sightseeing ended as the sun began to set.

lessons.title: The Journey Home and a Promise

activities.prompt: What did Minam and her grandfather discover on their journey home?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Happy Journey Home
activities.body: Minam and her grandfather began their journey home. On the way down, they heard a Santoor under a tree. They saw mountain goats jumping from rock to rock. The goats could climb to hard places. At dusk, Minam felt tired but happy. She thanked her grandfather. He asked her to respect and protect the mountains. Minam promised to care for them and share their magic.
keyPoints: Minam and her grandfather journeyed home.
They saw goats and heard a Santoor.
Minam promised to care for the mountains.
activities.explanation: The journey brought Minam happiness and led to a caring promise.

activities.prompt: Why can Minam feel tired and very happy after her journey?
steps: They went home from the magical mountains, because Minam had visited them.
They arrived as it got dark, because their journey continued until then.
The journey made Minam tired, because travelling through mountains took effort.
She thanked her grandfather, because the happy visit mattered more than tiredness.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Minam Promised
activities.body: Minam thanked her grandfather for taking her to the magical mountains. Her grandfather said that mountains teach people about strength, beauty and the wonders of nature. He asked Minam to respect and protect the mountains. Minam promised to care for the mountains and share their magic.
keyPoints: The mountains teach strength, beauty and nature.
Minam's grandfather asked her to protect them.
Minam promised to care for and share their magic.
activities.explanation: Minam's promise showed that she valued her journey.

activities.prompt: Who was playing the Santoor?
options: An old man
Her grandfather
A family of goats
Minam
activities.explanation: The old man sitting under a tree was playing the Santoor.

activities.prompt: They reached their village before it started getting dark.
activities.explanation: They reached their village as it was getting dark.

activities.prompt: They reached their village as it was getting ______.
activities.hint: Choose the word from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Minam and her grandfather arrived while it was getting dark.

activities.prompt: Match each person or group with what they did.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a person or group with the action described.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Her grandfather spoke about the mountains.
Her grandfather asked Minam to respect them.
Minam promised to care for them.
activities.explanation: The order follows the events from Minam's happiness to her promise.

activities.prompt: Which promise did Minam make?
options: Care for the mountains and share their magic.
Care for the goats and share their magic.
Protect the village and share the music.
Respect the journey and leave the mountains.
activities.explanation: She promised to care for the mountains and share their magic.

activities.prompt: What did her grandfather ask Minam to do?
options: Respect and protect the mountains.
Care for the goats and share their magic.
Protect the village and play the Santoor.
Learn about beauty and leave nature alone.
activities.explanation: He asked her to respect and protect the mountains.

activities.prompt: Minam hears musical notes under a tree while going down. Why?
options: An old man is playing a Santoor nearby.
The mountain goats are making music together.
Her grandfather is playing a Santoor for her.
The village is playing music behind them.

why.The mountain goats are making music toge: The goats were jumping; the story does not say they made music.
why.Her grandfather is playing a Santoor for: It was the old man, not Minam's grandfather, who was playing.
why.The village is playing music behind them: The music came from the man under the tree, not the village.

activities.explanation: The notes come from the old man playing the Santoor.

activities.prompt: Minam feels tired but happy after the journey. What does this show?
options: The trip affected both her body and her feelings.
The trip changed only her body, not her feelings.
Feeling tired means the trip was not worth it.
Feeling happy means she did not really feel tired.

why.The trip changed only her body, not her: Her happy feeling also changed, so this misses part of the meaning.
why.Feeling tired means the trip was not wor: She was happy, so tiredness did not make the trip worthless.
why.Feeling happy means she did not really f: She felt both feelings at the same time, not just one.

activities.explanation: Her tiredness and happiness show the journey changed her in two ways.

lessons.title: Words, Meanings and Mountain Helpers

activities.prompt: What helpers might Minam meet during her mountain walk?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Mountain Words and Their Meanings
activities.body: Minam learned from her grandfather during a mountain walk. She saw yaks and mountain goats helping people. A Sherpa is a guide and helper for people climbing mountains. Yaks are large, strong animals found in mountains. A journey means travel from one place to another. Magical means wonderful, amazing or enchanting. Memories are things we remember and cherish. Minam promised to protect the mountains.
keyPoints: Minam learned from her grandfather during their walk.
Yaks and mountain goats helped people in the mountains.
A Sherpa guides and helps people climbing mountains.
activities.explanation: Wonderful! These words and meanings help you understand Minam's mountain journey.

activities.prompt: Minam promises to protect the mountains. What does her promise show?
steps: Minam has promised to protect the mountains.
Because protecting means trying to keep them safe, she will care for them.
Therefore, her promise shows that she cares about the mountains.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Remembering the Mountains
activities.body: The Himalayas are the tallest mountain range in the world. Minam promised to protect the mountains. She learned from her grandfather during their walk. She saw yaks and mountain goats helping people. A Sherpa is a guide and helper for people climbing mountains. The word magical can mean wonderful, amazing or enchanting. Memories are things we remember and cherish.
keyPoints: The Himalayas are the tallest mountain range in the world.
Minam promised to protect the mountains.
Magical means wonderful, amazing or enchanting.
activities.explanation: Nice work! You can now connect the meanings with Minam's mountain story.

activities.prompt: What did Minam enjoy during her walk?
options: Learning from her grandfather
Climbing with a Sherpa
Finding magical flowers
Watching a tall city
activities.explanation: Minam enjoyed learning from her grandfather during their walk.

activities.prompt: A Sherpa is a guide and helper for people climbing mountains.
activities.explanation: Yes! Sherpas guide and help people who climb mountains.

activities.prompt: A ______ means travel from one place to another.
activities.hint: This word names the travel.
activities.explanation: Great! A journey is travel from one place to another.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: Travel from one place to another
A guide and helper for people climbing mountains
activities.explanation: You matched all four meanings correctly. Well done!

activities.prompt: Who did Minam see helping people in the mountains?
options: Sherpas and yaks
Yaks and mountain goats
Grandfather and Sherpas
Mountains and goats
activities.explanation: Minam saw yaks and mountain goats helping people in the mountains.

activities.prompt: Which pair of statements uses both word meanings correctly?
options: A journey is strong, and magical means tall.
Magical means amazing, and memories are cherished.
A Sherpa is a journey, and yaks are memories.
Memories are strong, and magical means a helper.
activities.explanation: Magical means wonderful, amazing or enchanting. Memories are things we remember and cherish.

activities.prompt: Minam smiles when she recalls learning from her grandfather. What does this show?
options: She cherishes that happy memory.
She has forgotten that learning time.
She dislikes walking with her grandfather.
She wants to forget her grandfather.

why.She dislikes walking with her grandfathe: This mistakes enjoying learning with disliking the walk.
This wrongly reads the happy memory as dislike.

activities.explanation: Her smile shows that she treasures the memory of learning.

activities.prompt: Minam sees yaks and mountain goats helping people in the mountains. What can she work out?
options: Both animals can help mountain people.
Only yaks can help mountain people.
Only mountain goats can help people.
Neither animal can help people.

This leaves out the mountain goats.
This turns the help she saw into no help.

activities.explanation: says both yaks and mountain goats helped people.

lessons.title: Body Parts, Conjunctions and Class Activities

activities.prompt: Ready to discover surprising names and fun ways to join ideas?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Body-part names and conjunctions
activities.body: Body-part names describe objects. A table has legs, and a clock has hands. A mountain has a foot, while a bottle has a neck. Conjunctions join words, phrases or sentences. AND adds information. OR gives a choice. BUT shows contrast. BECAUSE gives a reason. The speaking activity has groups A and B. A child from group B completes the sentence. The writing activity uses a dictionary. Children make colourful charts.
keyPoints: Body-part names can describe objects.
Conjunctions join words, phrases or sentences.
Class activities include speaking, writing and chart-making.
activities.explanation: This card introduces body-part names, conjunctions and class activities.

activities.prompt: A table has legs AND a clock has hands. What is special?
steps: Because clocks have hands, body-part names can describe objects.
AND joins the examples because the clock adds more information.
Both examples share an idea because they use body-part names.
Therefore, body-part names can describe other objects.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which object has the body-part name hands?
options: a clock
a table
a bottle
a mountain
activities.explanation: The hands of a clock are named after body parts.

activities.prompt: The foot of a mountain is a body-part name for an object.
activities.explanation: A mountain can be described as having a foot.

activities.prompt: Match each body-part name with its object.
activities.explanation: These objects are described using names of body parts.

activities.prompt: The conjunction that adds information to a sentence is ______.
activities.hint: It joins extra details.
activities.explanation: AND is the conjunction that adds information.

activities.prompt: Which conjunction gives a choice?
options: AND
OR
BUT
BECAUSE
activities.explanation: OR gives the reader a choice.

activities.prompt: BECAUSE shows a contrast or difference.
activities.explanation: BECAUSE gives a reason. BUT shows a contrast or difference.

activities.prompt: A table has legs. A bottle has a neck. A mountain has a foot. What do these names show?
options: Body-part names can describe parts of other objects.
These objects have real human body parts.
Only people can use names from the body.
The names show what each object can do.

why.These objects have real human body parts: This child thinks named objects have real body parts.
This child believes only people can use body-part names.
This child thinks the names explain actions instead of parts.

activities.explanation: The examples show body-part names used for other objects.

activities.prompt: You need glue AND paper for the craft. Both items are needed. What does AND do here?
options: It joins two needed items together.
It gives a reason for using one item.
It shows that the two items differ.
It offers a choice between two items.

This child mistakes AND for BECAUSE, which gives a reason.
This child mistakes AND for BUT, which shows a contrast.
This child mistakes AND for OR, which offers a choice.

activities.explanation: AND joins both items and adds the second needed item.

activities.prompt: A child may paint OR draw after class. Only one activity will happen. What does OR show?
options: It gives a choice between two activities.
It joins two activities that both happen.
It shows a contrast between two activities.
It gives the reason for choosing an activity.

why.It joins two activities that both happen: This child mistakes OR for AND, which joins both activities.
why.It shows a contrast between two activiti: This child mistakes OR for BUT, which shows a contrast.
why.It gives the reason for choosing an acti: This child mistakes OR for BECAUSE, which gives a reason.

activities.explanation: OR tells us there is a choice between the two activities.

activities.prompt: A child felt cold BUT the room felt warm. Why use BUT?
options: It shows a contrast between two facts.
It gives a choice between two facts.
It joins two reasons for one fact.
It adds a similar fact to the first.

This child mistakes BUT for OR, which offers a choice.
This child mistakes BUT for BECAUSE, which gives a reason.
This child mistakes BUT for AND, which adds information.

activities.explanation: BUT marks the contrast between feeling cold and feeling warm.

activities.prompt: Children design a colourful chart with drawings, pictures and captions. Why add captions to pictures?
options: Captions help explain what the pictures show.
Captions take the place of the pictures.
Pictures show nothing unless captions are added.
Captions make the whole chart less colourful.

This child thinks captions replace the pictures.
why.Pictures show nothing unless captions ar: This child thinks pictures cannot show meaning alone.
why.Captions make the whole chart less colou: This child thinks captions remove colour instead of adding information.

activities.explanation: Captions explain what the pictures show on the class chart.

lessons.sceneAlt: Lachung village sits beside the Lachung River, surrounded by Himalayan mountains in North Sikkim, India.
lessons.sceneCaption: Lachung village and its river valley are surrounded by the magnificent Himalayas.
